title: MDMx: Multi-dimensional Mortality
text:
How the book is organised
This book is the computational companion to
It reproduces every figure, table and number in the paper from the Human Mortality Database, and explains each step of the analysis in more detail than a journal article can.
crumbs: 1  Preface

title: MDMx: Multi-dimensional Mortality
text:
Part I — Data pipeline (chapters d1–d6, paper §2) takes the HMD download to the four-way mortality tensor: verifying the release, reading the files, curation, the event dictionary of wars and pandemics, adaptive temporal pooling, and assembling the tensor. Every change made to the published data is recorded in results/ledger/data-changes.csv.
Part II — Analysis has one chapter per section of the paper’s methods and results: 04 (the Tucker decomposition, paper §3), 06 (a typology of age patterns, §4), 07 (reconstruction at arbitrary mortality levels, §5), 08 (exceptional mortality, §6), 09 (life table fitting, §7), 10 (prediction from summary indicators, §8), 11 (the two forecasters, §9, and what the flow field says about mortality change, §11.4) and 12 (the forecast evaluation, §10). The chapters’ file names keep their own numbers (04, 06, …), which do not follow the paper’s sections. Each chapter also shows results that the paper leaves out.
Appendices describe the computing environment and show the provenance of every result.

title: MDMx: Multi-dimensional Mortality
text:
How to read a chapter
Each chapter starts with a box naming the paper sections it reproduces and the figures and tables it writes. Code is shown next to the prose that explains it; the routine machinery lives in the mdmx Python package (src/mdmx/), whose functions are documented line by line.
crumbs: 1  Preface

title: MDMx: Multi-dimensional Mortality
text:
How results reach the paper
Chapters write figures to results/figures/, tables to results/tables/ and every number the paper quotes to results/numbers/ (as LaTeX macros). The paper reads only those files, so the paper and the book can never disagree. results/manifest.json records, for every one of these files, the chapter that produced it and the checksums of its inputs.
crumbs: 1  Preface

title: 2  Acquiring the data
text:
2.1 The Human Mortality Database release
All analyses use the period life tables of the Human Mortality Database (HMD). The HMD is revised continually — new years are added and past estimates are sometimes corrected — so “the HMD” is not a fixed data set. To make the analysis reproducible we therefore pin one specific release: the bulk download (“all statistics” zip archive) dated 29 October 2026.
The HMD licenses its estimates (life tables, death rates, exposures) under CC BY 4.0, but asks users to obtain the data from its website rather than from third parties. This repository therefore does not contain the data. You download the zip yourself (a free registration is required) and save it, unopened and unrenamed apart from the name below, as
The file raw/MANIFEST.json — which is part of the repository — records the release, where it came from, and SHA-256 checksums of the zip and of the four files inside it that the analysis reads. A checksum is a 64-character fingerprint of a file’s exact bytes: if a single byte differs, the fingerprint differs. Verifying it proves that you are running the analysis on exactly the data the paper used.
Chapter setup: imports and provenance tracking
# Every chapter starts the same way: import the project package, declare
# which chapter is running (so every artefact, figure, table and number it
# produces is attributed to it), and load the analysis parameters.
import json

import pandas as pd

from mdmx import artifacts, data, latex, paths, provenance
from mdmx.config import params

provenance.start_chapter("d1-acquire")
P = params()
print(f"Project root : {paths.root().name}/")          # the folder's name: the full path is the reader's own
print(f"HMD release  : {P.data.hmd_release}")

title: 2  Acquiring the data
text:
2.3 Verifying the release
mdmx.data.verify_release() locates the release and recomputes every checksum. It accepts either the zip exactly as downloaded or — for convenience — a folder raw/hmd/20261029/ holding just the four files with their paths as inside the zip. In both cases each of the four files must match the manifest, and if the zip is present its own checksum must match too. Any mismatch stops the pipeline with an error.


Verify the checksums and register the release as the root artefact
report = data.verify_release(P.data.hmd_release)
print(f"Release found at: {report['source']}")
if report["zip_sha256"]:
    print(f"Zip checksum     : OK ({report['zip_sha256'][:16]}…)")
for member, res in report["members"].items():
    print(f"  {member:<45s} {'OK' if res['ok'] else 'MISMATCH'}")

# Record the verified release as the root of the provenance graph.  Its
# content is the release label and the checksums of the four member files —
# deliberately NOT the file location or the zip's own checksum, so that the
# cache is identical whether the data were read from the zip or from an
# extracted folder, on any computer.  Every downstream artefact is thereby
# tied to exactly these bytes.
artifacts.save(
    "hmd_release",
    {"release": P.data.hmd_release,
     "members": {m: r["sha256"] for m, r in report["members"].items()}},
    params={"release": P.data.hmd_release},
    desc="Verified HMD bulk release: checksums of the four files used",
)

title: 2  Acquiring the data
text:
2.4 The populations
The HMD covers 50 populations in this release. Several are not independent: the United Kingdom total (GBR_NP) contains England & Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland; Germany (DEUTNP) contains East and West Germany for the years they overlap; and New Zealand (NZL_NP) contains its Māori and non-Māori populations. The HMD also publishes civilian-only series for France and England & Wales, which omit military deaths in war years. The register below records these relationships; it lives in config/populations.csv, so it can be read and edited without touching code.


The population register
pops = data.load_populations()
artifacts.save("populations", pops, inputs=["hmd_release"],
               desc="Population register: HMD codes, names, aggregates, inclusion")
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 60)
used = pops[pops["included"] == "yes"]
latex.report("dataNCountries", int((used["aggregate_of"] == "").sum()),
             desc="Countries and territories: the populations used that are not part of another")

title: 3  Ingesting the life tables
text:
3.1 What the files look like
Each HMD bulk file holds every population in one whitespace-separated table. The first line names the series and gives its “Last modified” stamp, the second is blank, and the third is the column header. Missing values are written as a single dot, and the oldest age group is written 110+ (the open interval: everyone aged 110 or more).

import pandas as pd

title: 3  Ingesting the life tables
text:
3.2 Reading the files
mdmx.data.ingest_life_tables() reads the female and male files with pandas (splitting on runs of whitespace and treating . as missing), converts 110+ to the integer 110, and stacks the two sexes into one long table with one row per population × sex × year × age. A long table is the natural format for a data pipeline: every filter, join and summary is a one-liner, and each row is one fact. ingest_deaths_exposures() does the same for the death counts and exposures, which are published with female, male and total columns side by side and are reshaped to the same long form.
Both tables are saved as artefacts — Parquet files in work/companion/artifacts/ with a provenance record that names their input (the verified release) — so later chapters load them in a fraction of a second instead of re-parsing 200 MB of text.


Parse the four HMD files into long tables (cached)
def _ingest():
    lt, lt_report = data.ingest_life_tables(source)
    de, de_report = data.ingest_deaths_exposures(source)
    return {"lt": lt, "de": de, "report": {**lt_report, **de_report}}

raw = artifacts.stage("hmd_raw", _ingest, inputs=["hmd_release"], code=[_ingest, data],
                      desc="HMD 1x1 period life tables, deaths and exposures, long format")
lt_raw, de_raw = raw["lt"], raw["de"]

for member, rep in raw["report"].items():
    print(f"{member:<45s} {rep['rows']:>9,} rows   [{rep['title'][:60]}]")
print()
print(lt_raw.head())

title: 3  Ingesting the life tables
text:
3.3 A first look
The figures in this section show the data as published by the HMD, before any curation. They use the 48 populations retained for the analysis (the two civilian-only duplicate series are left out, see chapter d1).


Restrict the descriptive figures to the retained populations
pops = artifacts.load("populations")
keep = set(pops.loc[pops["included"] == "yes", "code"])
names = dict(zip(pops["code"], pops["name"]))
lt48 = lt_raw[lt_raw["pop"].isin(keep)]
e0 = (lt48[lt48["age"] == 0][["pop", "sex", "year", "ex"]]
      .rename(columns={"ex": "e0"}).reset_index(drop=True))


  [artefact] loaded  populations



3.3.1 Coverage
The HMD is ragged: Sweden’s series begins in 1751, but many populations enter only in the second half of the twentieth century. This raggedness is the central data problem the decomposition has to deal with (chapter 04).


Code

3.3.3 The age pattern of mortality
The probability of dying, \(q_x\), has the familiar U (or J) shape: high in infancy, lowest around age 10, then rising roughly exponentially with age. The logit transform, \(\operatorname{logit}(q) = \log\{q/(1-q)\}\), maps probabilities onto the whole real line; on that scale the old-age rise is close to linear, variability is more even across ages, and differences between schedules are additive — which is why the whole analysis works with \(\operatorname{logit}(q_x)\) (paper §2.2, “The quantity modelled”).


Schedules used to illustrate the age pattern
# Russia's HMD series ends in 2014, so its most recent table is used.
SELECTION = [("SWE", 1800), ("SWE", 1900), ("SWE", 2020), ("JPN", 2020),
             ("USA", 2020), ("RUS", 2014)]
def schedule(pop, year, sex):
    s = lt48[(lt48["pop"] == pop) & (lt48["year"] == year) & (lt48["sex"] == sex)
             & (lt48["age"] <= P.data.age_max)].sort_values("age")
    return s["age"].to_numpy(), s["qx"].to_numpy()




Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharey=True)
for ax, sex in zip(axes, data.SEXES):
    for pop, year in SELECTION:
        age, q = schedule(pop, year, sex)
        ax.semilogy(age, np.clip(q, 1e-6, None), lw=1.1, label=f"{names[pop]} {year}")
    ax.set_title(sex.title()); ax.set_xlabel("Age"); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$q_x$ (log scale)")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s1-qx-profiles")
plt.show()

Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharey=True)
for ax, sex in zip(axes, data.SEXES):
    for pop, year in SELECTION:
        age, q = schedule(pop, year, sex)
        ax.plot(age, lifetable.logit(q, P.data.q_min), lw=1.1, label=f"{names[pop]} {year}")
    ax.set_title(sex.title()); ax.set_xlabel("Age")

title: 4  Curation
text:
4.1 The rules
A life table enters the analysis only if it passes all of the following checks. Each rule removes a whole country-year — both sexes — because the tensor needs a female and a male table for every country-year it holds. The rules are applied in order, and each removed country-year is recorded with the first rule that removed it.
The thresholds are parameters in config/params.toml ([data] section).
Apply the curation rules (cached)
def _curate():
    curated, exclusions = data.curate(
        lt_raw,
        populations_excluded=P.data.populations_excluded,
        flat_tail_ages=tuple(P.data.flat_tail_ages),
        age_max=P.data.age_max,
    )
    # Keep only the columns used downstream.  e_x is kept for the published
    # HMD e0 (age 0) used in descriptive summaries.
    curated = curated[["pop", "sex", "year", "age", "mx", "qx", "ax", "ex"]]
    return {"lt": curated, "exclusions": exclusions}

cur = artifacts.stage("lt_curated", _curate, inputs=["hmd_raw"],
                      params=P.section("data"), code=[_curate, data.curate],
                      desc="Curated life tables (ages 0-109) and the exclusion record")
lt_cur, exclusions = cur["lt"], cur["exclusions"]

title: 4  Curation
text:
Excluded populations. The civilian-only series FRACNP and GBRCENW (chapter d1).
Missing values. A table with any missing \(m_x\), \(q_x\) or \(a_x\).
Flat old-age tail. A table whose \(q_x\) is identical at ages 105 and 109. When the underlying data are too thin to estimate mortality at the oldest ages, the HMD’s old-age model can return the same value across the whole tail; such a tail carries no age information. The rule looks only at two high ages because ties at younger ages are common and harmless: the HMD publishes \(q_x\) to five decimals, so two adjacent ages with \(q_x \approx 0.0001\) often have the same value.
Sex pairing. Both sexes must be present.
Age range. Ages above 109 (the open interval 110+, where \(q_x = 1\) by definition) are dropped from every table.

title: 5  Exceptional years
text:
5.1 Why exceptional years are set aside
Wars and pandemics produce short, sharp mortality shocks with their own age–sex signatures. The Tucker decomposition is meant to describe the baseline mortality surface — the slow secular transition — so the years in which a population was hit by such an event are removed from the data the decomposition sees, and kept aside for the disruption model of paper §6 (chapter 08). A country-year is exceptional if, and only if, it appears in the event dictionary.

title: 5  Exceptional years
text:
5.2 The event dictionary
The dictionary is a plain table, config/events.csv, with one row per event and group of populations: the event, its type, first and last calendar year, the HMD population codes affected, and a source. ALL means every population with data during the event (used for the influenza pandemics of 1957–58 and 1968–69 and for COVID-19). Keeping the dictionary as data, rather than as code, means the same file drives both the masks used in the analysis and the dictionary’s tables at the end of this chapter, so the two can never disagree.

5.2.1 How the dictionary is compiled
Four choices shape the dictionary; where an entry needs a reason, the note column above gives it.

The United Kingdom (GBR_NP) is listed with its parts. It is a population in its own right (chapter d1), so every war entry that lists England & Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland lists it too. Otherwise its war years, 1939–45 for example, would count as normal years while those of its parts are masked.
Entry dates. Each belligerent is flagged from the year it entered the war, so that its years before entry stay in the baseline: Italy and Bulgaria in World War I from 1915, the United States and Greece from 1917; Italy and Greece in World War II from 1940 (the same entry lists Hungary and Bulgaria, which entered in 1941; their HMD series begin after the war), the United States from 1942; France and Britain in the Crimean War from 1854 and Sardinia (Italy) from 1855. Two entries start earlier for some of the populations they list: World War II from 1939 for every population of its main entry, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Denmark and Norway (invaded in 1940) included, and the Napoleonic Wars from 1803 for Sweden, at war from 1805. The populations that sent forces to the Second Boer War and the Korean War are flagged for those wars too, though little excess mortality is expected at home.
Sweden in the Seven Years’ War is flagged for 1757–1762, the years of its own (Pomeranian) war within the war of 1756–1763.
A fourth type, “other”, records four mortality crises that are neither wars nor the three pandemic types: the Swedish famine and dysentery epidemic of 1772–73 (the lowest life expectancy in the HMD), the Icelandic measles epidemics of 1846 and 1882, and the 1871 smallpox epidemic in the Netherlands and Belgium. These years are excluded from the baseline like other exceptional years, but they are too few and too heterogeneous to estimate a disruption profile, so the disruption model does not use them.

text:
5.3 Labelling every country-year
Each curated country-year receives a label \(d_{c,t}\): 0 = none, 1 = war, 2 = respiratory pandemic, 3 = enteric pandemic, 4 = other. When a country-year is in more than one entry the label is chosen by priority war > respiratory > enteric > other (paper §2.3): in 1918, for example, a belligerent is labelled war. All matching entries are kept in the all_events column for transparency.


Expand the dictionary and label every curated country-year (cached)
def _label():
    coverage = (lt_cur.groupby("pop")["year"].agg(["min", "max"])

    country_years = lt_cur[["pop", "year"]].drop_duplicates().sort_values(["pop", "year"])
    return data.label_country_years(country_years, expanded)

text:
5.4 A screen for crises the dictionary might miss
The dictionary is compiled from historical sources, so it can miss events. As a check, the code below lists every unlabelled country-year whose life expectancy (average of the sexes) falls more than 5.0 years below the median of the same population’s surrounding ±5 years. This is a diagnostic only — nothing is changed automatically. The four “other” crises were identified this way and confirmed against historical sources. The country-years still listed below remain in the baseline: most are in the very small Icelandic population, where single-year life expectancy is volatile, and the rest are isolated dips without an established cause in the sources used for the dictionary. They are listed so that any reader can judge them.


List unlabelled years with unusually low e0

               params=P.section("data"), desc="Unlabelled country-years with unusually low e0")

5  Exceptional years

title: 6  Adaptive temporal pooling
text:
6.1 The problem: zeros in small populations
Between late childhood and middle age, the annual probability of dying is of the order of \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-3}\). In a population the size of Iceland or Luxembourg that means a handful of deaths — or none — at each single age in a given year. When the HMD records no deaths, \(m_x\) and \(q_x\) are exactly zero, and their logit is \(-\infty\) (in practice, the floor \(\operatorname{logit}(10^{-8}) \approx -18.4\), far below any real value near \(-7\)). Left in the tensor, such cells are enormous outliers that the decomposition would spend rank on.
crumbs: Part I — Data pipeline
6  Adaptive temporal pooling

title: 6  Adaptive temporal pooling
text:
6.2 The remedy: pool adjacent years
Following Clark (2001), we pool adjacent years: deaths and exposures are summed over a block of years and the pooled rate \(m_x = \sum_t D_{x,t} / \sum_t E_{x,t}\) replaces the single-year rates. A block is just wide enough to contain at least one death at every affected age, so large populations are not pooled at all and small ones only as much as they need. The algorithm, implemented in mdmx.data.adaptive_pooling(), is:

Valley ages. Ages whose median \(q_x\) across all populations, sexes and years is below \(q_{\text{thresh}} =\) 0.005.
Flag. A population–sex is pooled only if one of its non-exceptional years has \(m_x = 0\) at a valley age. Its pooling ages are the valley ages plus any other age below 80 at which it has a zero rate (in the very smallest populations zeros also occur a few years above the valley). Above that age the HMD’s rates are smoothed by a model and are never zero.
Blocks. The flagged population–sex’s non-exceptional years are taken in calendar order and split into runs wherever more than 3 calendar years are missing (so 2019 and 2023 belong to the same run across the COVID years 2020–22, but a long gap breaks the run). Within a run, years are added to a block until every pooling age has at least one death in the block; the block is then closed and the next begins. Years left over at the end of a run join the previous block.
Pool and rebuild. In a block of two or more years, the pooled rate \(\sum_t D_{x,t}/\sum_t E_{x,t}\) is computed at each pooling age, and in every year of the block \(q_x\) at those ages is recomputed from the pooled rate and that year’s own \(a_x\): \(q_x = m_x / \{1 + (1-a_x)\,m_x\}\).
Everything else is untouched. Outside the pooling ages, every year keeps the HMD’s published \(q_x\); single-year blocks (years that already have deaths at every pooling age) and unflagged populations are not changed at all; and exceptional years are never pooled.



Find the valley ages and pool (cached)
def _pool():
    valley = data.valley_ages(lt_cur, P.data.valley_q_threshold)
    pooled, blocks = data.adaptive_pooling(
        lt_cur, de, labels, valley,
        max_gap=P.data.pool_max_gap, raw_rate_age_limit=P.data.pool_raw_rate_age_limit)
    return {"lt": pooled, "blocks": blocks, "valley_ages": valley}

res = artifacts.stage("lt_pooled", _pool, inputs=["lt_curated", "hmd_raw", "event_labels"],
                      params=P.section("data"),

The widest blocks belong to the smallest populations — Iceland, the Māori population of New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Estonia and Luxembourg — where a block of a decade or more is needed before every single age between 1 and the late forties has recorded a death. Thin grey lines: the published single-year schedules of the years in one block; blue line: the pooled result for one year of the block. Orange shading marks the pooling ages. How much noise does pooling remove? A good measure is the year-to-year change in \(\operatorname{logit}(q_x)\) at each age: real mortality changes slowly, so large jumps between consecutive years are mostly noise. The figure compares the median absolute year-to-year change, before and after pooling, over the same country-years (all non-exceptional years of the pooled populations, zero-free cells only so that the floor does not dominate the “before” curve).


Code
pooled_ps = set(map(tuple, blocks[["pop", "sex"]].drop_duplicates().to_numpy()))
nonexc = labels.loc[labels["label"] == 0, ["pop", "year"]]
def yearly_change(lt):
    df = lt.merge(nonexc, on=["pop", "year"])
    df = df[[ (p, s) in pooled_ps for p, s in zip(df["pop"], df["sex"])]].copy()
    df["z"] = lifetable.logit(df["qx"], P.data.q_min)
    df = df.sort_values(["pop", "sex", "age", "year"])
    g = df.groupby(["pop", "sex", "age"], observed=True)
    df["dz"] = g["z"].diff().abs()
    df["consecutive"] = g["year"].diff() == 1
    return df.set_index(["pop", "sex", "age", "year"])
before, after = yearly_change(lt_cur), yearly_change(lt_pool)
ok = before["consecutive"] & (before["qx"] > 0) & (before.groupby(level=[0, 1, 2]).shift(1)["qx"] > 0)
med_before = before.loc[ok, "dz"].groupby(level="age").median()
med_after = after.loc[ok[ok].index, "dz"].groupby(level="age").median()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(med_before.index, med_before.to_numpy(), color=plotting.COLORS["grey"], lw=1.6, label="Before pooling")
ax.plot(med_after.index, med_after.to_numpy(), color=plotting.COLORS["respiratory"], lw=1.6, label="After pooling")
ax.axvspan(valley.min() - 0.5, valley.max() + 0.5, color="#fdae61", alpha=0.2, label="Valley ages")
ax.set_xlabel("Age"); ax.set_ylabel(r"median |Δ logit$(q_x)$| between consecutive years")
ax.legend()
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s2-smoothing-by-age")
plt.show()

reduction = 1 - med_after[valley_mask].mean() / med_before[valley_mask].mean()
latex.report("dataPoolNoiseReduction", 100 * reduction, digits=0,
             desc="Percent reduction in median year-to-year |Δlogit q| at valley ages, pooled populations")

title: 7  The mortality tensor
text:
7.1 From long tables to a four-way array
The tensor \(\mathcal{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{S \times A \times C \times T}\) holds \(\operatorname{logit}(q_x)\) for every sex \(s\) (female, male), single-year age \(a\) (0–109), population \(c\) and calendar year \(t\). The year axis runs over every calendar year in which at least one population has data. Before the logit, \(q_x\) is clipped to \([q_{\min}, 1-q_{\min}]\) with \(q_{\min} = 10^{-8}\) so that every value is finite. After pooling, the floor is needed only in exceptional years of very small populations (which are not part of the baseline); no observed baseline cell is at the floor.
Not every population has data in every year. Three \(C \times T\) masks record what each cell holds:
Cells that are not observed are left empty (NaN) here. How the decomposition treats them — it fills them iteratively with its own reconstruction — is the subject of chapter 04.
Build the tensor and masks (cached)
def _tensor():
    return data.build_tensor(pooled["lt"], labels, q_min=P.data.q_min,
                             min_observed_years=P.data.min_observed_years, populations=pops)

tensor = artifacts.stage("tensor", _tensor, inputs=["lt_pooled", "event_labels", "populations"],
                         params=P.section("data"), code=[_tensor, data.build_tensor, lifetable.logit],
                         desc="logit(qx) tensor (S,A,C,T) with present/observed/exceptional masks")
M, observed, exceptional, present = (tensor[k] for k in ("M", "observed", "exceptional", "present"))
S, A, C, T = M.shape
years = tensor["years"]
print(f"Tensor shape (S, A, C, T) = {M.shape}  →  {M.size:,} cells")
print(f"Country-years: present {present.sum():,}, observed {observed.sum():,}, "
      f"exceptional {exceptional.sum():,}, empty {(~present).sum():,}")
print(f"Cells floored at q_min: {tensor['n_floored']:,} "
      f"(observed: {int((np.isclose(M, lifetable.logit(0.0, P.data.q_min)) & observed).sum())})")
print(f"Populations dropped by the minimum-years rule: {tensor['dropped_pops'] or 'none'}")

for key, value, desc in [
    ("dataS", S, "Sexes"), ("dataA", A, "Ages"), ("dataC", C, "Populations in the tensor"),
    ("dataT", T, "Years in the tensor"), ("dataNCells", M.size, "Cells in the tensor"),
    ("dataNPresent", int(present.sum()), "Country-years with data"),
    ("dataNObserved", int(observed.sum()), "Observed (non-exceptional) country-years"),
    ("dataNExceptionalTensor", int(exceptional.sum()), "Exceptional country-years in the tensor"),
    ("dataNFloored", tensor["n_floored"], "Cells floored at q_min (all in exceptional years)"),
]:

7.5 Where are the empty cells?
Of the \(C \times T\) country-year cells, most are empty simply because a population’s series had not started. The table accounts for every unobserved cell.


Table: classification of the unobserved country-year cells
excl = cur["exclusions"]
excl = excl[excl["pop"].isin(tensor["pops"])]
excluded_keys = set(zip(excl["pop"], excl["year"]))
cats = {"Outside the population's HMD series": 0,
        "Exceptional (masked for the disruption model)": 0,
        "Removed in curation": 0,
        "Gap inside the HMD series (not published)": 0}
for i, pop in enumerate(tensor["pops"]):
    hmd = lt_raw.loc[lt_raw["pop"] == pop, "year"]
    first, last = hmd.min(), hmd.max()
    for j, y in enumerate(years):
        if observed[i, j]:
            continue
        if exceptional[i, j]:

        elif (pop, y) in excluded_keys:

7.6 The change ledger
Every change made to the published HMD data on the way to the tensor is listed in one file, results/ledger/data-changes.csv, with one row per change: the step, the rule, the population, sex and years affected, and the details. 7  The mortality tensor

title: 8  The Tucker decomposition
text:
8.1 What the decomposition is for
The decomposition has two jobs (paper §3). The first is to find a shared basis in which every mortality schedule can be written: a sex factor matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) (\(2 \times r_1\)) and an age factor matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) (\(110 \times r_2\)) that are the same for every population and every year. Writing each schedule in that common basis gives every output of the system — model life tables, fitted schedules, predictions, forecasts — what we call shared-basis coherence: both sexes’ schedules are combinations of the same age patterns. The basis itself does not tie the two sexes together (with \(r_1 = 2\) the sex factor imposes nothing; see below); they are tied by the low-rank models built on the cores downstream, such as the forecasters’ few principal components and the regimes’ deviations. The coordinates of a country-year’s schedule in the basis form its effective core, the \(r_1 \times r_2\) matrix
\[
\mathcal{G}_{c,t} \;=\; \mathbf{S}^{\top}\, \mathcal{M}_{c,t}\, \mathbf{A},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
\mathcal{M}_{c,t} \;\approx\; \mathbf{S}\, \mathcal{G}_{c,t}\, \mathbf{A}^{\top}
\]
where \(\mathcal{M}_{c,t}\) is the \(2 \times 110\) matrix of \(\operatorname{logit}(q_x)\) for population \(c\) in year \(t\). Every later chapter works with these effective cores.
The second job is to describe how mortality varies across populations and over time — the country and year modes of the tensor — and, in doing so, to say something about the country-years for which we have no (non-exceptional) data. That is a completion problem: about 70% of the country-year cells are unobserved.
The two jobs are done in turn, so that values filled in for the unobserved country-years never shape the basis or the cores of the observed ones. The sex and age bases are estimated from observed schedules only, which needs no imputation, and every observed country-year is represented by its exact projection on that basis (steps 1–3). The unobserved country-years are then filled by a low-rank model of the country and year modes, fitted to observed data only by EM, with its ranks chosen by out-of-sample prediction (step 4).

8  The Tucker decomposition

title: 8  The Tucker decomposition
section: 8.2 Step 1 — the shared sex and age bases
text:
8.2 Step 1 — the shared sex and age bases
Each observed country-year contributes one complete \(2 \times 110\) schedule. Stacking those schedules side by side gives the age unfolding \(\mathbf{M}_{(2)}\) (\(110 \times 2N_{\text{obs}}\)) and the sex unfolding \(\mathbf{M}_{(1)}\) (\(2 \times 110 N_{\text{obs}}\)) of the observed data, with no gaps. Their left singular vectors are the factor matrices (the paper’s shared bases, §3.2). The sex mode has only two levels and is kept at full rank, \(r_1 = 2\). The age rank \(r_2\) is the smallest number of components that captures a share \(\tau =\) 0.9999 of the variance of \(\mathbf{M}_{(2)}\) (the paper’s rank rule, in §3.2). Computing an SVD of a \(110 \times 9{,}000\) matrix is quick; we use the equivalent eigen-decomposition of the \(110 \times 110\) matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{(2)} \mathbf{M}_{(2)}^\top\) (mdmx.tensor.leading_left_vectors). Singular vectors are only defined up to sign; mdmx.tensor.fix_signs makes the largest entry of each positive so that results are identical on every computer. The first age vector is then turned, where needed, to point the same way as the mean observed schedule, so that it has the shape of a \(\operatorname{logit}(q_x)\) schedule (negative at almost every age) and its core entry rises as mortality falls.


Estimate the shared sex and age bases from observed schedules (cached)
def _bases():
    return tz.sex_age_bases(Mz, observed, tau=P.tucker.tau,
                            age_bounds=tuple(P.tucker.age_rank_bounds))

bases = artifacts.stage("tucker_bases", _bases, inputs=["tensor"], params=P.section("tucker"),
                        code=[_bases, tz.sex_age_bases, tz.leading_left_vectors, tz.select_rank,
                              tz.fix_signs], desc="Shared sex and age bases from observed schedules")
U_sex, U_age_raw = bases["U_sex"], bases["U_age"]
latex.report("tuckerTau", P.tucker.tau, text=f"{P.tucker.tau:g}", desc="Variance share tau of the rank rule for r2")
r1, r2 = U_sex.shape[1], U_age_raw.shape[1]
print(f"r1 (sex) = {r1}, r2 (age) = {r2}")
print(f"Variance of the age unfolding captured by {r2} components: {bases['cumvar_age'][r2 - 1]:.6f}")
print("Sex factor matrix S (rows: female, male):")
print(np.round(U_sex, 3))
latex.report("tuckerRankSex", r1, desc="Sex rank r1")
latex.report("tuckerRankAge", r2, desc="Age rank r2 (tau rule on observed schedules)")
latex.report("tuckerVarAge", 100 * bases["cumvar_age"][r2 - 1], digits=3,
             desc="Percent of age-unfolding variance captured by r2 components")
latex.report("tuckerVarAgeFirst", 100 * bases["cumvar_age"][0], digits=1,
             desc="Percent of age-unfolding variance captured by the first component")

8  The Tucker decomposition

title: 8  The Tucker decomposition
text:
8.3 Step 2 — smoothing the age basis
The leading age components are smooth, but the higher-order ones pick up some single-year wiggle where the data are noisy. Following paper §3.2, each column except the first is smoothed with a Gaussian kernel whose width grows with age, so that the infant peak, the childhood minimum and the young-adult “accident hump” are smoothed lightly and the old-age tail more strongly. Components 2–5 have their own settings; all higher components share one narrow, constant bandwidth. Ages 0 and 1 are reset to their unsmoothed values, and the basis is then re-orthonormalised (QR). mdmx.smoothing implements the kernel as a matrix, so smoothing a column is one matrix–vector product.


Smooth the age basis and re-orthonormalise (cached)
def _smooth():
    U, diag = smoothing.smooth_age_basis(
        U_age_raw, P.tucker.smooth_components, P.tucker.smooth_rest_sigma,
        P.tucker.smooth_preserve, P.tucker.smooth_orth_tol)
    return {"U_age": U, "diagnostics": diag}

sm = artifacts.stage("tucker_age_smoothed", _smooth, inputs=["tucker_bases"],
                     params=P.section("tucker"), code=[_smooth, smoothing],
                     desc="Smoothed, orthonormal age basis")
U_age = sm["U_age"]

text:
8.4 Step 3 — the effective cores of the observed country-years
With \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\) fixed, the effective core of each observed country-year is a projection, \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t} =
\mathbf{S}^\top \mathcal{M}_{c,t}\mathbf{A}\), and the schedule implied by it is \(\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{c,t} = \mathbf{S}\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\mathbf{A}^\top\). The only approximation is the truncation of the age basis to \(r_2\) components, so the reconstruction of observed data is very close.


Project every observed schedule onto the shared basis; measure the fit
Y_obs = tz.effective_cores(Mz, observed, U_sex, U_age)            # (r1, r2, C, T), NaN if unobserved
M_rec = tz.schedules_from_cores(np.nan_to_num(Y_obs), U_sex, U_age)
err = (M_rec - Mz)[obs4]
r2_obs = 1 - np.sum(err ** 2) / np.sum((Mz[obs4] - Mz[obs4].mean()) ** 2)
rel_err = np.linalg.norm(err) / np.linalg.norm(Mz[obs4])
e0_obs = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(Mz, 1, -1))[:, observed]
e0_rec = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(M_rec, 1, -1))[:, observed]
de0 = np.abs(e0_rec - e0_obs)
print(f"Observed cells: RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean(err ** 2)):.4f}, R² {r2_obs:.6f}, "
      f"relative error {rel_err:.4f}")
print(f"|Δe0| between observed and reconstructed schedules: mean {de0.mean():.3f}, max {de0.max():.3f} years")
latex.report("tuckerObsRMSE", float(np.sqrt(np.mean(err ** 2))), digits=3, desc="RMSE (logit) on observed cells")
latex.report("tuckerObsRsq", float(r2_obs), digits=5, desc="R-squared on observed cells")
latex.report("tuckerObsRelErr", float(rel_err), digits=4, desc="Relative Frobenius error on observed cells")
latex.report("tuckerObsMeanAbsDeZero", float(de0.mean()), digits=3, desc="Mean |delta e0|, observed vs reconstructed")
latex.report("tuckerObsMaxAbsDeZero", float(de0.max()), digits=2, desc="Max |delta e0|, observed vs reconstructed")

title: 8  The Tucker decomposition
text:
8.5 Step 4 — completing the unobserved country-years
To describe the country and year modes, and to say what the model implies for country-years without baseline data, we fit a Tucker model to the effective cores in which the country and year modes are compressed to ranks \(r_3\) and \(r_4\):
\[
\mathcal{G}_{c,t} \;\approx\; \mathcal{G} \times_3 \mathbf{c}_c^\top \times_4 \mathbf{t}_t^\top ,
\]
with \(\mathbf{C}\) (\(C \times r_3\)) and \(\mathbf{T}\) (\(T \times r_4\)) orthonormal. It is fitted to observed country-years only, by the EM algorithm (mdmx.tensor.complete_cores): start with the country means of the observed cores, fit the model, replace only the unobserved slices by the fit, and repeat until the filled values stop changing. At convergence the observed slices are data, the unobserved slices are the model’s own prediction, and the factors are those of the completed array — so the made- up values exert no pull of their own. One limit follows: a calendar year in which no population is observed — every year of the influenza pandemics and of COVID-19, for example, is exceptional in every population with data — gives its year loading nothing to be estimated from, so EM leaves it close to where it started and the model returns roughly each country’s mean schedule there (for Sweden the same e₀ in 1918 as in each of 2020–22; chapter 08). The model’s values in such years are not predictions; chapter 08 builds the baselines of exceptional years differently.

8.5.1 Choosing the ranks by prediction
A variance threshold cannot choose \(r_3\) and \(r_4\) here: most of the array is missing, and the share of variance a component “explains” depends on how the gaps were filled. Instead we ask how well each candidate pair predicts data it has not seen. A random 5% of the observed country-years is hidden, the model is fitted to the rest, and the hidden schedules are predicted.


Hold-out search over the completion ranks (cached; a few minutes)
grid = [(rc, rt) for rc in P.tucker.completion_country_ranks for rt in P.tucker.completion_year_ranks]

def _loss(Y_completed, hidden):
    rec = tz.schedules_from_cores(Y_completed, U_sex, U_age)
    h4 = np.broadcast_to(hidden[None, None], M.shape)
    e0p = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(rec, 1, -1))[:, hidden]
    e0t = lifetable.e0_from_logit(np.moveaxis(Mz, 1, -1))[:, hidden]
    return {"rmse": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((rec[h4] - Mz[h4]) ** 2))),
            "e0_mae": float(np.mean(np.abs(e0p - e0t)))}

def _search():
    rows = tz.holdout_rank_search(Y_obs, observed, grid, share=P.tucker.holdout_share,
                                  seed=P.tucker.holdout_seed, max_iter=P.tucker.search_max_iter,
                                  tol=P.tucker.em_tol, loss=_loss)
    # Country-mean imputation, a naive benchmark, on the same hidden cells.
    rows.append({"r_country": 0, "r_year": 0, "iterations": 0,
                 **_loss(tz.country_mean_impute(np.nan_to_num(Y_obs), observed & ~_hidden()), _hidden())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def _hidden():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(P.tucker.holdout_seed)
    ci, ti = np.nonzero(observed)
    pick = rng.choice(len(ci), size=max(1, int(round(P.tucker.holdout_share * len(ci)))), replace=False)
    h = np.zeros_like(observed); h[ci[pick], ti[pick]] = True
    return h

search = artifacts.stage("tucker_rank_search", _search, inputs=["tucker_bases", "tucker_age_smoothed", "tensor"],
                         params=P.section("tucker"),
                         code=[_search, _loss, _hidden, tz.complete_cores, tz.holdout_rank_search],
                         desc="Hold-out prediction error of the completion model by rank")
cand = search[search["r_country"] > 0]
best = cand.loc[cand["rmse"].idxmin()]
ref = search[search["r_country"] == 0].iloc[0]
r3, r4 = int(best["r_country"]), int(best["r_year"])
print(cand.pivot(index="r_country", columns="r_year", values="rmse").round(3))
print(f"\nSelected ranks: r3 = {r3}, r4 = {r4}  (hold-out RMSE {best['rmse']:.3f}, e0 MAE {best['e0_mae']:.2f} y)")
print(f"Country-mean imputation on the same cells: RMSE {ref['rmse']:.3f}, e0 MAE {ref['e0_mae']:.2f} y")

def _sci(x: float) -> str:
    """x as a power of ten in text-mode LaTeX, e.g. $5.5 \\times 10^{-5}$ (not for use inside math)."""
    mantissa, exponent = f"{x:.1e}".split("e")
    power = f"10^{{{int(exponent)}}}"
    return f"${power}$" if mantissa == "1.0" else f"${mantissa} \\times {power}$"

8.5.3 The HOSVD or higher-order orthogonal iteration
Each iteration of the completion model computes \(\mathbf{C}\) and \(\mathbf{T}\) by a truncated HOSVD of the filled array: the leading left singular vectors of its country and year unfoldings. A truncated HOSVD is quasi-optimal, not optimal. Its squared error is at most the sum, over the truncated modes, of the squared singular values each one discards, so with two modes truncated its error is at most \(\sqrt{2}\) times that of the best approximation with the same ranks. Higher-order orthogonal iteration can come closer to the best: it updates each factor matrix in turn, given the other, by least squares. To see whether that would serve the completion model better, the same EM is fitted with one sweep of it in place of the HOSVD at every iteration (mdmx.hooi.complete_cores_hooi), at the selected ranks and with the same settings, and the two are compared twice: by the residual of the observed cores after the final model’s 1,500 iterations, and by how well they predict hidden country-years. The second comparison uses 10 random splits, each hiding 5% of the observed country-years as the rank search does, drawn with their own seed rather than the one whose split chose the ranks.


The completion model with higher-order orthogonal iteration (cached; about a minute)
CK = P.section("checks")


def _hooi_check():
    done, fac, core, hist = hooi.complete_cores_hooi(Y_obs, observed, r3, r4,
                                                     max_iter=P.tucker.em_max_iter, tol=P.tucker.em_tol)
    fit = pd.DataFrame({
        "method": ["HOSVD", "HOOI"],
        "resid_obs": [hooi.observed_residual(comp["G_ct"], observed, [comp["U_country"], comp["U_year"]],
                                             comp["core"]),
                      hooi.observed_residual(done, observed, fac, core)],
        "iterations": [len(comp["history"]), len(hist)]})
    rng = np.random.default_rng(CK["hooi_seed"])
    ci, ti = np.nonzero(observed)
    rows = []
    for split in range(CK["hooi_splits"]):
        pick = rng.choice(len(ci), size=max(1, int(round(P.tucker.holdout_share * len(ci)))), replace=False)
        hidden = np.zeros_like(observed)
        hidden[ci[pick], ti[pick]] = True
        for name, complete in (("HOSVD", tz.complete_cores), ("HOOI", hooi.complete_cores_hooi)):
            Yc = complete(Y_obs, observed & ~hidden, r3, r4, max_iter=P.tucker.search_max_iter,
                          tol=P.tucker.em_tol)[0]
            rows.append({"split": split + 1, "method": name, **_loss(Yc, hidden)})
    return {"fit": fit, "holdout": pd.DataFrame(rows)}


hc = artifacts.stage("tucker_hooi_check", _hooi_check,
                     inputs=["tensor", "tucker_bases", "tucker_age_smoothed", "tucker_completion"],
                     params={"r3": r3, "r4": r4, "em_max_iter": P.tucker.em_max_iter,
                             "search_max_iter": P.tucker.search_max_iter, "em_tol": P.tucker.em_tol,
                             "holdout_share": P.tucker.holdout_share, "splits": CK["hooi_splits"],

                           tz.complete_cores],

                          "fit to the observed cores and prediction of hidden country-years")

Higher-order orthogonal iteration fits the observed cores more closely, as it must: one sweep never moves the model away from the filled array, so the residual of the observed cores cannot rise from one iteration to the next. The closer fit does not carry over to country-years the model has not seen: in 10 of the 10 splits it predicts them less well than the HOSVD. The completion model keeps the HOSVD, which also keeps each iteration in closed form.

8  The Tucker decomposition

title: 9  A typology of mortality age patterns
text:
9.1 What this chapter does
The decomposition of chapter 04 represents every observed schedule by its effective core \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\), a \(2 \times r_2\) matrix of coordinates in the shared sex and age bases. Paper §4 uses these coordinates to sort country-years into a typology of mortality age patterns; each type is called a regime, here and in the chapters that use it. A regime is a deviation pattern relative to the typical schedule at the same life expectancy: two country-years belong to the same cluster when their schedules depart in the same way from the schedule that is typical for their e₀. Level is removed twice over: the level coordinate (the first age column of \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\)) is dropped, and from every remaining coordinate we subtract its average at the country-year’s e₀.
Part A chooses which part of the effective core carries the shape signal, builds the level-free features, fits Gaussian mixtures for \(K = 2, \ldots, 15\), chooses the largest \(K\) whose partition is reproducible (reporting BIC and how the clusters fare when populations are resampled), cross-checks with Ward’s method, and describes the clusters — their deviation patterns, members, relation to level, time and place, and whether any of them merely collects noisy schedules of small populations. Part B classifies how the level changes within each country (it does not use the clustering features). The artefact saved at the end lets later chapters build a schedule for any cluster at any e₀.

10.1 Step 1 — the unit of clustering
The objects clustered are country-years: each observed pair \((c, t)\) with \(O_{c,t} = 1\) is one data point (paper §4.1). Country-years without data, and exceptional years set aside for the disruption model, are not clustered. mdmx.clustering.observed_index lists them in a fixed order (by population, then year); every per-observation array in this chapter uses that order. Each country-year’s life expectancy at birth is computed from its observed schedule with the project’s single life-table function and averaged over the sexes; it is checked against the HMD’s published e₀ and against the e₀ of the schedule implied by the effective core.

section: 10.2 Step 2 — the smooth, low-order part of the effective core
text:
10.2 Step 2 — the smooth, low-order part of the effective core
The schedule implied by an effective core is a sum of terms, one per entry of \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\) (paper §4.1): the first age column multiplies \(\mathbf{a}_1\), which is close to the average logit(\(q_x\)) schedule, and so carries the level; the later columns carry the shape. Not all shape columns are equally useful. The age basis has \(r_2\) = 50 columns because the decomposition must reproduce every observed schedule almost exactly (chapter 04), including the year-to-year jitter of single-year rates in small populations. That jitter lives in the high-order columns. Clustering on them groups country-years by how noisy their data are, not by how their mortality differs.
We therefore keep only the first \(c_{\text{feat}}\) age columns, with \(c_{\text{feat}}\) the smallest number of age components that together capture a share τ = 0.999 of the sum of squares of the observed schedules — the τ rule that chapter 04 uses for \(r_2\), at a less demanding threshold (mdmx.clustering.column_energy_share, choose_n_columns). Two further measures, computed for every column, show whether the rule separates signal from noise:

the roughness of the basis function \(\mathbf{a}_j\) — the sum of its squared second differences over ages 2–109 (basis_roughness): smooth age patterns have values near zero;
the year-to-year noise ratio of each core entry (year_to_year_noise): the mean squared change between consecutive observed years of a population, divided by twice the entry’s overall variance. An entry that moves smoothly over time scores near 0; one whose values are independent from year to year scores near 1.



Choose the number of age columns k, with the evidence

text:
10.3 Step 3 — level-free features
The features are built from the entries of columns 2–6 of \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\), for both sex components: the level column is dropped. Dropping the level column is not enough to make the remaining coordinates independent of level, because the shape of the schedule changes systematically as mortality falls (the “rotation” of the age pattern of decline; paper §4.1). So, for each entry \(m\), we estimate its e₀-conditional mean \(\mu_m(e_0)\) — a LOWESS curve of the entry against e₀ fitted across all observed country-years, with a span of 0.1 of the points and 3 robustifying iterations (mdmx.clustering.conditional_mean) — and subtract it:
\[
f_{c,t,m} \;=\; \mathcal{G}_{c,t}[i_m, j_m] \;-\; \mu_m\!\left(e_{0,c,t}\right),
\qquad j_m \in \{2, \ldots, k\},\; i_m \in \{1, 2\}.
\]
The feature vector \(\mathbf{f}_{c,t}\) (length \(2(k-1)\) = 10) says how this country-year’s schedule departs from the schedule that is typical at its e₀. The same LOWESS is applied to every entry of the effective core, including the level column and the columns beyond \(c_{\text{feat}}\); this conditional-mean core \(\bar{\mathcal{G}}(e_0)\) is stored on a grid of e₀ values (step 0.1 years) so that later chapters can build the typical schedule \(\mathbf{S}\bar{\mathcal{G}}(e_0)\mathbf{A}^\top\) at any e₀.


Conditional means on e0, residual features, and checks of level independence

The level coordinate is almost a linear function of e₀ (r = 0.97; its sign is a convention of the decomposition). The first shape coordinate is far from level-free (r = -0.86), and the entries of all age columns 2–50, with only the level column dropped, predict e₀ with R² = 0.91. After the conditional mean is removed, the 10 features predict e₀ with R² = 0.009, and no feature correlates with e₀ by more than |r| = 0.066: the features are free of level in their mean. They are not identically distributed at every e₀, however: the root-mean-square size of the residual vector is 4.8 in the noisiest e₀ band and 2.0 above e₀ = 75 (table above), so allowing squared terms gives R² = 0.10. High-mortality schedules vary more around their typical shape.
The typical schedule \(\mathbf{S}\bar{\mathcal{G}}(x)\mathbf{A}^\top\) has an e₀ within 0.9 years of \(x\) over the observed range (mean difference +0.47): the mean of logit schedules is not exactly the schedule with the mean e₀, because the life table is not linear. Chapters that need an exact e₀ should adjust the level coordinate after adding a cluster’s deviation.

text:
10.5 Step 5 — Gaussian mixtures and the choice of K
A Gaussian mixture model (paper §4.2) treats the rows of the reduced feature matrix as draws from \(K\) multivariate normal distributions, each with its own mean vector and its own unrestricted (“full”) covariance matrix. It is fitted by EM for each \(K\) = 2, …, 15, with 20 EM starts from k-means solutions (seed in the parameter file). The usual choice of \(K\) minimises
\[
\mathrm{BIC}(K) = -2\,\ell(\hat\theta_K) + p_K \log n_{\text{obs}},
\qquad p_K = (K-1) + K d + K\,\tfrac{d(d+1)}{2}
\]
(mdmx.clustering.bic_sweep checks the formula against scikit-learn). Shared (“tied”) and diagonal covariance matrices are compared in the supplementary section. Clusters are numbered by increasing mean e₀ of their members (order_clusters), which makes the numbering reproducible.


Fit mixtures for K = 2 … 15 and compute BIC (cached)
k_values = list(range(PG["k_min"], PG["k_max"] + 1))
gmm_settings = {k: PG[k] for k in ("covariance_type", "n_init", "max_iter", "tol", "reg_covar", "seed")}
# The code that turns the data into the features X (Steps 1–4); every stage fitted to X lists it.
FEATURE_CODE = [clus.observed_index, clus.observed_cores, clus.observed_e0, lifetable.e0_from_logit,
                clus.column_energy_share, clus.choose_n_columns, clus.feature_index, clus.cores_to_features,
                clus.e0_grid, clus.conditional_mean, clus.pca_fit, tz.fix_signs]


def _ordered(gm):
    """A fitted mixture with its clusters numbered by increasing mean e0 of their members."""
    raw = gm.predict(X)
    order = clus.order_clusters(raw, e0, gm.n_components)               # order[new] = old
    covariances = gm.covariances_ if PG["covariance_type"] == "tied" else gm.covariances_[order]
    return {"labels": np.argsort(order)[raw], "posterior": gm.predict_proba(X)[:, order],
            "weights": gm.weights_[order], "means": gm.means_[order], "covariances": covariances}


def _fit_mixtures():
    table, models = clus.bic_sweep(X, k_values, **gmm_settings)
    return {"table": table, "fits": {str(k): _ordered(gm) for k, gm in models.items()}}


fit = artifacts.stage(
    "clustering_gmm", _fit_mixtures, inputs=["tucker", "tensor"],
    params={"features": PF, "gmm": PG},
    code=[_fit_mixtures, _ordered, *FEATURE_CODE, clus.bic_sweep, clus.fit_gmm, clus.gmm_n_parameters,
          clus.order_clusters],
    desc="Gaussian mixtures on the level-free features for every K, with BIC")
bic_table = fit["table"]

      .round(1).to_string(index=False))

      f"runner-up K = {k_second}, {bic_margin:,.0f} BIC units worse.")

BIC alone is not a sufficient guide: a partition is worth describing only if the method gives it again, and it is more useful if it would also appear in another set of populations. We check both.
Reproducibility. The likelihood of a mixture has many local maxima, and EM started from other k-means solutions can end at a different partition of almost the same likelihood. For every \(K\) the mixture is refitted from 5 seeds — the chapter’s and those listed under seeds in the parameter file, each with 20 EM starts — and the partitions are compared in pairs with the adjusted Rand index (ARI: 1 = identical, 0 = chance agreement). The chapter uses the largest \(K\) whose refits agree at a mean ARI of at least 0.9, as do the refits of every smaller \(K\) (mdmx.clustering.choose_k_reproducible); its partition is that \(K\)’s fit from the sweep above.


Refit every K from other seeds and choose K (cached)

        **{k_: PG[k_] for k_ in ("covariance_type", "n_init", "max_iter", "tol", "reg_covar")})
    return {"table": table, "labels": {str(k): lab for k, lab in refits.items()}}

Resampling of populations. Reproducibility is a property of the method on these data. Whether the clusters would also appear in another set of populations is a different question. Following Hennig (2007), we resample whole population families — a population together with its HMD parts, such as the United Kingdom with England & Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland (svdcomp.population_families), because the years of one population are not independent — with replacement, refit the mixture to each of 50 resamples (each with the 20 EM starts of the chapter’s partition, so that the check measures the populations and not the starting values), and record for every cluster its Jaccard similarity with its best match in the refit, on the country-years in the resample (mdmx.clustering.group_bootstrap, cluster_jaccard). A cluster’s mean Jaccard is read as in Hennig’s fpc::clusterboot: at least 0.75 a stable cluster, from 0.6 a pattern whose members are doubtful, below that a cluster not to be trusted. The check is reported for every \(K\); it does not choose \(K\).


Resample population families and refit every K (cached)

            for k in k_values}

low, high = (ari_next if ari_next is not None else 0.0), min(ari_at[k] for k in k_values if k <= K)
print(f"BIC is lowest at $K$ = {K_bic}"
      f"{' (the upper bound of the range)' if K_bic == PG['k_max'] else ''}, but the refits from other "
      f"starting values agree at a mean ARI of at least {thr} only up to $K$ = {K} ({ari_at[K]:.2f}{after}).  "
      "A partition that another seed would change is not worth describing, so the rule stops at the first "
      f"$K$ whose refits disagree; any threshold above {low:.2f} and up to {high:.2f} gives the same $K$.  "
      f"The chapter therefore uses $K$ = {K} clusters, {bic_at[K] - bic_at[K_bic]:,.0f} BIC units above "
      f"the minimum.  Cluster sizes range from {sizes.min():,} to {sizes.max():,} country-years, and "
      f"{100 * uncertain:.0f}% of country-years have a largest posterior probability below 0.9.\n")
if stable_k:
    stable_text = (f"Only $K$ = {', '.join(str(k) for k in stable_k)} keep every cluster stable "
                   f"(mean Jaccard ≥ {PSt['jaccard_stable']}) when whole population families are resampled.")
else:
    stable_text = (f"When whole population families are resampled, no $K$ keeps every cluster stable (mean "
                   f"Jaccard ≥ {PSt['jaccard_stable']}); the best is $K$ = {int(best_row['K'])}, whose least "
                   f"stable cluster reaches {best_row['jaccard_min']:.2f}.")
print(f"{stable_text}  At $K$ = {K} the clusters' mean Jaccard similarities range from {jac_K.min():.2f} to "
      f"{jac_K.max():.2f} ({n_untrusted} of {K} below {PSt['jaccard_doubtful']}), and the refits agree with "
      f"the chapter's partition at a mean ARI of {boot_ari_K:.2f}, against {ari_at[K]:.2f} for refits to all "
      "populations from other starting values: most of the instability comes from which populations are in "
      "the sample — a cluster made up mostly of a few populations cannot form in a resample without them.  "
      "If anything the check is lenient, because the typical schedule (Step 3) and the PCA are fitted to "
      "all populations and held fixed; only the mixture is refitted.  The clusters are a reproducible "
      f"description of these {C} populations — a typology in the spirit of the regional model life tables "
      "of @CoaleDemeny1966 — not regimes that any set of populations would reproduce.\n")

BIC is lowest at \(K\) = 13, but the refits from other starting values agree at a mean ARI of at least 0.9 only up to \(K\) = 5 (1.00; at \(K\) = 6 they agree only at 0.63, and no other \(K\) does (at most 0.71)). A partition that another seed would change is not worth describing, so the rule stops at the first \(K\) whose refits disagree; any threshold above 0.63 and up to 0.98 gives the same \(K\). The chapter therefore uses \(K\) = 5 clusters, 2,674 BIC units above the minimum. Cluster sizes range from 212 to 1,369 country-years, and 43% of country-years have a largest posterior probability below 0.9.
When whole population families are resampled, no \(K\) keeps every cluster stable (mean Jaccard ≥ 0.75); the best is \(K\) = 2, whose least stable cluster reaches 0.60. At \(K\) = 5 the clusters’ mean Jaccard similarities range from 0.41 to 0.57 (5 of 5 below 0.6), and the refits agree with the chapter’s partition at a mean ARI of 0.29, against 1.00 for refits to all populations from other starting values: most of the instability comes from which populations are in the sample — a cluster made up mostly of a few populations cannot form in a resample without them. If anything the check is lenient, because the typical schedule (Step 3) and the PCA are fitted to all populations and held fixed; only the mixture is refitted. The clusters are a reproducible description of these 48 populations — a typology in the spirit of the regional model life tables of Coale and Demeny (1966) — not regimes that any set of populations would reproduce.

10.6 Step 6 — Ward’s hierarchical clustering as a check
This check, which is in the companion only, compares the mixture with Ward’s minimum-variance clustering on the same reduced features. The tree is built on all 4,056 country-years, cut into \(K\) groups, and matched to the mixture clusters to maximise agreement (matched_agreement); we report the share of country-years on which they agree and the adjusted Rand index (ARI: 0 for chance, 1 for identical partitions).


Ward’s method on the same features, and its agreement with the mixture
Z_ward, ward_raw = clus.ward_clustering(X, K)
ward_agree, ward_conf, ward_map = clus.matched_agreement(ward_raw, labels, K)
ward_labels = ward_map[ward_raw]
ward_ari = adjusted_rand_score(labels, ward_raw)
print(f"Ward vs mixture: matched agreement {ward_agree:.3f}, ARI {ward_ari:.3f}")
latex.report("clusWardAgree", 100 * ward_agree, digits=0, desc="Percent of country-years on which Ward and GMM agree (matched labels)")
latex.report("clusWardARI", float(ward_ari), digits=2, desc="Adjusted Rand index between Ward and GMM partitions")

10.7 Step 7 — what the clusters are
Each cluster is summarised by its mean deviation \(\bar{\mathbf{f}}_k\), the mean of its members’ features (mdmx.clustering.cluster_means). Mapped back to core coordinates (features_to_cores: the feature entries filled in, zeros elsewhere) it is a matrix \(\mathbf{D}_k\), and the cluster’s schedule at any life expectancy \(x\) is
\[
\mathcal{M}_k(x) \;=\; \mathbf{S}\,\bigl[\bar{\mathcal{G}}(x) + \mathbf{D}_k\bigr]\,\mathbf{A}^\top,
\]
the typical schedule at \(x\) plus the cluster’s deviation \(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{D}_k\mathbf{A}^\top\), which is the same at every \(x\). The members’ own schedules, and their e₀, vary widely within a cluster; what they share is the deviation.


Cluster deviations, and the noise and population-size measures
residual_mean = clus.cluster_means(R, labels, K)                              # (K, p)
residual_core = clus.features_to_cores(residual_mean, fidx, r1, r2)          # (K, r1, r2)
deviation = tz.schedules_from_cores(np.moveaxis(residual_core, 0, -1), U_sex, U_age)   # (S, A, K)
member_mean_core = clus.cluster_means(G_obs, labels, K)                       # (K, r1, r2)

# Noise measures (Step 8): roughness of each observed schedule relative to the
# typical roughness at the same e0, and population size (total HMD exposure).

text:
10.8 Step 8 — level, time, and noise
Level and time. The features have no mean dependence on e₀, but the clusters can still differ in e₀ if different groups of populations are observed at different levels of mortality — below e₀ = 40 only a handful of populations are in the HMD. The correlation ratio \(\eta^2\) (the share of a variable’s variance explained by cluster membership; mdmx.clustering.eta_squared) measures this for e₀ and for calendar year; the number of clusters present at each level of e₀ shows whether the clusters are level strata.


How much of e0 and calendar time the clusters explain
eta_e0 = clus.eta_squared(e0, labels)
eta_year = clus.eta_squared(obs_year.astype(float), labels)
e0_band = pd.cut(e0, np.arange(15, 95, PD["e0_bin"]))
per_band = pd.crosstab(e0_band, labels)
clusters_per_band = (per_band >= PD["band_min_members"]).sum(axis=1)

Where the data allow a test, the clusters are not level strata: every 5-year e₀ band with at least 100 country-years contains at least 3 clusters, and the bands between e₀ = 65 and 80 contain 4–5 of the 5. Cluster membership explains \(\eta^2\) = 0.23 of the variance of e₀ and \(\eta^2\) = 0.25 of the variance of calendar year. This is not level leaking back into the features, whose mean does not depend on e₀ (Step 3). What association there is comes from composition — below e₀ ≈ 45 only a few populations with long early series are observed, so the deviation patterns found there are theirs, and populations that enter the HMD late are observed only at high e₀ — and from spread: the residuals are larger at high mortality, and clusters that differ mainly in how widely their members scatter (see Step 7) differ in e₀ and period with it. The clusters are therefore free of level in the sense intended — they are defined by deviations from the typical schedule at the same e₀ — but they are not uncorrelated with level or period.
Noise. A cluster can form around the noisy schedules of small populations, above all when the features include the high-order age columns (Step 2). We check every cluster with two measures: the roughness ratio — the median roughness of its members’ observed schedules (mean squared second difference of logit \(q_x\) over ages 1–59, mdmx.clustering.roughness) relative to typical schedules at the same e₀ (a LOWESS of log roughness on e₀) — and the share of its members from the smallest quarter of country-years by population size (total HMD exposure). A cluster is flagged as a noise cluster if its roughness ratio exceeds 2.0 and more than 50% of its members come from the smallest quarter (mdmx.clustering.noise_diagnostics).

section: 11.1 The level signal and its direction
text:
11.1 The level signal and its direction
The level coordinate \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}[1,1]\) removed in Part A is used here to describe how fast mortality is changing (the level epochs, which are in the companion only). Its sign is that of the singular vectors \(\mathbf{s}_1\) and \(\mathbf{a}_1\), which is a convention: in this decomposition \(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}[1,1]\) falls as e₀ rises, but another linear-algebra library or sign rule could flip it. To make “improvement” mean improvement whatever the convention, we multiply the level coordinate by the sign of its correlation with e₀ (mdmx.clustering.level_orientation):
\[
\ell_{c,t} = \sigma\, \mathcal{G}_{c,t}[1,1], \qquad
\sigma = \operatorname{sign}\operatorname{corr}\bigl(\mathcal{G}_{c,t}[1,1],\, e_0\bigr),
\]
so that \(\ell\) rises when mortality improves whatever the orientation of the bases (with the decomposition chapter’s orientation, \(\sigma = +1\)). The thresholds below are stated for \(\ell\). To express them in years of life expectancy, we regress e₀ on \(\ell\) across all observed country-years: one unit of \(\ell\) corresponds to \(b\) years of e₀.


Orient the level signal by e0 and translate the thresholds into e0 units
sigma = clus.level_orientation(level, e0)
ell = sigma * level
e0_per_ell, e0_at_zero = np.polyfit(ell, e0, 1)
print(f"σ = {sigma:+d}: the level coordinate G[1,1] {'falls' if sigma < 0 else 'rises'} as e0 rises")
print(f"e0 ≈ {e0_at_zero:.1f} + {e0_per_ell:.3f} ℓ   (R² = {np.corrcoef(ell, e0)[0, 1] ** 2:.3f})")
print(f"δ = {PE['delta']} ℓ/year ≈ {PE['delta'] * e0_per_ell:.3f} years of e0 per year; "
      f"δ_rapid = {PE['delta_rapid']} ℓ/year ≈ {PE['delta_rapid'] * e0_per_ell:.3f}")

title: 9  A typology of mortality age patterns
text:
11.2 The classification
The procedure takes every setting from the parameter file:

Smooth. For each population with at least 15 observed years, smooth \(\ell\) and e₀ over its observed years by LOWESS (mdmx.clustering.lowess_at), with a span of 0.2 of the population’s years but never fewer than 10 years, and 3 robustness iterations.
Slopes. Slide a window of \(W\) = 15 calendar years across the series one year at a time; in each window with at least 8 observed years, fit a least-squares line to the smoothed \(\ell\) and keep its slope (mdmx.clustering.window_slopes).
Classify each window slope \(s\): rapid improvement if \(s > \delta_{\text{rapid}}\), slow improvement if \(\delta < s \le \delta_{\text{rapid}}\), stagnation if \(|s| \le \delta\), slow worsening if \(-\delta_{\text{rapid}} \le s < -\delta\), rapid worsening if \(s < -\delta_{\text{rapid}}\) (classify_slopes).
Assign years. Each calendar year from the population’s first to last observed year takes the most common category among the windows that contain it (yearly_categories, which uses majority_label); ties go to the category listed first above, i.e. towards rapid improvement. Years in the middle of a series are covered by \(W\) windows; years near either end by fewer, so their category rests on less evidence.
Epochs are maximal runs of consecutive calendar years with the same category (runs).



Classify level epochs for every population
ep = clus.classify_epochs(c_idx, obs_year, ell, e0, pops, **PE)
win, yrs_cat, epochs = ep["windows"], ep["years"], ep["epochs"]

Improvement dominates: 63% of the classified country-years are in rapid and 24% in slow improvement, 11% in stagnation and only 1.6% in worsening. Stagnation marks the long pre-transition periods of the earliest series (Sweden, France, England & Wales, Norway) and the Eastern European plateau of the 1960s–1980s. The worsening epochs are few and recognisable: Iceland (1838–1866, 29 years); Estonia (1970, 1 year); Belarus (1972–1998, 22 years); Ukraine (1987–1997, 11 years); Russia (1990–1999, 10 years); United States (2024, 1 year). The post-Soviet mortality crisis is therefore captured. For the United States the last three epochs are slow improvement 2004–2016, stagnation 2017–2023, slow worsening 2024; the final year of a series is covered by only 1 window (years near either end of a series always rest on fewer windows than years in the middle), so the recent slowdown of mortality improvement in the United States appears essentially as stagnation rather than worsening. Because the level and e₀ slopes agree in sign in 97.9% of windows, the direction assigned to each window is unambiguous almost everywhere.

crumbs: Part II — Analysis (one chapter per paper section)
9  A typology of mortality age patterns

title: 10  Reconstruction at arbitrary mortality levels
text:
10.1 What this chapter does
A model life table system must produce a complete schedule of mortality at any level, including levels not observed in any country-year. Paper §5 does this for a regime \(k\) and a target life expectancy \(x\). Life expectancy alone does not determine a schedule — infinitely many schedules share an e₀ (paper §5.1) — so the regime supplies the shape.
Chapter 06 defines a regime as a deviation pattern from the typical schedule at the same e₀. The natural generator is therefore
\[
\mathcal{G}_k(x) \;=\; \bar{\mathcal{G}}(x) + \mathbf{D}_k(x),
\qquad
\mathbf{z}_k(x) \;=\; \mathbf{S}\,\mathcal{G}_k(x)\,\mathbf{A}^\top ,
\]
the typical effective core at \(x\) — the e₀-conditional mean of chapter 06, whose schedule is the paper’s typical schedule \(\bar{\mathcal{M}}(x)\) (Eq. 10) — plus the regime’s deviation, mapped to logit(\(q_x\)) for both sexes (the paper’s trajectory of a regime, Eq. 13 in §5.2). The chapter asks how the deviation should depend on \(x\), answers by a hold-out over populations, and then examines what the resulting trajectories show: the sex differential, the change in the age pattern as e₀ rises, and how well a schedule’s regime and e₀ can be recovered from the schedule.

section: 10.2 Step 1 — the typical schedule and the level calibration
text:
10.2 Step 1 — the typical schedule and the level calibration
The typical effective core \(\bar{\mathcal{G}}(x)\) is chapter 06’s e₀-conditional mean: a LOWESS of every core entry against the e₀ of the observed schedules (span 0.1), stored on a grid of 662 e₀ values from 19.9 to 86.0. Its schedule’s e₀ is close to \(x\) but not equal to it: the mean of the cores at a given e₀ is not a core with exactly that e₀, because the life table is not linear in logit(\(q_x\)). mdmx.trajectories.calibrate_level therefore shifts the level coordinate \(\mathcal{G}[1,1]\), which moves logit(\(q_x\)) up or down at almost every age at once, until the schedule’s sex-average e₀ equals \(x\); the coordinates that carry the shape are left alone. The shift is found by bisection, and the step stops with an error rather than returning an uncalibrated schedule if the target cannot be bracketed.

section: 10.3 Step 2 — the deviation, chosen by a hold-out over populations
text:
10.3 Step 2 — the deviation, chosen by a hold-out over populations
How should a regime’s deviation depend on the level of mortality? The candidates:

typical — no deviation: every regime gets the typical schedule (the baseline: the typical schedule of all populations, paper Eq. 10);
constant — the regime’s mean deviation at every e₀ (the definition of a regime in chapter 06);
LOWESS — a LOWESS of the regime members’ features against e₀, so that the deviation changes with the level of mortality (a per-regime trajectory in level-free form), with span 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1 of the regime’s members;
neural — one small network for all regimes from the regime and e₀ to the features (mdmx.nn; settings in the parameter file), trained with early stopping on whole held-out families.

Each of the last three is tried on chapter 06’s feature positions alone and with the sex contrast of the level column added (mdmx.trajectories.deviation_positions). Chapter 06 builds the regimes without the level column, so on its features alone a regime keeps its shape but takes the typical overall sex differential; the sex contrast of the level column — how far apart male and female mortality sit overall — lets it keep its own: without it, the female advantage of the Central-Eastern European regime comes out too small (Step 3 measures by how much). Adding the sex contrast to chapter 06’s clustering features instead turned the regimes into eras, so it enters through the deviation. Outside a regime’s central e₀ range (its support: the 5–95 % range of its members) a deviation is held at its value at the boundary.
The candidates are compared on schedules the fits have not seen. Whole population families — a population with its HMD parts, because the years of one population are not independent — are dealt into 10 folds (svdcomp.assign_folds). For each fold, the typical schedule and every candidate are estimated from the other folds; each held-out country-year’s schedule is then generated from its regime at its observed e₀, calibrated to that e₀, and compared with the observed schedule: the RMSE of logit(\(q_x\)) over both sexes and ages 0–109 (mdmx.trajectories.holdout_scores). The rule, fixed before the run: the candidate with the lowest pooled held-out RMSE over the non-noise regimes is used. The deviations are estimated from the non-noise regimes only, as in the model the chapter keeps; the noise cluster is scored in a separate run (without the neural candidate) for information. The regime labels come from chapter 06’s clustering of all data, so the hold-out asks how well a schedule is rebuilt given its regime — as in an application where the user chooses the regime. The LOWESS span is the best of its grid on the same folds, which favours the LOWESS slightly.


The hold-out over population families (cached; a few minutes)
def cand_name(kind, frac=None, sex=False):
    """Hold-out name of a candidate, e.g. 'lowess 0.8 + sex level'."""
    base = f"lowess {frac:g}" if kind == "lowess" else kind
    return base + (" + sex level" if sex else "")

Each held-out country-year above is rebuilt with the regime the clustering gave it, and the clustering saw that year’s own schedule: the gain over the typical schedule is how much the regimes describe, given the regime. Every candidate deviation rebuilds held-out schedules better than the typical schedule alone (pooled RMSE 0.241). On chapter 06’s feature positions, a constant deviation reaches 0.222, the best LOWESS 0.220 and the neural network 0.222; with the sex level added, 0.220, 0.217 and 0.219. By the rule fixed in advance the chapter uses the e₀-dependent deviation (LOWESS, span 0.5) with the sex level, 10.0% below the typical schedule. Against the constant deviation with the sex level the pooled RMSE is 0.0032 lower (95% interval over families -0.0001 to 0.0071; 61% of families rebuilt better): a difference within the uncertainty. Against the same deviation without the sex level the pooled RMSE is 0.0034 lower (95% interval over families 0.0011 to 0.0068; 68% of families rebuilt better): a small but clear gain.
The neural network is about as accurate but does not beat the chosen deviation (difference -0.0023, 95% interval over families -0.0050 to +0.0003). It would have been kept only if it won, so it is not used. For the noise cluster no deviation helps: the typical schedule alone rebuilds its schedules best (RMSE 0.511) — another reason to leave it out.

10.4 Step 3 — the model
The chosen deviation is estimated once more, on all country-years of the non-noise regimes, around chapter 06’s typical schedule. The result, the artefact trajectories, holds everything a later chapter needs to generate a schedule: the e₀ grid, the typical core, each regime’s deviation on the grid, the regimes’ supports and the bases (see the end of the chapter).


The model on all data (cached artefact trajectories)
def _model():
    positions = tr.deviation_positions(fidx, U_sex.shape[1], sex_level=SEX)
    typical_core = clusters_art["conditional_mean"]["core"]
    # Residuals from the typical schedule's LOWESS values at the data, as in the hold-out (chapter 06's
    # grid curve is that LOWESS interpolated; the two differ by at most 0.02).
    typical_at, _ = clus.conditional_mean(e0, G_obs, grid=grid, **TYPICAL)
    R_all = clus.cores_to_features(G_obs, positions) - clus.cores_to_features(typical_at, positions)
    dev, support = tr.estimate_deviation(R_all, e0, labels, family, REGIMES, grid, CHOSEN,
                                         iterations=PF["conditional_iterations"],
                                         delta_share=PF["conditional_delta"],
                                         support_quantiles=PT["support_quantiles"])
    model = tr.build_model(grid, typical_core, dev, support, REGIMES, positions, U_sex, U_age, CHOSEN["kind"])
    return {**model, "candidate": BEST, "holdout_rmse": pooled.to_frame("rmse").reset_index()}


model = artifacts.stage(
    "trajectories", _model, inputs=["clustering", "tucker", "populations", "trajectories_holdout"],
    params={"chosen": CHOSEN, "support": PT["support_quantiles"], "typical": TYPICAL},
    code=[_model, tr, clus, mnn],
    desc="Typical schedule plus regime deviations: generates a schedule for any regime at any e0")
support = {k: model["support"][i] for i, k in enumerate(REGIMES)}
latex.report("trajSupportLowerPct", 100 * PT["support_quantiles"][0], digits=0,
             desc="Quantile (percent) of the members' e0 at the lower end of a regime's support")
latex.report("trajSupportUpperPct", 100 * PT["support_quantiles"][1], digits=0,
             desc="Quantile (percent) of the members' e0 at the upper end of a regime's support")
for k in REGIMES:
    latex.report(f"trajSupportLow{WORDS[k]}", float(support[k][0]), digits=1,
                 desc=f"Lower end of the e0 support of {cname(k).lower()}")
    latex.report(f"trajSupportHigh{WORDS[k]}", float(support[k][1]), digits=1,
                 desc=f"Upper end of the e0 support of {cname(k).lower()}")
