For each regime, the generated schedules at its members’ own e₀ — before calibration, how far their e₀ is from the target; after it, their female and male e₀ — against the members’ observed female and male e₀ (both averaged over the members). This is an in-sample check: the deviations were estimated from these members; the out-of-sample evidence is the hold-out of Step 2.


Table: generated against observed, at each member’s own e0
rows = []
for k in REGIMES:
    m = np.flatnonzero(labels == k)
    e0_fm = tr.sex_e0(tr.generate(model, k, e0[m], bracket=BRACKET))           # (n_k, S)
    gap_k = tr.uncalibrated_e0_gap(model, k, e0[m])
    rows.append({"Cluster": k + 1, "Country-years": int(m.size),
                 r"Support ($e_0$)": f"{support[k][0]:.1f}--{support[k][1]:.1f}",
                 r"Mean $|\Delta e_0|$ before calibration": float(np.abs(gap_k).mean()),
                 r"Female $e_0$": float(e0_fm[:, 0].mean()), r"Male $e_0$": float(e0_fm[:, 1].mean()),
                 r"Observed female $e_0$": float(e0_sex[m, 0].mean()),
                 r"Observed male $e_0$": float(e0_sex[m, 1].mean())})
verify = pd.DataFrame(rows)
verify["gap error"] = ((verify[r"Female $e_0$"] - verify[r"Male $e_0$"])
                       - (verify[r"Observed female $e_0$"] - verify[r"Observed male $e_0$"]))

# The same, for the chosen deviation estimated with the other treatment of the sex level (how much it matters).
other_pos = tr.deviation_positions(fidx, U_sex.shape[1], sex_level=not SEX)
typical_at_data, _ = clus.conditional_mean(e0, G_obs, grid=grid, **TYPICAL)
R_other = clus.cores_to_features(G_obs, other_pos) - clus.cores_to_features(typical_at_data, other_pos)
dev_o, sup_o = tr.estimate_deviation(R_other, e0, labels, family, REGIMES, grid, CHOSEN,
                                     iterations=PF["conditional_iterations"], delta_share=PF["conditional_delta"],
                                     support_quantiles=PT["support_quantiles"])
other_model = tr.build_model(grid, model["typical"], dev_o, sup_o, REGIMES, other_pos, U_sex, U_age, CHOSEN["kind"])
gap_error_other = {}
for k in REGIMES:
    m = np.flatnonzero(labels == k)
    e0_fm = tr.sex_e0(tr.generate(other_model, k, e0[m], bracket=BRACKET))
    gap_error_other[k] = float((e0_fm[:, 0] - e0_fm[:, 1]).mean() - (e0_sex[m, 0] - e0_sex[m, 1]).mean())
print("Sex-gap error (generated − observed, years) with the chosen positions:",
      dict(zip(verify["Cluster"], verify["gap error"].round(2))), "; with the other treatment of the sex level:",
      {k + 1: round(v, 2) for k, v in gap_error_other.items()})
VERIFY_HEAD = {"Cluster": "Regime", "Country-years": "Country-\nyears", r"Support ($e_0$)": "Support\n($e_0$)",
               r"Mean $|\Delta e_0|$ before calibration": "Mean $|\\Delta e_0|$\nbefore calibration",
               "Female $e_0$": "Generated $e_0$: Female", "Male $e_0$": "Generated $e_0$: Male",
               "Observed female $e_0$": "Observed $e_0$: Female", "Observed male $e_0$": "Observed $e_0$: Male"}
verify_tex = verify.drop(columns="gap error").rename(columns=VERIFY_HEAD)
latex.save_table(
    verify_tex, "tbl-s6-recon-verification",
    "The generated schedules of each regime at its members' own $e_0$, against the members' observed "
    "schedules (means over the members).  \\emph{Support}: the "
    f"{100 * PT['support_quantiles'][0]:.0f}--{100 * PT['support_quantiles'][1]:.0f}\\% range of the members' "
    "$e_0$, outside which the deviation is held constant.  $|\\Delta e_0|$: the distance between the $e_0$ "
    "of the uncalibrated schedule (typical core plus deviation) and the target, in years; after "
    "calibration the sex-average $e_0$ equals the target, so the generated and observed female and male "

10.6 Step 5 — the sex differential along the trajectories
The female and male schedules are generated together, so the sex differential along a trajectory comes from the data, not from an assumption: the typical schedule carries the sex differential observed at each level of mortality, and each regime adds its own: its deviation includes the sex contrast of the level column, so the overall difference between female and male mortality is the regime’s, not the typical one.

section: 10.7 Step 6 — does the age pattern of decline rotate?
text:
10.7 Step 6 — does the age pattern of decline rotate?
Paper §5.2 motivates the trajectories by the rotation of mortality decline — as e₀ rises, gains shift from young to old ages — and §5.4 measures it. We examine it along the typical schedule in two ways (mdmx.trajectories.age_contributions): the slope of logit(\(q_x\)) per year of e₀ at three levels — the paper’s measure — and the share of a gain in e₀ that comes from each age group, from the exact derivative of e₀ with respect to logit(\(q_x\)) times that slope. Both use central differences over ±2.5 years of e₀, wide enough not to follow the small irregularities of the typical schedule (chapter 06’s short smoothing span follows the mix of populations observed at each level); over such a step the shares are rescaled to add up to one.


Slopes of logit(q_x) and age shares of e0 gains along the typical schedule
h_rot = PT["rotation_step"]
lev = np.asarray(PT["rotation_e0"], dtype=float)
slope, _ = tr.age_contributions(model, None, lev, bracket=BRACKET, h=h_rot)                  # (L, S, A)
x_rot = curve_x(x_typ[0] + h_rot, x_typ[-1] - h_rot)
_, share_rot = tr.age_contributions(model, None, x_rot, bracket=BRACKET, h=h_rot, normalise=True)  # (q, S, A)
starts = PT["age_groups"]
groups = [(a, b) for a, b in zip(starts, starts[1:] + [len(ages)], strict=True)]
if PT["young_below"] not in starts or PT["old_from"] not in starts:
    raise ValueError("young_below and old_from must be first ages of age groups (age_groups).")
share_grp = np.stack([share_rot[:, :, a:b].sum(axis=(1, 2)) for a, b in groups], axis=1)   # (q, G)
young = share_grp[:, [b <= PT["young_below"] for a, b in groups]].sum(axis=1)
old = share_grp[:, [a >= PT["old_from"] for a, b in groups]].sum(axis=1)
at = [int(np.argmin(np.abs(x_rot - v))) for v in lev]
print(pd.DataFrame(share_grp[at], index=[f"e0 {v:g}" for v in lev], columns=PT["age_group_labels"]).round(3).to_string())
a_hi, a_lo = PT["slope_ratio_ages"]
s_avg = slope.mean(axis=1)                                                               # (L, A) sex average
ratio = s_avg[:, a_hi] / s_avg[:, a_lo]                                                  # (L,)
ad_lo, ad_hi = PT["adult_ages"]
adult = s_avg[:, ad_lo:ad_hi + 1].mean(axis=1) / s_avg[:, a_lo]                          # (L,)
print(f"Slope at age {a_hi} relative to age {a_lo}, by level:", np.round(ratio, 2).tolist())
print(f"Mean slope at ages {ad_lo}–{ad_hi} relative to age {a_lo}, by level:", np.round(adult, 2).tolist())
for i, word in ((0, "Low"), (len(lev) // 2, "Mid"), (len(lev) - 1, "High")):
    v = f"{lev[i]:g}"
    latex.report(f"trajShareYoung{word}", 100 * young[at[i]], digits=0,
                 desc=f"Percent of an e0 gain from ages below {PT['young_below']} at e0 = {v}")
    latex.report(f"trajShareOld{word}", 100 * old[at[i]], digits=0,
                 desc=f"Percent of an e0 gain from ages {PT['old_from']} and over at e0 = {v}")
    latex.report(f"trajSlopeRatio{word}", float(ratio[i]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Slope of logit qx at age {a_hi} relative to age {a_lo} along the typical schedule at e0 = {v}")
    latex.report(f"trajAdultRatio{word}", float(adult[i]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Mean slope of logit qx at ages {ad_lo}-{ad_hi} relative to age {a_lo} at e0 = {v}")
    latex.report(f"trajRotation{word}", lev[i], digits=0, desc=f"{word} e0 level of the rotation analysis")
latex.report("trajRotationStep", h_rot, digits=1,
             desc="Half-width (years of e0) of the central differences of the rotation analysis")

Measured as the paper does — the slope of logit(\(q_x\)) per year of e₀ — mortality at ages 50–70 falls 0.53, 0.17, 0.80 times as fast as at age 0 at e₀ = 45, 65, 80 (at age 85: 0.08, 0.09, 0.61 times): between e₀ = 45 and 65 the decline moves towards the young ages; between e₀ = 65 and 80 the decline moves towards the older ages. Where the gains in life expectancy come from does rotate: at e₀ = 45, 65, 80 the shares from ages below 15 are 68, 59, 6% and from ages 65 and over 4, 6, 58%, most of the shift happening between e₀ = 65 and 80. The rotation is therefore supported for the sources of gains in e₀; the age pattern of the decline itself does not move steadily towards older ages.

text:
10.8 Step 7 — from a schedule back to its regime and e₀
Chapter 09 fits model schedules to data, which needs the inverse of the generator (paper §5.1; the results below are in the companion only): the regime and e₀ whose generated schedule is closest to a given schedule (mdmx.trajectories.invert: for each regime, a search over e₀ for the smallest RMSE of logit(\(q_x\)), then the best regime). A random sample of 400 observed country-years of the non-noise regimes shows how well this recovers their regime and e₀. It is an in-sample check: the model and the regime labels were estimated from these same schedules.


Invert a sample of observed schedules (cached)
def _invert():
    pool = np.flatnonzero(np.isin(labels, REGIMES))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(PT["invert_seed"])
    sample = np.sort(rng.choice(pool, size=min(PT["invert_sample"], pool.size), replace=False))
    rows = []
    for i in sample:
        found = tr.invert(z_obs[i], model, bracket=BRACKET, step=PT["invert_step"])
        rows.append({"row": int(i), "regime": int(labels[i]), "found": found["regime"],
                     "e0": float(e0[i]), "e0_found": found["e0"], "rmse": found["rmse"]})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


inv = artifacts.stage(
    "trajectories_inversion", _invert, inputs=["clustering", "tucker", "tensor", "trajectories"],
    params={"sample": PT["invert_sample"], "seed": PT["invert_seed"], "step": PT["invert_step"],
            "bracket": BRACKET, "regimes": REGIMES},
    code=[_invert, tr, clus, lifetable],
    desc="Regime and e0 recovered from a sample of observed schedules")
pool_all = np.isin(labels, REGIMES)
agree = float(np.mean(inv["found"] == inv["regime"]))
chance = float(np.max(np.bincount(labels[pool_all]) / pool_all.sum()))
e0_err = inv["e0_found"] - inv["e0"]
print(pd.crosstab(inv["regime"] + 1, inv["found"] + 1, rownames=["labelled"], colnames=["recovered"]))
print(f"\nRegime recovered for {100 * agree:.0f}% (largest regime's share: {100 * chance:.0f}%); "
      f"e0 error mean {e0_err.mean():+.2f}, mean absolute {e0_err.abs().mean():.2f} years")
latex.report("trajInvertAgree", 100 * agree, digits=0, desc="Percent of sampled schedules whose regime is recovered by inversion")
latex.report("trajInvertChance", 100 * chance, digits=0, desc="Share of the largest regime among non-noise country-years (percent)")

The regime is recovered for 68% of the sampled schedules, against 36% for always guessing the largest regime. The regimes are summaries of a continuum of deviation patterns (chapter 06), so a single schedule’s regime can be ambiguous. The e₀ of the best-matching generated schedule differs from the schedule’s own e₀ by 0.75 years on average: the closest schedule in logit(\(q_x\)) is not always the one with the same life expectancy. Whether a fit should match the schedule or fix e₀ to the data’s is a question for chapter 09.

title: 11  Exceptional mortality
text:
11.1 What this chapter does
The decomposition and the regimes describe the slow, secular change of mortality. Wars and epidemics are short, sharp departures from it, so the country-years they affect were set aside (chapter d4) and are modelled here. Paper §6 writes an exceptional country-year as
\[
y_{s,a,c,t} \;=\; \hat y_{s,a,c,t} + \lambda_{c,t}\,\delta_{d,s,a},
\]
its baseline \(\hat y\) — the schedule it would have had without the event — plus a disruption: the profile \(\boldsymbol\delta_d\) of the event’s type \(d\) (a unit vector over sex and age) scaled by an intensity \(\lambda_{c,t}\). Everything rests on the baseline, which is never observed. The chapter chooses it by asking which candidate best recovers schedules we do know, then estimates the profiles and intensities, checks how well one profile per type describes the events, and shows what a disruption does to life expectancy.

section: 11.3 Step 2 — the baseline, chosen on pseudo-events
text:
11.3 Step 2 — the baseline, chosen on pseudo-events
The baseline of an exceptional year is the schedule the population would have had without the event. The candidates (paper §6.1; the first two never read the exceptional year’s own schedule):

temporal interpolation of the population’s effective cores (paper §6.1) — linear between the nearest observed years on either side (at a series end either carrying the last core or extending a 10-year trend), or a local-linear smoother in calendar year over ±5, ±10, ±20 years;
the neural core (a reference candidate, not in the paper): a network from the country’s loading and nine features of calendar year to the core, trained on the observed country-years, with early stopping on whole held-out calendar years;
the naïve projection (paper §6.1): the schedule in the population’s slice of the completion model closest to the observed exceptional schedule;
the penalised projection (paper §6.1, Eq. 15): the same, pulled towards an interpolation with weight α (one of 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100). As α grows it tends to the projection of the interpolation onto that slice, not to the interpolation itself;
the completion model of chapter 04, for reference.

To compare them on schedules whose truth is known, every event is moved, as one block across all its populations, to the normal years just beyond its own span on each side (mdmx.disruption.pseudo_events). Those pseudo-events are hidden from every candidate; a spell with data on one side only keeps that property, and an event that hits every population leaves no population observed in the shifted year either. A normal year that chapter d5 pooled with its neighbours is not used: they carry its deaths, which the neighbours of a real exceptional year never do. The completion model and the neural core are refitted without the hidden years. Each pseudo-event then receives the residual of a real exceptional country-year of the same type from another population family (mdmx.disruption.inject; the residuals come from linear interpolation), and every candidate estimates the baseline from the disrupted schedule. The score is the RMSE of logit(\(q_x\)) between the estimate and the clean schedule, over both sexes and all ages. The rule, fixed before the run: the candidate with the lowest pooled RMSE over the injected pseudo-events is used. The same candidates are also scored without injection, for comparison.


The pseudo-event hold-out (cached; about a minute)

for rule in PE["end_rules"]:

def cand_label(name):
    spec = SPECS[name]
    if spec["kind"] == "linear":
        return f"Linear interpolation ({'carry' if spec['end_rule'] == 'carry' else 'trend'} at ends)"
    if spec["kind"] == "local":
        return f"Local-linear in year, $\\pm${spec['window']:g} y"
    if spec["kind"] == "penalized":
        return f"Penalised projection, $\\alpha = {spec['alpha']:g}$"
    return {"projection": "Na\\\"{\\i}ve projection", "neural": "Neural core",
            "completion": "Completion model (\\cref{sec:preprocessing:imputation})"}[spec["kind"]]


def short_label(name):
    """cand_label without LaTeX, for axis labels."""
    return (cand_label(name).replace("$\\pm$", "±").replace("$\\alpha = ", "α = ").replace("$", "")
            .replace('Na\\"{\\i}ve', "Naïve").replace(" (\\cref{sec:preprocessing:imputation})", ""))


def plain_label(name):
    """A candidate's name for the book's prose."""
    spec = SPECS[name]
    if spec["kind"] == "linear":
        return ("linear interpolation with the last core carried at a series end" if spec["end_rule"] == "carry"
                else "linear interpolation with a trend extended at a series end")
    if spec["kind"] == "local":
        return f"local-linear interpolation over ±{spec['window']:g} years"
    if spec["kind"] == "penalized":
        return f"penalised projection with α = {spec['alpha']:g}"
    return {"projection": "naïve projection", "neural": "neural core", "completion": "completion model"}[spec["kind"]]

Figure 11.1: Baseline candidates on pseudo-events. Left: RMSE of logit(q_x) without (open) and with (filled) an injected real disruption; the naïve projection is accurate on clean years but absorbs a disruption. Right: the penalised projection as its weight α grows, against the interpolation it is pulled towards (dashed).





On clean pseudo-events the projections, which read the year’s own schedule, do well — the naïve projection has RMSE 0.119, ahead of every interpolation (best 0.140) — because that schedule here is the baseline. With a real disruption added its error grows 2.0-fold, to 0.235 — it absorbs part of the disruption, exactly the bias paper §6.1 describes — and its e₀ error reaches 1.60 years. A hold-out on clean years alone would have chosen the penalised projection with α = 0.3 (0.116), which with a disruption scores 0.194. The completion model is far off (0.323, and 0.365 for the pandemic years, in which no population is observed), and the neural core (0.194) cannot follow a population’s own trend from smooth functions of calendar year; it is not used. The chosen baseline is the penalised projection with α = 10 towards linear interpolation with the last core carried at a series end, with RMSE 0.138 and e₀ MAE 0.81 years. Its edge over local-linear interpolation over ±10 years (0.140) is small: −0.0015, 95 % family-bootstrap interval −0.0062 to +0.0028 (which includes zero), and it was picked as the best of 36 candidates, so its own score is slightly optimistic. On e₀ it ranks lower: its mean absolute error (0.81 years) is above that of linear interpolation with the last core carried at a series end (0.74), linear interpolation with a trend extended at a series end (0.76), local-linear interpolation over ±5 years (0.79), local-linear interpolation over ±10 years (0.81). It absorbs a little of a disruption: its mean e₀ error is −0.04 years with an injected disruption against +0.04 without — small next to the losses of several years that the events cause. Where a spell has data on one side only the error is larger (0.156): the baselines of COVID-19 at the end of a series are extrapolations.

11.4 Step 3 — baselines and residuals of the exceptional years
The chosen candidate is applied to every exceptional country-year, using all observed years (and the completion model of chapter 04, fitted without the exceptional years). The residual is the observed minus the baseline logit(\(q_x\)) (paper §6.2). A cell is left out when its observed \(q_x\) was zero (floored) or when the deaths expected under the linear interpolation — HMD exposure × its death rate — are below 5; the second rule removes the upward bias of keeping only the small cells that happened to have deaths, without looking at the deaths themselves.

Why the second rule is needed: exceptional years are never pooled (chapter d5), so small populations have cells with no deaths or only one or two. 11.5 Step 4 — profiles and intensities
The profile of a type is its mean residual scaled to unit length (paper §6.3), smoothed along age by a Savitzky–Golay filter (window 11 ages, degree 3) for each sex with the end ages kept, and rescaled. The type “other” (6 country-years of famine, measles and smallpox) is too heterogeneous for a profile; its years keep their residuals. The intensity of a country-year is the least-squares coefficient of its residual on its type’s profile (paper §6.3), over the cells not left out.


Profiles, intensities, explained fractions and the null band
def smooth(delta):
    return ds.sg_smooth(delta, window=PP["sg_window"], poly=PP["sg_poly"])


raw, prof, n_empty = {}, {}, {}
for d in PROFILE_TYPES:
    raw[d], n_empty[d] = ds.profile(R[types == d])
    prof[d] = smooth(raw[d])
lam = np.full(n_exc, np.nan)
fit = np.zeros_like(R)
for d in PROFILE_TYPES:
    m = types == d
    lam[m] = ds.intensities(R[m], prof[d])
    fit[m] = lam[m, None, None] * prof[d]
expl_row = np.full(n_exc, np.nan)
expl = {}
for d in PROFILE_TYPES:
    m = types == d
    expl_row[m], expl[d] = ds.explained_fraction(R[m], fit[m])

# The null band: intensities of the clean pseudo-events (true intensity 0) under the chosen baseline.

The war profile is concentrated in young men, peaking at age 22, with a much smaller and flatter excess for women. The respiratory profile is broad and irregular: it averages pandemics with opposite age patterns (Step 5). Its female half keeps an excess at ages 5–14 (peak at 14), but this one is genuine: it comes from the Spanish influenza 1918–1920 (mean residual of girls +0.27), the other pandemics being within ±0.04. The enteric profile is raised over childhood and adult ages, peaking at 36 (women) and 36 (men), not concentrated in infants and young children as cholera would suggest. Smoothing changes the profiles little — cosines of raw and smoothed 0.998 (war), 0.967 (respiratory) and 0.982 (enteric) — but the cosine exceeds 0.99 only for war, not for respiratory and enteric.
The null bands are wide — an intensity must exceed +1.08 for a war, +0.91 for a respiratory and +2.20 for an enteric pandemic to stand out from the year-to-year noise of a baseline. Of the 138 negative intensities only 17 fall below their band: almost all are country-years whose event left no detectable mark, not deficits. That is common: 101 of 190 war country-years and 59 of 308 respiratory ones lie above the band. By event (table above), the influenza pandemics of 1889–90, 1957–58 and 1968–69 barely register at annual resolution; 1918 and the World Wars do. The Boer and Korean Wars — expeditionary wars fought far from home — have a median intensity of 0.37 and no country-year above the band; leaving them out changes the war profile very little (cosine 0.9984).

11.6 Step 5 — one profile per type, per event, or per sub-cluster?
Step 4 estimates a single profile per type. The heatmaps suggest that events of one type differ, and Ward sub-clusters of the residuals are one way to capture it. Three alternatives are compared, each estimated without the population family it is scored on (mdmx.disruption.holdout_heterogeneity): (a) one profile per type; (b) one profile per historical event — the dictionary entries grouped into wars and pandemics (World War I, World War II, 1918, COVID-19, the cholera pandemics, …) — where the event has at least 10 country-years in the training families, the type’s profile otherwise; (c) Ward sub-clusters (PCA to at most 20 components, the first 10 clustered, K from 2–7 by silhouette, sub-clusters of at least 5), with a held-out country-year fitted by whichever sub-profile fits it best — a choice made with the held-out residual itself, which favours (c). The score is the pooled explained share of the held-out residuals’ sum of squares.


Held-out comparison of the three alternatives (cached; under a minute)
HSET = {"profile_types": PROFILE_TYPES, "min_event_n": PH["min_event_n"], "sg_window": PP["sg_window"],
        "sg_poly": PP["sg_poly"], "k_range": PH["k_range"], "min_size": PH["min_size"],
        "max_pca": PH["max_pca"], "n_use": PH["n_use"]}


def _heterogeneity():
    scores_, prof_ = ds.holdout_heterogeneity(R, types, groups, families, HSET)
    labels_ = {str(d): ds.ward_subclusters(R[types == d], k_range=HSET["k_range"], min_size=HSET["min_size"],
                                           max_pca=HSET["max_pca"], n_use=HSET["n_use"])[0] for d in PROFILE_TYPES}
    return {"scores": scores_, "sub_labels": labels_,
            "profiles": {"type": {str(k): v for k, v in prof_["type"].items()}, "group": prof_["group"],
                         "sub": {str(k): v for k, v in prof_["sub"].items()}}}


# The residuals are computed in this chapter, so their content (not just the input artefacts) keys the cache.
het = artifacts.stage("disruption_heterogeneity", _heterogeneity, inputs=["disruption_holdout"],
                      params={"settings": HSET, "data": artifacts.content_hash(
                          {"R": R, "types": types, "groups": groups, "families": families})},
                      code=[_heterogeneity, ds, clus.ward_clustering],
                      desc="One profile per type, per event or per Ward sub-cluster, scored on held-out population families")

                         desc=f"Percent explained ({samp}), {alt} profiles, {TYPES[d]}")
latex.report("excMinEventN", PH["min_event_n"], desc="Country-years an event needs for a profile of its own")
for d in PROFILE_TYPES:
    latex.report(f"excKSub{WORD[d]}", K_SUB[d], desc=f"Number of Ward sub-clusters, {TYPES[d]} (all data)")
_ks = [int(K_SUB[d]) for d in PROFILE_TYPES]
latex.report("excKSubText", "/".join(map(str, _ks)),
             text=(f"{latex.number_word(_ks[0]).lower()} sub-clusters in each type" if len(set(_ks)) == 1
                   else ", ".join(map(str, _ks[:-1])) + f" and {_ks[-1]} sub-clusters for "
                   + ", ".join(TYPES[d] for d in PROFILE_TYPES[:-1]) + f" and {TYPES[PROFILE_TYPES[-1]]}"),
             desc="The numbers of Ward sub-clusters of the types, as words")
# What Ward's sub-clusters separate: their events, their intensities, and how different their profiles are.
sub_lab = {int(k): v for k, v in het["sub_labels"].items()}
sub_rows = []
for d in PROFILE_TYPES:

                         "years": f"{years[ti[mk]].min()}–{years[ti[mk]].max()}",
                         "main events": ", ".join(f"{group_name(g)} {c}" for g, c in top.head(3).items()),
                         "cos with sub-cluster 1": cos(subs[k], subs[0])})
sub_tab = pd.DataFrame(sub_rows)
print(sub_tab.round(3).to_string(index=False))
small = sub_tab.loc[sub_tab.groupby("type")["n"].idxmin()].set_index("type")
large = sub_tab.loc[sub_tab.groupby("type")["n"].idxmax()].set_index("type")
for d in PROFILE_TYPES:
    t_ = TYPES[d]
    latex.report(f"excSubLamSmall{WORD[d]}", float(small.loc[t_, "median λ"]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Median intensity of the smaller Ward sub-cluster, {t_}")
    latex.report(f"excSubLamLarge{WORD[d]}", float(large.loc[t_, "median λ"]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Median intensity of the larger Ward sub-cluster, {t_}")
    latex.report(f"excSubCos{WORD[d]}", float(cos(*het["profiles"]["sub"][str(d)][:2])) if K_SUB[d] > 1 else 1.0,
                 digits=3, desc=f"Cosine of the first two Ward sub-cluster profiles, {t_}")
latex.report("excGainEventResp", float(contrib.loc[2, "event"]), digits=1,
             desc="Points of the held-out gain of per-event profiles contributed by respiratory pandemics")
latex.report("excGainEventAll", float(contrib["event"].sum()), digits=1, desc="Held-out gain of per-event profiles (points)")
latex.report("excGainSubResp", float(contrib.loc[2, "subcluster"]), digits=1,
             desc="Points of the held-out gain of Ward sub-profiles contributed by respiratory pandemics")
latex.report("excGainSubWar", float(contrib.loc[1, "subcluster"]), digits=1,
             desc="Points of the held-out gain of Ward sub-profiles contributed by wars")
latex.report("excGainSubAll", float(contrib["subcluster"].sum()), digits=1, desc="Held-out gain of Ward sub-profiles (points)")
for w, g in PFIG["quoted_events"].items():
    if g not in het["profiles"]["group"]:

    pg = het["profiles"]["group"][g]

        latex.report(f"excPeak{w}{sx}", int(ages[np.argmax(pg[s])]),
                     desc=f"Age at the peak of the {EVENT_NAME[g]} profile, {sx.lower()}s")

Figure 11.10: Ward sub-cluster profiles within each type (all data): female (top) and male (bottom); the grey line is the type’s profile. The legend gives each sub-cluster’s size and the range of its years.





Held out, one profile per type explains 53 % of the residuals’ sum of squares, per-event profiles 56 % and the best Ward sub-profile 58 % (+3 and +5 percentage points). Weighted by their share of the residuals, respiratory pandemics give 2.6 of the 2.8 points that per-event profiles gain, and 3.4 of the 5.0 that Ward’s sub-profiles gain, wars 1.6. Per type (table): respiratory 19 → 27 (event) and 29 % (Ward); war 72, 73, 75 %; enteric 58, 58, 61 %. The event profiles show why a single respiratory profile does badly: COVID-19’s profile rises with age to peaks at 75 (women) and 67 (men), while the 1918 influenza’s peaks at young adults (28 and 29).
Ward’s method picks K = 2, 2 and 2 for war, respiratory and enteric pandemics, and in each type the smaller sub-cluster holds the most intense country-years (median intensity 7.38, 2.52 and 3.16 against 0.70, 0.20 and 0.19 in the larger; table above). For wars the two sub-profiles are nearly parallel (cosine 0.958): Ward separates the severity of a war, not the shape of its excess, and both sub-clusters mix World War I and II. For respiratory pandemics the shapes differ (cosine 0.195): the small sub-cluster is 21 of the 35 country-years of the Spanish influenza 1918–1920 (median intensity 2.5 against 0.9 for the event’s other country-years) — part of an event, chosen by its size. For enteric pandemics the cosine is 0.723. A held-out country-year is moreover assigned to whichever sub-profile fits it best, a choice made with its own residual, which flatters the sub-clusters. In sample every richer model looks better than it does held out.






NoteThe profiles used



The paper uses one profile per historical event where the event has enough country-years (event_profile in the artefact) and the type’s profile otherwise. Ward sub-clustering is reported here, held out, but is not used: its clusters split severity rather than kind of event, select part of one event, and need a country-year’s own residual to be assigned.

A war and a pandemic in the same year can be represented by two terms that act additively on the log-odds, a property of the model shown in the companion only. Only 6 country-years carry both a war and a pandemic — 1918 in the belligerents with data — so the test is small. Adding the respiratory profile raises the held-out explained share from 86 % to 88 % (+2 points). A second non-negative term can only fit better on the data it is fitted to; what matters is whether the gain is large and the intensities plausible (table above). The composite equation is kept as a property of the model, and this test is consistent with it but weak.

At its median positive intensity a war costs men 1.8 years of e₀ and women 0.7; a respiratory pandemic 0.4 and 0.3; an enteric one 0.6 and 0.5. Because the disruption adds to the logit, the same λ·δ can be applied to any baseline — the model’s baseline independence — but how much e₀ it costs depends on the baseline: the same log-odds ratio removes more years where mortality at the affected ages is higher.

11  Exceptional mortality

title: 12  Life-table fitting
text:
12.1 What this chapter does
The previous chapters build a model that generates a schedule: a regime \(k\), a life expectancy \(e_0^*\) (chapter 07) and, optionally, a disruption of profile \(\delta_h\) and intensity \(\lambda\) (chapter 08):
\[
\mathbf y = \mathbf z_k(e_0^*) + \lambda\,\boldsymbol\delta_h + \boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad \lambda \ge 0 .
\]
Paper §7 runs the model backwards: given one schedule and nothing else — no country, no year — which regime and \(e_0^*\) describe it, and does it carry a disruption? The chapter fits every observed schedule this way, with a generator and profiles built without the schedule’s own population family, and measures how often the fitter is right.
crumbs: Part II — Analysis (one chapter per paper section)

title: 12  Life-table fitting
text:
12.2 Step 1 — the fit
For a schedule \(\mathbf y\), regime \(k\) and hypothesis \(h\) (none, or one of the profiles), the fitter minimises the residual sum of squares over the cells it uses,
\[
\mathrm{RSS}_{k,h}(e_0) = \sum_{\text{cells}} \bigl(y - z_k(e_0) - \hat\lambda\,\delta_h\bigr)^2,
\qquad \hat\lambda = \max\!\Bigl(0, \frac{\boldsymbol\delta_h^\top(\mathbf y - \mathbf z_k)}{\boldsymbol\delta_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_h}\Bigr),
\]
over a grid of e₀ 0.1 years apart (each regime’s schedules on the grid are computed once), refined between grid points by a parabola (mdmx.fitting.fit_many). Each fit is turned into a Laplace approximation of its log evidence with a half-normal prior on \(\lambda\) (mdmx.fitting.laplace_log_bf):
\[
\log \mathrm{BF}_{k,h} = \tfrac p2 \log\frac{\mathrm{RSS}_{k,0}}{\mathrm{RSS}_{k,h}}
+ \log\frac{2}{\sigma_h\sqrt{2\pi}} - \frac{\hat\lambda^2}{2\sigma_h^2}
+ \tfrac12\log 2\pi - \tfrac12 \log I_h,
\qquad I_h = \frac{\boldsymbol\delta_h^\top\boldsymbol\delta_h}{\mathrm{RSS}_{k,h}/p},
\]
where \(p\) is the number of cells used, \(\sigma_h\) is the prior scale of hypothesis \(h\) (the root mean square of the positive intensities, measured as in chapter 08, of its training country-years), \(\mathrm{RSS}_{k,0}\) is the null model’s own minimum over e₀, and \(\log 2\) is subtracted when \(\hat\lambda = 0\) (the maximum on the boundary). The second term, the prior’s normalising constant, makes a wider prior cost evidence. The best pair over all regimes and hypotheses is the fit; the score of a schedule is the log Bayes factor of its best disrupted fit against its best undisrupted one. Floored cells are always left out; when the exposures are known (as here) the schedule is fitted again without the cells whose deaths expected under its first undisrupted fit are fewer than 5. This is chapter 08’s rule, with its threshold. Only the baseline differs: chapter 08 interpolates the population’s neighbouring years, whereas a single schedule handed to the fitter has none, so its own first fit without disruption serves. The rule never reads a cell’s deaths, although that baseline depends on the schedule as a whole.
The likelihood treats the 220 cells as independent, which they are not; the score is therefore not a calibrated probability. That is why the decision threshold is set on normal schedules (Step 4) rather than at log BF = 0.

12.3 Step 2 — how far a disruption can be told from a change of e₀
A disruption raises mortality at some ages, and so does a lower e₀. The more a profile resembles the direction in which a regime’s schedule moves as e₀ falls — the trajectory tangent \(\mathbf z'_k\), a central difference in the level \(\xi\) — the harder it is to tell the two apart from one schedule (the article’s §7.2). The table gives, over every regime and e₀ in its support, the cosine \(\cos\vartheta\) of the angle between each profile and the tangent, the share of the profile orthogonal to it, \(\lvert\sin\vartheta\rvert\), and the variance inflation \(1/\sin^2\vartheta\).

text:
12.4 Step 3 — every schedule, fitted out of sample
Whole population families are dealt into 10 folds. For each fold the generator (chapter 07’s chosen deviation, mdmx.fitting.fold_model) is estimated from the other folds’ observed country-years, the profiles and prior scales (fold_profiles) from their exceptional ones, and then every schedule of the fold is fitted (mdmx.fitting.evaluate_folds): 4,056 observed normal schedules and 540 exceptional ones, each under both hypothesis sets — one profile per type, or one per historical event with at least 10 training country-years plus the type profiles (always allowed, since the fitter does not know the event). An event whose training country-years are on average a deficit rather than an excess is not a hypothesis. Each schedule is fitted twice (fit_two_pass): without its exposures (only floored cells left out) and with them (cells with few expected deaths left out too); both procedures are calibrated, so that the app can use either.
Three things are not held out, and are stated here: the sex and age bases of the decomposition (chapter 04) and chapter 06’s regime labels come from all data, and the label “detectable” (Step 4) uses chapter 08’s intensities, whose profiles include the country-year itself. The label is never used to fit anything — it only says which disruptions count as visible.

12.5 Step 4 — the decision, and which hypotheses to test
A schedule is called disrupted when its score exceeds a threshold. For the schedules of each fold, the threshold is the score exceeded by only 5 % of the other folds’ normal schedules (mdmx.fitting.cross_fitted_thresholds). A disruption counts as detectable when chapter 08 measured its intensity above its type’s null band (169 of the 534 exceptional country-years of the three types with a profile; the 6 country-years of type “other” are fitted but not scored). The hypothesis set with the higher detection of detectable disruptions at this budget is used — the rule fixed before the run; a tie goes to the type profiles.


Detection, false positives and accuracy at each operating point, for both hypothesis sets and both procedures
def evaluate(set_name, budget, passes="two"):
    """Metrics and flags of one hypothesis set and procedure at one false-positive budget."""
    f = fits[(fits["set"] == set_name) & (fits["passes"] == passes)]
    nr = f[f["kind"] == "normal"].sort_values("row").reset_index(drop=True)
    ex = f[f["kind"] == "exceptional"].sort_values("row").reset_index(drop=True)
    m, n_flag, e_flag = ft.operating_point(nr, ex, budget, truth=types, detectable=detectable,
                                           profile_types=PTYPES, labels=labels, regimes=REGIMES,
                                           e0_data=e0_obs, e0_base=e0_base_exc)
    return m, n_flag, e_flag, nr, ex

Figure 12.3: What the fitter decides at the false-positive budget (chosen hypothesis set): rows are the truth (normal schedules and the three disruption types), columns the decision; shares of each row, counts in brackets. Left: all schedules, normal ones included; right: detectable disruptions only.





At a budget of 5 % of normal schedules (actually flagged out of fold: 5.4 %), the fitter with type profiles detects 49 % of the detectable disruptions (83 of 169): 59 % of wars (60 of 101), 25 % of respiratory (15 of 59) and 89 % of enteric pandemics (8 of 9). Of all war and pandemic years — many of which left no measurable mark — 19 % are detected. Of the detected detectable ones, 78 % get the right type.
The two hypothesis sets are nearly tied: type profiles detect 83 detectable disruptions and event profiles 81 (2 apart), and their ROC curves cross near the budget (figure), with AUCs of 0.82 and 0.84. The rule, which looks at detection only, chose type profiles. Where the two differ is the type: with type profiles 4 of the 15 detected respiratory disruptions get the right type, with event profiles 13 of 18 — COVID-19 and 1918 have profiles of their own.
Respiratory pandemics are the weak point. Almost all of their detectable years belong to two events (Spanish influenza 1918–1920 28, COVID-19 2020–2022 28), of which the fitter detects 11 of 28, 4 of 28: the type profile averages the young-adult excess of 1918 and the old-age excess of COVID-19 (chapter 08), so neither fits it well. Over the whole range of thresholds the trade-off is smooth (figures): from 30 % detected at 1 % false positives to 56 % at 10 %. Of the 217 normal schedules flagged, 55 % are called enteric — the profile least distinguishable from a change of e₀ (Step 2). The threshold itself is a log Bayes factor of about 49, not 0: the likelihood treats the cells of a schedule as independent and the generator does not fit normal schedules perfectly, so the raw score overstates the evidence.
The normal schedules that set the threshold are the observed ones, whose small populations chapter d5 pooled across neighbouring years at the ages where deaths are rare (639 country-years); raw single-year schedules — exceptional years, or a user’s schedule — are noisier. Pooled normal schedules are flagged at 2.5 %, the others at 5.9 %; the false-positive rate of raw schedules from small populations may be higher than the budget. Without exposures (floored cells left out, no expected-deaths rule) and with its own threshold, the fitter flags 5.2 % of normal schedules and detects 49 % of detectable disruptions.
The fit also recovers the schedule’s level and, less reliably, its regime: for normal schedules the fitted e₀* is 1.05 years from the schedule’s own e₀ on average, and the regime is chapter 06’s for 66 % of them. The regimes are a typology of a continuum (chapter 06), and chapter 06 assigns them by the level-free features of a year’s core while the fitter compares whole schedules, so the two need not agree on schedules near the boundaries. For exceptional years, the fitted baseline e₀* is 1.73 years from chapter 08’s baseline on average, against 2.10 years for a fit without disruption: allowing a disruption brings the estimate of the counterfactual e₀ closer.

title: 13  Predicting schedules from summary indicators
text:
13.1 The task
The previous chapters build mortality schedules from the decomposition. This chapter addresses a different, very practical question (paper §8): given only a summary indicator of mortality, what is the most likely complete schedule? In much of the world, child mortality ₅q₀ — the probability of dying before age 5 — is the only well-measured indicator, sometimes together with adult mortality ₄₅q₁₅, the probability that a 15-year-old dies before age 60. Model life-table systems turn such indicators into full life tables; the best known are Coale–Demeny, the Log-Quad model of Wilmoth et al. (2012) and SVD-Comp (Clark 2019).
MDMx reformulates SVD-Comp in the Tucker framework. Every schedule — the \(2 \times 110\) matrix of \(\operatorname{logit}(q_x)\) for one country-year — is written in the shared sex basis \(\mathbf{S}\) and age basis \(\mathbf{A}\) of chapter 04 as \(\mathcal{M}_{c,t} = \mathbf{S}\,\mathcal{G}_{c,t}\,\mathbf{A}^\top\). Stacking the female and then the male schedule into one vector \(\mathbf{z}\) of length \(2A = 220\), the reconstruction is linear in the core,
\[
\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{R}\,\operatorname{vec}(\mathcal{G}), \qquad
\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{S} \otimes \mathbf{A}_{c}
\qquad\text{(paper Eq. 21)},
\]
where \(\mathbf{A}_{c}\) keeps only the first \(c_{\text{age}}\) columns of the age basis. A small neural network \(f_\theta\) maps the logit of the input indicators to the \(2 c_{\text{age}}\) core weights (paper Eq. 22), trained so that \(\mathbf{R} f_\theta(\cdot)\) — the whole schedule — matches the observed schedule, with extra weight on ages 0–4. Finally, the predicted core weights are moved by (to first order) the smallest amount that makes the schedule reproduce its inputs exactly, as Log-Quad does (paper §8.3, Eq. 23). Two models are fitted (§8.2):
Both predict both sexes at once, so the sex differential comes from one model in one basis.

section: 13.3 Step 2 — the truncated basis, and what truncation alone costs
text:
13.3 Step 2 — the truncated basis, and what truncation alone costs
The network predicts only the first \(c_{\text{age}}\) age components of the \(r_2\) = 50 in the basis. Two arguments favour a small \(c_{\text{age}}\) such as 6 (12 core weights): the higher components describe fine-grained structure that one or two summary indicators cannot be expected to predict, and the first few capture nearly all of the age-specific variance. Both arguments can be checked. For these checks the chapter uses fixed settings, \(c_{\text{age}}\) = 6 and a weight \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 10 on ages 0–4 in the loss (Step 3); the final models’ settings are chosen by nested cross-validation (Step 8).
The second argument depends on what “variance” means. An oracle helps. For every observed schedule, take the core weights that reproduce it as closely as possible in the truncated basis — the least-squares projection (mdmx.svdcomp.truncation_oracle). No predictor of truncated core weights can come closer to the schedule in squared error, so the oracle’s squared error is the price of the truncation alone (in \(e_0\) it is a reference, not a bound). We measure it three ways: the share of the uncentred sum of squares of logit(q_x) captured (what a variance threshold on the decomposition measures, dominated by the overall level of mortality); the share of the variation around the mean schedule captured; and, most interpretably, the error in life expectancy.
The oracle also reveals a side-effect of the loss. The loss of Step 3 up-weights ages 0–4 by \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\); with weights, the best truncated core is the weighted least-squares fit, which buys a closer fit at ages 0–4 at the expense of every other age. We therefore compute the oracle both without weights (\(w_{\mathrm{child}} = 0\)) and with the fixed setting \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 10.0.


Truncation oracle for each c_age, without and with the ages 0–4 weights
cores_obs = sc.project_cores(Z, sc.reconstruction_matrix(U_sex, U_age, PS["c_age"]))
ss_total = np.sum(Z ** 2)
ss_about_mean = np.sum((Z - Z.mean(axis=0)) ** 2)
oracle_rows = []
for c in PS["c_age_grid"]:
    for alpha in PS["alpha_grid"]:
        w = sc.loss_weights(A, alpha, PS["young_ages"])
        Z_orc = sc.truncation_oracle(Z, U_sex, U_age, c, w)
        acc_orc = sc.accuracy_by_sex(Z_orc, Z, A, AGE_GROUPS)
        ss_resid = np.sum((Z_orc - Z) ** 2)
        oracle_rows.append({"c_age": c, "alpha": alpha,
                            "share_uncentred": 1 - ss_resid / ss_total,
                            "share_about_mean": 1 - ss_resid / ss_about_mean,
                            "e0_mae_F": acc_orc.loc["female", "e0_mae"],
                            "e0_mae_M": acc_orc.loc["male", "e0_mae"],
                            "rmse_F": acc_orc.loc["female", "rmse_all"],
                            "rmse_M": acc_orc.loc["male", "rmse_all"]})
oracle = pd.DataFrame(oracle_rows)
orc_main = oracle[(oracle.c_age == PS["c_age"]) & (oracle.alpha == 0)].iloc[0]
orc_fixed = oracle[(oracle.c_age == PS["c_age"]) & (oracle.alpha == PS["alpha"])].iloc[0]

section: 13.4 Step 3 — the network and its training
text:
13.4 Step 3 — the network and its training
The network (mdmx.nn.MLP) has the paper’s architecture: inputs → two hidden layers of 64 ReLU units → a linear output of \(2 c_{\text{age}}\) values. Three design choices make it train reliably:

Inputs are standardised (mdmx.nn.Standardizer) to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, using the training rows only.
Outputs are standardised core weights. The core weights have very different scales: across the observed schedules the first averages 73 (standard deviation 12), whereas the 6th varies around zero with a standard deviation of 0.76. The network predicts each weight in standard-deviation units, and the fixed affine map back to core weights is folded into the reconstruction: \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{R}\,(\text{out} \odot \boldsymbol{\sigma} + \boldsymbol{\mu})\).
The loss is measured on the schedule (mdmx.nn.LinearDecoderLoss): the weighted squared error between \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) and the observed \(\mathbf{z}\), with every cell weighted \(1/(2A)\) and the ten cells at ages 0–4 weighted an extra \(w_{\mathrm{child}}/10\) (the loss of the article’s §8.2).

Training (mdmx.nn.fit_mlp) is mini-batch Adam with weight decay, and early stopping: 10% of the training rows — whole population families, so that validation also measures prediction for unseen populations — are held out, the weights of the epoch with the lowest validation loss are kept, and training stops after 30 epochs without improvement. mdmx.nn is checked by unit tests (tests/test_nn.py): the hand-written gradients agree with finite differences, and training is reproducible from its seed.


How the loss weights divide attention between ages

      f"(ratio {w_fixed[0, 0] / w_fixed[0, 10]:.0f})")

section: 13.5 Step 4 — making the predictions reproduce their inputs
text:
13.5 Step 4 — making the predictions reproduce their inputs
A network trained to minimise a reconstruction loss does not reproduce its inputs exactly: the schedule it predicts for ₅q₀ = 0.05 implies a ₅q₀ near, but not equal to, 0.05. A user who supplies ₅q₀ and ₄₅q₁₅ expects them back — Log-Quad guarantees it by construction — and errors in the indicators propagate into life expectancy. MDMx therefore ends with a correction step (mdmx.svdcomp.enforce_indicators).
Let \(\mathbf{g}_0\) be the network’s core weights for one country-year and \(t_1, \dots, t_m\) its input indicators (\(m = 2\) for Model 1: ₅q₀ of each sex; \(m = 4\) for Model 2: also ₄₅q₁₅ of each sex). For a schedule \(\mathbf{z}\), write \(h_j(\mathbf{z}) = 1 - \prod_{a \in W_j} \bigl(1 -
\operatorname{expit}(z_a)\bigr)\) for the indicator over the ages \(W_j\) of one sex (ages 0–4, or 15–59), and \(f_j(\mathbf{g}) = \operatorname{logit} h_j(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{g}) - \operatorname{logit} t_j\) for its error. Since \(\partial \operatorname{logit} h_j / \partial z_a =
q_a / h_j\) for ages \(a\) in \(W_j\) (and 0 elsewhere), the Jacobian \(\mathbf{J} = \partial \mathbf{f} / \partial \mathbf{g}\) (\(m \times 2c_{\text{age}}\)) is cheap to compute.
The directions. To first order, the smallest change of core weights that removes the errors is \(\Delta\mathbf{g} = -\mathbf{J}^\top(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^\top)^{-1}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{g}_0)\), a combination of the \(m\) columns of \(\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{g}_0)^\top\). Column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{D}\) is the gradient of indicator \(j\) with respect to the schedule, projected onto the truncated basis: the change of schedule that moves indicator \(j\) furthest per unit of change, concentrated in that indicator’s age window as far as the basis allows.
The coefficients. The corrected core weights are
\[
\mathbf{g}^\star = \mathbf{g}_0 + \mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad\text{with } \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^m \text{ solving }
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{g}_0 + \mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \mathbf{0},
\]
\(m\) equations in \(m\) unknowns, solved by Newton’s method from \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0}\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\mu} - \bigl(\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{g})\,\mathbf{D}\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{g})\), halving a step whenever it would not reduce the largest error. The predicted schedule is \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{g}^\star\). Three properties make this the natural choice:

It stays inside the MDMx representation. The correction is a change of core weights, so the corrected schedule is still a combination of the shared sex and age basis functions — smooth across age, and built from the same components for both sexes.
It is (to first order) the smallest possible change to the predicted schedule. The columns of \(\mathbf{R}\) are orthonormal, so \(\lVert \mathbf{g} - \mathbf{g}_0 \rVert\) is exactly the root-sum-of-squares change of the whole logit(q_x) schedule; the directions \(\mathbf{D}\) are those of the smallest change, and the coefficients make the indicators exact rather than approximately right. The predicted age pattern is altered as little as the constraints allow, and only where it must be. (Re-computing the directions at every step would converge to the exactly smallest change, but that iteration can fail when the start is far from the targets; tests/test_svdcomp.py checks that our change is within 5% of the exactly smallest one, and in practice it is within about 1%.)
It respects the sexes. The span of \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{S} \otimes
\mathbf{A}_c\) is “any female schedule in the span of \(\mathbf{A}_c\), and any male schedule in the span of \(\mathbf{A}_c\)”, so the direction of a female indicator alters only the female schedule, and both sexes are corrected in the same age basis.

The directions are fixed at \(\mathbf{g}_0\), so each Newton step solves an \(m \times m\) system per country-year: the correction is vectorised over country-years and takes well under a second for all 4,056 of them. Iteration stops when every \(|\operatorname{logit} h_j - \operatorname{logit} t_j|\) is below 1e-10; a country-year that has not converged after 50 iterations is counted and reported (Step 8). tests/test_svdcomp.py also checks that the inputs are reproduced to machine precision and that a female-only constraint leaves the male schedule untouched.
What does the correction look like? It is a combination of the directions \(\mathbf{D}\): the figure shows, for the mean schedule, the smallest change that raises logit ₅q₀ by 0.1 while keeping ₄₅q₁₅ fixed, and the smallest change that raises logit ₄₅q₁₅ by 0.1 while keeping ₅q₀ fixed. With six components the change is smooth and spreads somewhat beyond the age window (a bump confined to ages 0–4 cannot be built from six smooth curves); with more components it becomes more local. This figure is for the book only.

section: 13.6 Step 5 — cross-validation blocked by population family
text:
13.6 Step 5 — cross-validation blocked by population family
An honest estimate of how well a model predicts a schedule it has not seen must hold out data that are genuinely new. Neighbouring years of the same population are nearly identical, so holding out years at random tests interpolation, not prediction. We hold out whole populations instead — and more than that, whole population families: some HMD series overlap (the United Kingdom contains England & Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland; Germany contains East and West Germany; New Zealand contains its Māori and non-Māori populations), and a model trained on England & Wales has effectively seen the United Kingdom. A family is a population plus every population it contains, read from the population register.
The 41 families are dealt into 10 folds, largest first, each to the fold with the fewest country-years so far (mdmx.svdcomp.assign_folds). Every model — MDMx and the benchmarks — is trained on 9 folds and predicts the remaining one, 10 times; each country-year’s prediction therefore comes from a model that has never seen its population.

13.7 Step 6 — the fixed settings, out of fold, with and without the correction
We first cross-validate the models at the fixed settings of Step 2 (\(c_{\text{age}}\) = 6, \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 10.0), together with the two benchmarks (explained in §Step 9). The MDMx models are trained exactly as the final models are, including early stopping; fold \(k\) uses the seed seed \(+ k\). Every network of the cross-validations is trained in sex and age bases estimated from its own training rows only, so that the held-out populations play no part in the bases either (Step 10 explains why this matters); the final models use the bases of chapter 04. Because the correction is applied after the network, each cross-validation yields both the network’s own schedules (“raw”) and the corrected ones, from the same networks.


Cross-validate the fixed settings and the benchmarks on the same folds (cached; a few minutes)
SETTINGS = sc.model_settings(PS)          # the fixed c_age and alpha (config/params.d/svdcomp.toml)
INPUTS = {"one": ["5q0_F", "5q0_M"], "two": ["5q0_F", "5q0_M", "45q15_F", "45q15_M"]}
OWN_INPUTS = {"one": ["5q0"], "two": ["5q0", "45q15"]}
CV_KEYS = (*sc.MODEL_KEYS, "seed", "n_folds", "fold_seed", "logquad_v_ages",
           "svdcomp_components", "svdcomp_offset")
cv_params = {k: PS[k] for k in CV_KEYS}
# The bases of a fit come from its training rows, with chapter 04's
# smoothing and the age rank held at its value on all the data (as the
# forecasters of chapter 11 hold it at every origin), so that c_age means
# the same in every fold.
BASIS_PARAMS = {"tucker": P.section("tucker"), "age_rank": int(U_age.shape[1])}
_BASES: dict[bytes, tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]] = {}


def train_bases(train):
    """Sex and age bases (2, 2) and (A, r₂) from the rows ``train`` (n,) of Z."""
    key = np.packbits(train).tobytes()
    if key not in _BASES:
        cells = np.zeros_like(observed)
        cells[cell[train, 0], cell[train, 1]] = True
        r2 = BASIS_PARAMS["age_rank"]
        b = tz.sex_age_bases(Mz, cells, tau=P.tucker.tau, age_bounds=(r2, r2))
        U_a, _ = smoothing.smooth_age_basis(b["U_age"], P.tucker.smooth_components,
                                           P.tucker.smooth_rest_sigma, P.tucker.smooth_preserve,
                                           P.tucker.smooth_orth_tol)
        _BASES[key] = (b["U_sex"], U_a)
    return _BASES[key]


S_all, A_all = train_bases(np.ones(len(Z), dtype=bool))
if not (np.allclose(S_all, U_sex, atol=1e-10) and np.allclose(A_all, U_age, atol=1e-10)):
    raise RuntimeError("train_bases on every row does not reproduce chapter 04's bases")


def _cv():
    preds, runs = {}, []
    for key, two in (("one", False), ("two", True)):
        res = sc.cross_validate_core_model(sc.features(ind, INPUTS[key]), Z, inputs=INPUTS[key],
                                           folds=FOLDS, groups=family, settings=SETTINGS,
                                           seed=PS["seed"], basis=train_bases)
        preds[f"paper_{key}"] = res["Z_hat"]
        preds[f"paperraw_{key}"] = res["Z_raw"]
        runs.append(res["runs"].assign(model=f"paper_{key}"))
        for method in ("logquad", "svdcomp"):
            preds[f"{method}_{key}"] = sc.cross_validate_benchmark(method, ind, Z, folds=FOLDS,
                                                                   two_parameter=two, settings=PS)
    # Out-of-fold schedules are stored in single precision (ample for
    # logit(q_x) to six significant digits) to halve the artefact's size.
    return {"Z_hat": {k: v.astype(np.float32) for k, v in preds.items()},
            "runs": pd.concat(runs, ignore_index=True), "folds": FOLDS}


cv = artifacts.stage("svdcomp_cv", _cv, inputs=["tensor", "tucker", "populations"],
                     params={**cv_params, **BASIS_PARAMS}, code=[_cv, train_bases, sc, lq, mnn, tz, smoothing],
                     desc="Out-of-fold schedules: MDMx at the fixed settings (raw, corrected), Log-Quad, SVD-Comp")
if not np.array_equal(cv["folds"], FOLDS):
    raise RuntimeError("stored folds differ from the folds computed now")
oof = {k: v.astype(float) for k, v in cv["Z_hat"].items()}
acc_cv = sc.summarise_accuracy(oof, Z, A, AGE_GROUPS, AB_STARTS)
# The stored method keys "paper_*" and "paperraw_*" are the fixed settings, corrected and raw.
show = acc_cv[acc_cv.method.str.startswith("paper")]
print(show[["method", "sex", "e0_mae", "e0_bias", "rmse_all", "rmse_15_59", "q5_mae", "q45_mae"]].round(3)
      .to_string(index=False))
for key, tag in (("one", "One"), ("two", "Two")):
    for variant, vtag in (("paperraw", "Raw"), ("paper", "Fixed")):
        r = acc_cv[acc_cv.method == f"{variant}_{key}"].set_index("sex")
        for sex, sx in zip(SEXES, "FM", strict=True):
            latex.report(f"svd{vtag}{tag}Ezero{sx}", float(r.loc[sex, "e0_mae"]), digits=2,
                         desc=f"Out-of-fold e0 MAE, fixed settings (c_age = {PS['c_age']}, alpha = "
                              f"{PS['alpha']:g}), {'without' if vtag == 'Raw' else 'with'} "
                              f"the correction, Model {1 if tag == 'One' else 2}, {sex}")

What the correction changes
cv_e0 = acc_cv.pivot_table(index="method", columns="sex", values="e0_mae")
enf_shift = {key: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((oof[f"paper_{key}"] - oof[f"paperraw_{key}"]) ** 2)))

RMS change of logit(q_x) made by the correction: {'one': 0.014, 'two': 0.087}


The correction is small — it changes logit(q_x) by 0.014 (Model 1) and 0.087 (Model 2) in root-mean-square terms — but it matters. For Model 2 it reduces the out-of-fold \(e_0\) error from 1.23 to 0.64 years for females and from 1.30 to 0.61 for males (by 48–53%): the network’s schedules missed the adult-mortality input, and honouring it removes about half of the \(e_0\) error. For Model 1, which has no adult input, the gain is smaller (1.66 → 1.53 and 2.05 → 1.92 years).

13.8 Step 7 — how many age components, and how much weight on ages 0–4?
With all \(r_2\) age components the predicted schedules could be noisy, since the higher-order weights can hardly be predicted from one or two summary indicators (Step 2); the weight \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) on ages 0–4 trades accuracy at those ages against accuracy elsewhere. We repeat the whole cross-validation for \(c_{\text{age}} \in\) [2, 6, 20, 50] and \(w_{\mathrm{child}} \in\) [0.0, 10.0], for both models, recording the accuracy with and without the correction. This describes the trade-offs; it is not how the settings are chosen (that is Step 8), because choosing by these out-of-fold errors and then quoting them would be optimistic.


Cross-validate Models 1 and 2 over c_age × alpha (cached; ten minutes or more)
sweep_params = {**cv_params, "c_age_grid": PS["c_age_grid"], "alpha_grid": PS["alpha_grid"]}


def _sweep():
    rows = []
    for key in ("one", "two"):
        X = sc.features(ind, INPUTS[key])
        for c in PS["c_age_grid"]:
            for alpha in PS["alpha_grid"]:
                res = sc.cross_validate_core_model(
                    X, Z, inputs=INPUTS[key], folds=FOLDS, groups=family,
                    settings=sc.model_settings(PS, c_age=c, alpha=alpha), seed=PS["seed"],
                    basis=train_bases)
                for variant, Z_v in (("corrected", res["Z_hat"]), ("raw", res["Z_raw"])):
                    a = sc.summarise_accuracy({f"mdmx_{key}": Z_v}, Z, A, AGE_GROUPS, AB_STARTS)
                    rows.append(a.assign(c_age=c, alpha=alpha, variant=variant,
                                         at_cap=int((res["runs"]["epochs_run"] == PS["max_epochs"]).sum()),
                                         not_converged=int(res["runs"]["not_converged"].sum())))
    return pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)


sweep = artifacts.stage("svdcomp_sweep", _sweep, inputs=["tensor", "tucker", "populations"],
                        params={**sweep_params, **BASIS_PARAMS},
                        code=[_sweep, train_bases, sc, mnn, tz, smoothing],
                        desc="Out-of-fold accuracy of MDMx Models 1-2 for each c_age and alpha, raw and corrected")

      [["e0_mae", "rmse_all", "rmse_abridged", "q5_mae", "q45_mae"]].mean().reset_index())   # mean of sexes

    no_w_full = d[(d.c_age == c_full) & (d.alpha == a_lo)].iloc[0]
    latex.report(f"svdSweep{tag}NoWeightEzero", float(no_w["e0_mae"]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Out-of-fold e0 MAE, c_age = {PS['c_age']}, alpha = {a_lo:g}, corrected, Model {tag}")
    latex.report(f"svdSweep{tag}NoWeightFullEzero", float(no_w_full["e0_mae"]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Out-of-fold e0 MAE, all age components, alpha = {a_lo:g}, corrected, Model {tag}")
    latex.report(f"svdSweep{tag}FullEzero", float(sweep_full[key]["e0_mae"]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Out-of-fold e0 MAE, all age components, alpha = {PS['alpha']:g}, corrected, Model {tag}")
    latex.report(f"svdSweep{tag}FixedEzero", float(sweep_fixed[key]["e0_mae"]), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Out-of-fold e0 MAE, fixed c_age and alpha ({PS['c_age']}, {PS['alpha']:g}), corrected "

Model 1 (corrected): fixed settings e0 MAE 1.72; all 50 components 1.75;  α=10 minus α=0 by c_age: 2: +0.74, 6: +0.06, 20: +0.06, 50: +0.08
Model 2 (corrected): fixed settings e0 MAE 0.63; all 50 components 0.75;  α=10 minus α=0 by c_age: 2: +0.00, 6: +0.10, 20: +0.26, 50: +0.22


Three things stand out.

A moderate truncation helps a little; predicting all components costs little. With the correction, the out-of-fold \(e_0\) error with \(c_{\text{age}}\) = 6 and with all 50 components is, for Model 1, 1.66 and 1.67 years (\(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 0) and 1.72 and 1.75 (\(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 10); for Model 2, 0.53 and 0.54, and 0.63 and 0.75. With early stopping the network learns small, smooth weights for components it cannot predict, so predicting all of them costs little; only very few components (two) clearly hurt.
The correction does most of the work for Model 2. The gap between the dashed (raw) and solid (corrected) lines is the value of honouring the inputs, and it is largest where the raw network misses ₄₅q₁₅ most.
With the correction, the extra weight on ages 0–4 does not help. Its purpose, reproducing ₅q₀, is served exactly by the correction. For \(c_{\text{age}} \ge\) 6, \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 10 raises the corrected \(e_0\) error of Model 2 by +0.10 to +0.26 years compared with \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 0 (without the correction: +0.49 to +0.57), and that of Model 1 by +0.06 to +0.08 years.

13.9 Step 8 — choosing the settings honestly: nested cross-validation
If \(c_{\text{age}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) were chosen as the best point of Step 7 and that point’s error quoted, the test folds would have helped choose the model that is then judged on them. A nested cross-validation avoids this (mdmx.svdcomp.nested_cross_validate_core_model). For each of the 10 outer folds:

the population families of the nine training folds are dealt into 3 inner folds;
every candidate \((c_{\text{age}}, w_{\mathrm{child}})\) in [6, 20] × [0.0, 10.0] is cross-validated over those inner folds, on training rows only, and scored by the mean (over both sexes) absolute error of \(e_0\) of its corrected predictions;
the best candidate is trained on all training rows of the outer fold and predicts the held-out fold.

The grid and the number of inner folds are kept small (four candidates, three inner folds: about 260 networks); the sweep of Step 7 shows that the omitted values of \(c_{\text{age}}\) would not change the picture. The sex-specific variant used in Step 9 is not tuned separately: in each outer fold it uses the setting chosen for the corresponding two-sex model, a choice that was also made without the test fold.


Nested cross-validation of Models 1 and 2, and the sex-specific variant (cached; the longest step)
GRID = [{"c_age": int(c), "alpha": float(a)} for c in PS["nested_c_age_grid"] for a in PS["nested_alpha_grid"]]
nested_params = {**cv_params, "nested_c_age_grid": PS["nested_c_age_grid"],
                 "nested_alpha_grid": PS["nested_alpha_grid"],
                 "nested_inner_folds": PS["nested_inner_folds"], "nested_inner_seed": PS["nested_inner_seed"]}


def _nested():
    out = {"Z_hat": {}, "runs": [], "inner": [], "fold_settings": {}}
    for key in ("one", "two"):
        res = sc.nested_cross_validate_core_model(
            sc.features(ind, INPUTS[key]), Z, inputs=INPUTS[key], folds=FOLDS, groups=family,
            settings=SETTINGS, grid=GRID, n_inner=PS["nested_inner_folds"],
            inner_seed=PS["nested_inner_seed"], seed=PS["seed"], basis=train_bases)
        out["Z_hat"][f"mdmx_{key}"] = res["Z_hat"].astype(np.float32)
        out["Z_hat"][f"mdmxraw_{key}"] = res["Z_raw"].astype(np.float32)
        out["runs"].append(res["runs"].assign(model=f"mdmx_{key}", sex="both"))
        out["inner"].append(res["inner"].assign(model=f"mdmx_{key}"))
        out["fold_settings"][key] = res["fold_settings"]
        own = sc.cross_validate_own_sex(ind, Z, indicator_names=OWN_INPUTS[key], folds=FOLDS,
                                        groups=family, settings=SETTINGS, seed=PS["seed"],
                                        basis=train_bases, fold_settings=res["fold_settings"])
        out["Z_hat"][f"own_{key}"] = own["Z_hat"].astype(np.float32)
        out["runs"].append(own["runs"].assign(model=f"own_{key}"))
    out["runs"] = pd.concat(out["runs"], ignore_index=True)
    out["inner"] = pd.concat(out["inner"], ignore_index=True)
    return out


nested = artifacts.stage("svdcomp_nested", _nested, inputs=["tensor", "tucker", "populations"],
                         params={**nested_params, **BASIS_PARAMS},

                         desc="Nested CV: out-of-fold schedules of Models 1-2 and the sex-specific variant "
                              "with c_age and alpha chosen inside each training set")

inner = nested["inner"]
choices = inner[inner.chosen].pivot_table(index="fold", columns="model", values=["c_age", "alpha"])
print("Settings chosen in each outer fold:")

          + int(sweep["at_cap"].sum()) // 4)
n_networks = len(all_runs) + int(inner["networks"].sum()) + n_sweep_nets

      f"converged (outer and inner): {failures}; most correction iterations: {max_iter_used}")

for key in ("one", "two"):

    best = d.loc[d["e0_mae"].idxmin()]
    final_choice[key] = {"c_age": int(best["c_age"]), "alpha": float(best["alpha"])}
    tag = "One" if key == "one" else "Two"
    agree = int(((choices[("c_age", f"mdmx_{key}")] == best["c_age"])
                 & (choices[("alpha", f"mdmx_{key}")] == best["alpha"])).sum())
    print(f"Model {1 if key == 'one' else 2}: final c_age = {final_choice[key]['c_age']}, "
          f"alpha = {final_choice[key]['alpha']:g} (chosen in {agree} of {PS['n_folds']} outer folds)")
    latex.report(f"svdChosen{tag}CAge", final_choice[key]["c_age"], desc=f"c_age of the final Model {tag}")
    latex.report(f"svdChosen{tag}Alpha", final_choice[key]["alpha"], text=f"{final_choice[key]['alpha']:g}",
                 desc=f"alpha of the final Model {tag}")
    latex.report(f"svdChosen{tag}Agree", agree, desc=f"Outer folds whose nested choice equals the final setting, Model {tag}")


def _final(key):
    model = sc.fit_core_model(sc.features(ind, INPUTS[key]), Z, inputs=INPUTS[key], U_sex=U_sex,
                              U_age=U_age, settings=sc.model_settings(PS, **final_choice[key]),
                              seed=PS["seed"], groups=family)
    model["description"] = (f"MDMx summary-indicator Model {'1' if key == 'one' else '2'} (the article's prediction from summary indicators): "
                            "logit of the inputs -> standardised truncated core weights -> smallest "
                            "change that reproduces the inputs -> logit(qx) schedules of both sexes; "
                            "see mdmx.svdcomp")
    return model


def _final_one():
    return _final("one")


def _final_two():
    return _final("two")

The two diagnostic figures show the out-of-fold behaviour of each model (nested cross-validation, corrected predictions): the training curve of the final model (top left; validation loss below the training loss simply means the held-out families are, on average, easier to fit), the reproduction of the input ₅q₀ (exact by construction), the predicted against the observed \(e_0\), the error by single year of age, the single-year errors at ages 0–4, the \(e_0\) error against the level of \(e_0\), and three example country-years at low, median and high child mortality.


Plotting helper for the diagnostic figures
def diagnostic_figure(model, Z_hat, title):
    """3 × 3 out-of-fold diagnostics of one model (Z_hat: its out-of-fold schedules)."""
    colours = [plotting.COLORS["female"], plotting.COLORS["male"]]
    ind_hat = sc.indicators(Z_hat, A)
    e0_obs, e0_hat = sc.e0_by_sex(Z, A), sc.e0_by_sex(Z_hat, A)
    err = (Z_hat - Z).reshape(-1, 2, A)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(13, 11.5))
    curve = model["history"]["curve"]
    ax = axes[0, 0]
    ax.plot(curve["epoch"], curve["train_loss"], lw=1, label="Training")
    ax.plot(curve["epoch"], curve["val_loss"], lw=1, label="Validation")
    ax.axvline(model["history"]["best_epoch"], color="grey", lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("Loss")
    ax.set_title("Final model: training curve"); ax.legend()
    ax = axes[0, 1]
    for s, sx in enumerate("FM"):
        ax.scatter(ind[f"5q0_{sx}"], ind_hat[f"5q0_{sx}"], s=3, alpha=0.25, color=colours[s],
                   label=SEXES[s].title())
    lim = [ind[["5q0_F", "5q0_M"]].min().min() * 0.8, ind[["5q0_F", "5q0_M"]].max().max() * 1.2]
    ax.plot(lim, lim, "k--", lw=0.7); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"Input $_5q_0$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$_5q_0$ of predicted schedule")
    ax.set_title(r"$_5q_0$ reproduction"); ax.legend()
    ax = axes[0, 2]
    for s in range(2):
        ax.scatter(e0_obs[:, s], e0_hat[:, s], s=3, alpha=0.25, color=colours[s], label=SEXES[s].title())
    lim = [e0_obs.min() - 2, e0_obs.max() + 2]
    ax.plot(lim, lim, "k--", lw=0.7)
    ax.set_xlabel("Observed $e_0$"); ax.set_ylabel("Predicted $e_0$"); ax.set_title("$e_0$"); ax.legend()
    ax = axes[1, 0]
    for s in range(2):
        ax.plot(ages, np.sqrt(np.mean(err[:, s] ** 2, axis=0)), color=colours[s], lw=1.4,
                label=SEXES[s].title())
    ax.set_xlabel("Age"); ax.set_ylabel(r"RMSE, logit$(q_x)$"); ax.set_title("Error by age"); ax.legend()
    ax = axes[1, 1]
    q_err = lifetable.expit(Z_hat.reshape(-1, 2, A)) - lifetable.expit(Z.reshape(-1, 2, A))
    for s, shift in ((0, -0.18), (1, 0.18)):
        ax.boxplot([q_err[:, s, a] for a in range(5)], positions=np.arange(5) + shift, widths=0.3,
                   showfliers=False, patch_artist=True,
                   boxprops={"facecolor": colours[s], "alpha": 0.5}, medianprops={"color": "black"})
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.5, ls="--")
    ax.set_xticks(range(5), [f"$q_{a}$" for a in range(5)])
    ax.set_ylabel("Predicted − observed $q_x$"); ax.set_title("Single-year errors, ages 0–4")
    ax = axes[1, 2]
    for s in range(2):
        d = e0_hat[:, s] - e0_obs[:, s]
        ax.scatter(e0_obs[:, s], d, s=3, alpha=0.2, color=colours[s])
        bins = np.linspace(e0_obs.min(), e0_obs.max(), 15)
        idx = np.digitize(e0_obs[:, s], bins)
        centres = [(e0_obs[idx == i, s].mean(), d[idx == i].mean()) for i in np.unique(idx)
                   if (idx == i).sum() >= 10]
        ax.plot(*zip(*centres, strict=True), color=colours[s], lw=2, label=f"{SEXES[s].title()}, binned mean")
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("Observed $e_0$"); ax.set_ylabel("Predicted − observed $e_0$")
    ax.set_title("$e_0$ error by level"); ax.legend()
    q5_avg = ind[["5q0_F", "5q0_M"]].mean(axis=1).to_numpy()
    order = np.argsort(q5_avg)
    for col, pct in enumerate((5, 50, 95)):
        ax = axes[2, col]
        i = order[int(len(order) * pct / 100)]
        for s in range(2):
            ax.plot(ages, Z[i, s * A:(s + 1) * A], ".", ms=2.5, color=colours[s], alpha=0.6)
            ax.plot(ages, Z_hat[i, s * A:(s + 1) * A], color=colours[s], lw=1.3, label=SEXES[s].title())
        rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((Z_hat[i] - Z[i]) ** 2))
        name = T["pop_names"][cell[i, 0]]
        ax.set_title(f"{name} {year_of_row[i]}: $_5q_0$ = {q5_avg[i]:.3f}, RMSE {rmse:.2f}", fontsize=9)
        ax.set_xlabel("Age"); ax.set_ylabel(r"logit$(q_x)$")
    axes[2, 0].legend()
    fig.suptitle(title, y=1.0)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

13.10 Step 9 — benchmarks: Log-Quad and SVD-Comp on the same folds
Comparing MDMx fairly with Log-Quad and SVD-Comp needs three things: the benchmarks must be fitted to the same training data, evaluated on the same held-out country-years, and given the same information.

Log-Quad (Wilmoth et al. (2012); mdmx.logquad) models the log death rate in each five-year age group as a quadratic in \(\log {}_5q_0\) plus an adult-mortality term \(v_x k\). It is re-estimated on each fold’s training schedules: \(a_x, b_x, c_x\) by least squares age group by age group, and \(v_x\) as the leading singular vector of the residuals at ages 5–89. With ₅q₀ only, \(k = 0\); with ₄₅q₁₅, \(k\) is solved so that the predicted ₄₅q₁₅ equals the input exactly. ₅q₀ is always reproduced exactly.
SVD-Comp [Clark (2019); mdmx.svdcomp.fit_svdcomp_classic] takes the SVD of each sex’s logit(q_x) matrix, keeps four components, and predicts their weights by regressions on eight polynomial terms in ₅q₀ and ₄₅q₁₅; with ₅q₀ only, ₄₅q₁₅ is first predicted from ₅q₀. It too is re-estimated on each fold’s training schedules, and, as published, it reproduces its inputs only approximately.

Using the published coefficients instead would be unfair to MDMx in the opposite direction: both were fitted to HMD life tables that include every population we test on. Re-estimation is possible because the model forms are fully specified; the re-implementations were checked during development against the originals: the SVD-Comp prediction code reproduces the R package svdComp5q0 to \(10^{-14}\) when given its packaged coefficients, and Log-Quad fitted to all observed HMD schedules recovers the published coefficients closely. tests/test_svdcomp.py checks that each benchmark recovers data generated by its own model.
The information difference. Log-Quad and SVD-Comp predict each sex from that sex’s indicators only. MDMx Models 1 and 2 use both sexes’ indicators — Model 1 sees the male ₅q₀ when predicting females. That is a legitimate feature of a joint model, but it makes a straight comparison unfair to the benchmarks. We therefore also report a sex-specific MDMx variant: one network per sex whose only inputs are that sex’s indicators, whose loss covers only that sex’s schedule, and whose predictions are corrected to reproduce those inputs. The table also shows MDMx at the fixed settings of Step 6.
All methods are compared on two scales: \(e_0\), and the RMSE of \(\operatorname{logit}({}_nq_x)\) over the standard abridged age groups (0, 1–4, 5–9, …, 105–109). The abridged scale is the one on which Log-Quad is defined, so it does not penalise Log-Quad for spreading each group’s rate evenly over single years; the single-year models are aggregated to the same groups.

With ₅q₀ alone the methods are close: the mean (over sexes) \(e_0\) error is 1.66 years for MDMx Model 1, 1.61 for the sex-specific variant, 1.68 for Log-Quad and 1.66 for SVD-Comp, and the abridged RMSE ranges from 0.319 to 0.331. One indicator, not the model, limits the accuracy.
Relative to Log-Quad, MDMx Model 1’s mean \(e_0\) error is 0.02 years smaller (95% interval -0.10 to +0.04), and relative to SVD-Comp 0.00 years larger (95% interval -0.05 to +0.04) — intervals from a bootstrap that resamples whole population families.
With ₅q₀ and ₄₅q₁₅ the \(e_0\) errors are 0.53 years (MDMx Model 2), 0.52 (sex-specific MDMx), 0.56 (Log-Quad) and 0.58 (SVD-Comp): MDMx Model 2’s error is 0.03 years smaller (95% interval -0.05 to -0.01) than Log-Quad’s and 0.05 years smaller (95% interval -0.08 to -0.01) than SVD-Comp’s. The smallest \(e_0\) error is that of the sex-specific MDMx variant and the smallest abridged RMSE that of SVD-Comp. Without the correction (Step 6) the network’s schedules have about twice the benchmarks’ error; reproducing the inputs exactly, as Log-Quad does by construction, together with settings chosen by nested cross-validation, is what makes MDMx competitive. Using both sexes’ indicators gives MDMx no advantage over the sex-specific variant.
On accuracy, then, MDMx is comparable to the established methods: with ₄₅q₁₅ its error is a few hundredths of a year below both Log-Quad’s and SVD-Comp’s, and with ₅q₀ alone it cannot be told from either. Its distinctive advantages are of structure: one model predicts both sexes coherently in one shared basis, every prediction reproduces its inputs, and further inputs can be added by widening the network’s input layer.
