13.11 Step 10 — the bases within each fold
The sex and age bases \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\) of chapter 04 come from every observed schedule, those of any held-out fold included. A cross-validation in those bases has a small leak: the bases have “seen” the test populations, whereas Log-Quad and SVD-Comp are estimated on the training folds alone. Every cross-validation of this chapter therefore re-estimates the bases from the training rows of each fit — the SVD of those schedules, then the same smoothing and re-orthonormalisation as in chapter 04, with the age rank held at its value on all the data. The check below shows what the leak would be worth: the plain cross-validation of Models 1 and 2 at their final settings, with the fold bases and with the bases from all the data.


Re-estimate the bases within each fold and cross-validate again (cached)
def _fold_bases():
    return {k: train_bases(FOLDS != k) for k in range(PS["n_folds"])}


def _basis_cv():
    bases = _fold_bases()
    c_max = max(final_choice[k]["c_age"] for k in final_choice)
    angles, rows = [], []
    for k, (_, U_a) in bases.items():
        # Largest principal angle between the leading age components
        # estimated with and without fold k (0 = the same subspace).
        cosines = np.linalg.svd(U_age[:, :c_max].T @ U_a[:, :c_max], compute_uv=False)
        angles.append({"fold": k, "max_angle_deg": float(np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cosines.min(), -1, 1))))})
    for key in ("one", "two"):
        settings = sc.model_settings(PS, **final_choice[key])
        for variant, basis in (("fold basis", train_bases), ("full-data basis", None)):
            res = sc.cross_validate_core_model(
                sc.features(ind, INPUTS[key]), Z, inputs=INPUTS[key], folds=FOLDS, groups=family,
                settings=settings, seed=PS["seed"], basis=basis,
                U_sex=None if basis else U_sex, U_age=None if basis else U_age)
            rows.append(sc.summarise_accuracy({f"mdmx_{key}": res["Z_hat"]}, Z, A, AGE_GROUPS, AB_STARTS)
                        .assign(variant=variant))
    return {"accuracy": pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True), "angles": pd.DataFrame(angles)}

                           params={**cv_params, **BASIS_PARAMS, "final_choice": final_choice},

                           desc="Out-of-fold accuracy of Models 1-2 (final settings) with bases from all data "
                                "or re-estimated in each fold")

# Principal angles for the fixed c_age as well as for the largest c_age
# used (the stage stored only the latter); the fold bases are cheap to rebuild.

c_used = max(final_choice[k]["c_age"] for k in final_choice)

                  np.linalg.svd(U_age[:, :c].T @ U_a[:, :c], compute_uv=False).min(), -1, 1))))
                  for _, U_a in fold_bases.values())
              for c in sorted({PS["c_age"], c_used})}
if not np.isclose(angle_by_c[c_used], basis_cv["angles"]["max_angle_deg"].max()):

Re-estimating the bases inside each fold changes the first 6 age components very little (the subspace they span rotates by at most 4.1 degrees); the first 20 move more (up to 53 degrees — the higher components are less well determined), yet the out-of-fold accuracy changes by at most 0.02 years of \(e_0\), because the network and the correction adapt to whichever basis they are given. text:
13.12 The final models, for the app
The final networks are trained on all 4,056 observed country-years with the settings chosen in Step 8 (Model 1: \(c_{\text{age}}\) = 20, \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 0; Model 2: \(c_{\text{age}}\) = 6, \(w_{\mathrm{child}}\) = 0), with the same early-stopping rule. Each is saved as a self-contained artefact — svdcomp_model1 and svdcomp_model2 — holding only arrays, numbers and strings, so that the Shiny app (or any other program) can reproduce the predictions exactly without this code. Its structure is documented in the mdmx.svdcomp module docstring:







key
contents




inputs
input names in order; the network input is the logit of each, and these are the indicators the prediction reproduces


x_scaler
mean and scale of the logit inputs


network
layer sizes and the weight matrices and bias vectors


core_scaler
mean and scale of the core weights: core = output × scale + mean


U_sex, U_age
the sex basis (\(2 \times 2\)) and the first \(c_{\text{age}}\) age components (\(110 \times c_{\text{age}}\))


enforce
tolerance and iteration limit of the correction


ages, loss_sexes, settings, history, description
ages, settings and training curve



A prediction is mdmx.svdcomp.predict_schedules(model, X): the network’s core weights \(\mathbf{g}_0\) = out ⊙ σ + μ for the standardised logit inputs, the correction of Step 4, and \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} = (\mathbf{S}
\otimes \mathbf{A}_c)\,\mathbf{g}^\star\); it raises an error if the correction does not converge. For example, for ₅q₀ = 0.05 (females) and 0.06 (males):

      np.round(lifetable.nqx(lifetable.expit(z), 0, 5), 10))

title: 14  Two forecasters
text:
14.1 What is forecast
Both forecasters forecast a population’s complete mortality schedule: single-year logit(q_x) for ages 0–109, female and male, every year ahead. Both work in the same space, the first principal components of the effective cores (Step 1 below), and both start from the population’s last observed schedule. They differ in how they move through that space: MDMx extrapolates each population’s own recent trend, damped and pulled towards the HMD-wide drift; the flow field moves every population along the paths that populations at the same level of mortality followed in the past.

Wherever an unqualified e₀ is quoted (an error, a bias, a coverage), it is the average of the female and the male e₀, \(\tfrac12(e_0^F + e_0^M)\), not the e₀ of a combined-sex life table.

text:
14.2 The MDMx forecaster, step by step

14.2.1 Step 1 — the space, re-estimated at every origin
Every observed schedule is represented by its effective core \(\G_{c,t} = \bS^\top \M_{c,t}\, \bA\) (chapter 04), an \(r_1 \times r_2\) matrix with 2 × 50 = 100 entries. Forecasting 100 numbers jointly is wasteful, because they move together: a principal-component analysis (PCA) of the vectorised cores of all observed country-years (paper §9.1, Eq. 24),
\[
\mathbf{s}_{c,t} = \mathbf{V}^\top\big(\operatorname{vec}(\G_{c,t}) - \bar{\mathbf{g}}\big)
\in \R^{N_{PC}},
\]
with \(N_{PC}\) = 5 components, reduces each core to a handful of scores, and the map back to a schedule is linear (paper Eq. 25): \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{z}_{\text{mean}} + \mathbf{L}\,\mathbf{s}\), where column \(j\) of \(\mathbf{L}\) is the female and male \(\logit(q_x)\) schedule \(\bS\,\mathbf{V}_j\,\bA^\top\) of the \(j\)-th loading.
A forecast made at origin \(o\) must not use any data after \(o\). The bases \(\bS\) and \(\bA\), the smoothing of \(\bA\), the effective cores and the PCA are therefore all re-estimated at each origin from the observed country-years up to that origin (mdmx.forecast.origin_space), exactly as chapter 04 estimates them from all the data. The age rank is held at the full-data value, \(r_2\) = 50, at every origin, so that the forecasts from different origins have the same structure. For the latest year in the tensor this reproduces the decomposition of chapter 04 exactly, which the next cell checks.


Re-estimate the bases and the PCA at every origin (cached)

The first component carries most of the variation — it is essentially the overall level of mortality — and the first 5 together carry 96.5% of the variance of the cores of all observed country-years (94.6–96.4% in the space estimated on the data up to each of the origins illustrated here, every 10 years from 1960 to 2010). The remainder is not lost for the history — it is in the observed data — but a forecast can only move in the space of the first 5 components. We return to what that costs at the forecast’s jump-off below.


14.2.2 Step 2 — the drift target
Each population’s own recent trend is informative, but noisy; the average trend of all HMD populations is stable, but ignores what is particular to the population. MDMx blends the two (paper §9.2.1):
\[
\boldsymbol\delta_{\text{hier}} = w_{\text{HMD}}\,\boldsymbol\delta_{\text{HMD}}
+ w_{\text{country}}\,\boldsymbol\delta_{c},
\]
with weights \(w_{\text{HMD}}\) = 0.8 and \(w_{\text{country}}\) = 0.2. A population’s drift \(\boldsymbol\delta_c\) is the average change of its scores per calendar year over the window \([o-W, o]\), with \(W\) = 20 years, measured between its first and last observed years in the window (mdmx.forecast.country_drifts); missing and exceptional years inside the window are simply not used, and the elapsed time is counted in calendar years. A population needs at least 10 observed years in the window for its drift to count. \(\boldsymbol\delta_{\text{HMD}}\) is the average of the drifts of all populations with a defined drift at that origin. The target has no regime level (paper §9.2.1), so this chapter does not depend on the clustering of chapter 06.


14.2.3 Step 3 — the drift-constrained Kalman filter
For each PCA score the model is a damped local linear trend whose drift reverts not to zero but to the target (paper §9.2.2, Eqs. 26–27):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_t &= \ell_{t-1} + \delta_{t-1} + \eta^{\ell}_t, &\operatorname{var}\eta^\ell &= q^\ell,\\
\delta_t &= \rho\,\delta_{t-1} + (1-\rho)\,\delta_{\text{hier}} + \eta^{\delta}_t,
  &\operatorname{var}\eta^\delta &= q^\delta,\\
y_t &= \ell_t + \varepsilon_t, &\operatorname{var}\varepsilon &= r,
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(y_t\) is the observed score in calendar year \(t\). With \(\rho<1\) the forecast drift converges geometrically to the target, so a long-range forecast follows the blended trend whatever the population did in its last few years. The covariances are diagonal, so the 5 components are independent two-state filters that share \(\rho\); mdmx.forecast.llt_filter writes this out and is checked against the textbook matrix filter in tests/test_forecast.py.
The filter runs over every calendar year from the population’s first observed year to the origin. In a year without an observed schedule — a war or epidemic year set aside as exceptional, or a year missing from the HMD series — the update step is skipped: the state is carried forward by the model and its uncertainty grows, exactly as in a forecast. The \(3N_{PC}+1\) = 16 parameters (\(q^\ell\), \(q^\delta\), \(r\) for each component, and the common \(\rho\), kept between 0.8 and 0.999) maximise the Gaussian likelihood of the observed years (prediction-error decomposition) by L-BFGS-B. Many of these maxima lie on a bound — a variance at its floor, which is effectively zero, or \(\rho\) at its lower bound — so the optimiser works on the standard deviations and on \(\rho\) itself, where such a maximum can be reached. It runs until \(-\log L\) stops decreasing at machine precision, and a fit counts as converged if the projected gradient there is below 0.001. The likelihood can have more than one local maximum — typically one with \(\rho\) at its lower bound and a higher one inside the range — so the optimiser is started from several points and the best fit is kept: moment-based starting values (\(q^\ell = \operatorname{var}\Delta y\), \(q^\delta = \operatorname{var}\Delta^2 y/4\), \(r = \operatorname{var}\Delta y/10\), within their bounds) with \(\rho\) in the middle of its range and at 7 fixed levels across it, and the 3 best points of the profile likelihood of \(\rho\) on a grid of 12 values. Given \(\rho\), the components are independent, so the profile is cheap: the standard deviations are found component by component by a grid search and then fitted exactly at every grid value of \(\rho\) at once. Several starts make a missed maximum unlikely, not impossible; the design was chosen by comparing search strategies. Chapter 12 reports convergence and the fitted \(\rho\) by origin for every fit of the evaluation, under both fitting periods. How often a single start would have missed the maximum is counted below for the fits of the long-run forecasts, one per population at the latest data year.
The cell below shows one fit: France at the 1960 origin, whose training series has gaps at both world wars.

14.2.4 Step 4 — from scores to schedules and e₀
A forecast of the scores is a forecast of the complete female and male schedules, \(\hat{\mathbf z}_{o+h} = \mathbf z_{\text{mean}} + \mathbf L\,
\hat{\mathbf s}_{o+h}\), and from those of e₀ for each sex. The forecast uncertainty of the scores at horizon \(h\) is that of a future observed score: the filter’s state variance plus the observation noise \(r\) (both diagonal). Because e₀ is a nonlinear function of the schedule, its standard deviation follows from the delta method (paper §9.2): \(\sigma^2_{e_0}(h) = \sum_j J_j^2 \operatorname{var}(s_j)\) with \(J = \partial e_0/\partial \mathbf s = (\partial e_0/\partial\mathbf z)\,\mathbf L\). The gradient \(\partial e_0/\partial\mathbf z\) is computed exactly from the life table (mdmx.forecast.e0_and_gradient): with \(e_0 = \sum_k w_k l_k\), \(\partial e_0/\partial z_x = -q_x\sum_{k>x} w_k l_k\). A Monte-Carlo check of the delta method is reported with the intervals.


14.2.5 Step 5 — the jump-off anchor
The Kalman filter starts the forecast from the filtered level of the scores, and the 5 scores represent a schedule only up to the PCA truncation. The schedule the forecast starts from therefore differs from the observed one, by a small amount at most ages but enough to move the female − male gap of e₀ at the jump-off. MDMx keeps the part of the observed schedule that its scores do not represent (paper §9.2.4, Eq. 28): the residual of the observed schedule at the job’s last training year from its projection on the scores, \(\varepsilon_{c} = \mathrm{logit}\,q_{c,t_0} - (\bar z + L\,s_{c,t_0})\), is added to every forecast schedule (forecast.mdmx_origin(anchor="persistent"), the persistent anchor, ρ = 1). The flow field uses the same anchor. A decaying anchor, with a half-life of 2 years, is a sensitivity in chapter 12.
The residual holds two things: the population’s own detail, which the anchor is there to keep, and the noise of that one year’s single-age rates, which it is not. Carried as observed, the noise would stay in every forecast schedule at every horizon. The residual is therefore smoothed over age before it is added, each sex’s by a Whittaker smoother with second differences, \(\tilde\varepsilon = \arg\min_{u} \sum_x (u_x - \varepsilon_x)^2 + \nu \sum_x (\Delta^2 u_x)^2\) over ages 1 and over, with ν = 1,000; age 0 keeps its observed value, because the step from infancy to childhood is real (forecast.smooth_residual). Both forecasters carry \(\tilde\varepsilon_c\). The smoothing was chosen on the evaluation’s origins up to 2000, among smoothers over age and over years, of the sex difference and of each sex; chapter 12 shows what it does to the comparison’s measures.
At every origin of the evaluation, the cell measures what the anchor keeps: the e₀ and the gap of the projection plus the smoothed residual minus those of the projection, and the share of the residual that the smoothing removes.

title: 14  Two forecasters
text:
14.3 The flow field
The flow field (paper §9.3) forecasts in MDMx’s space (Step 1), from data up to the origin only (mdmx.flowfield). Its state is the vector of PCA scores of a population-year, \(s = (s_1, \dots, s_5)\); the first score is the level of mortality, oriented so that a higher \(s_1\) is lower mortality.

The speed (flowfield.speed_function). Each population’s \(s_1\) is smoothed over its observed years, and its annual change is computed. The speed \(g(s_1)\) is a LOWESS of these changes against \(s_1\), pooled over the populations: how fast populations at each level of mortality improved. It is never allowed to reverse the improvement.
The frontier point (flowfield.orientation). \(s_1^*\) is the median \(s_1\) of the population-years whose e₀ is in the top 10%. Below it a forecast moves at the pace that populations at its level moved in the past. Beyond it there is no past to learn from.
The pace beyond the frontier (flowfield.frontier_level, frontier_speed, frontier_rule). In each year the 3 populations with the highest e₀ lead; their mean \(s_1\), chain-linked so that populations entering the data do not move it, gives the frontier’s pace \(V_s\) over the 50 years before the origin. Beyond \(s_1^*\) the speed is \(v_1 = \max\{0,\, w V_s + (1 - w)\, g(s_1^*)\}\), with \(w = n/(n + n_0)\), \(n_0\) = 3, for the \(n\) populations that led in those years.
The shape law (flowfield.shape_law). The other scores follow \(s_1\) along \(f_k(s_1)\), a LOWESS of \(s_k\) on \(s_1\) over the last 50 years (along its tangent beyond the frontier point of those years), and a population’s own deviation from \(f_k\) decays at the pooled rate \(\alpha_k\) a year.
The path (flowfield.integrate, forecast_origin). From the last observed scores, \(s_1\) moves one year at a time at the speed of its level, the other scores follow the shape law, and the schedules carry the jump-off anchor with its smoothed residual (Step 5).

The form (the speed on every year, the shape law on the last 50, the leaders’ pace beyond the frontier) was chosen in development studies on the development origins; chapter 12 describes how (the article’s §10.9 says on which origins the form was selected). The figure shows the flow fitted to every year up to the latest data.


The flow at the latest data year; the flow and the anchor’s residual at every origin of the evaluation (cached)

14.3.1 What the fitted flow says about mortality change
The flow field’s fitted objects can be read as statements about how mortality changes. Read together, the speed and the shape law trace one path through the space of schedules, the typical path: the level \(s_1\) moves at the speed \(g(s_1)\) and the other scores sit on the shape law. One year along it the level moves to \(s_1 + g(s_1)\), so the gain in e₀ that the flow implies at the level \(s_1\) is \(e(s_1 + g(s_1)) - e(s_1)\), where \(e(s_1)\) is the e₀ of the typical schedule at that level (paper §11.4, Eq. 37). Plotted against e₀, this implied gain is the flow field’s phase portrait of life expectancy: the counterpart of bayesLife’s gain function, estimated over the whole schedule and without a parametric form. The typical path also gives each sex’s e₀, so the gap between the sexes along the level of mortality.
The section describes the whole transition, so it uses the flow at the latest data year with the shape law estimated on every year (config/params.d/theory.toml). The forecaster’s shape law uses the last 50 years only, when few populations were at the lower levels. Observed gains are centred over 10 years.


The typical path of the flow fitted to every year, and the observed gains and gaps

# The dip of the implied gain inside a band of e0, and its recovery up to the frontier point.
def dip(path, band, front):
    """The smallest implied gain with e0 inside ``band`` and its e0; then the largest gain after it up to the
    frontier point, and its e0 (the recovery)."""
    seg = path[path["e0"].between(*band)]
    i = seg["gain"].idxmin()
    low, low_e0 = float(seg.loc[i, "gain"]), float(seg.loc[i, "e0"])
    after = path[(path["e0"] > low_e0) & (path["e0"] <= front)]
    j = after["gain"].idxmax()
    return low, low_e0, float(after.loc[j, "gain"]), float(after.loc[j, "e0"])

    latex.report(f"fcTheory{tag}GainRecoverEzero", high_e0, digits=0, desc=f"{what}: e0 at that largest gain (years)")

The implied gain rises with e₀ to 0.44 years a year at e₀ 59, dips to 0.09 at e₀ 71, recovers to 0.24 at 76 and declines to 0.19 at 80. The dip is mostly the populations of Central and Eastern Europe: their median observed gain at e₀ 65–70 is 0.03 years a year (median year 1980), against 0.37 for the other populations. Refitted without them, the flow’s gain is 0.23 at e₀ 70; its dip is 0.18 at 71 and it reaches 0.22 at 76. The gap between the sexes on the typical path is about 3.2 years at e₀ 45, peaks at 7.2 years at e₀ 70 (6.0 at 75 without Central and Eastern Europe) and narrows to 5.3 at 80. Paper §11.4 (“What the flow field says about mortality change”) interprets these against the literature.

section: 14.6 Sex differences in the long run
text:
14.6 Sex differences in the long run
MDMx forecasts both sexes at every age from one set of scores, so the age pattern of the sex difference is forecast jointly — not held fixed by assumption, as in the coherent FDM (whose sex ratios are stationary), nor left free, as in Lee–Carter and Hyndman–Ullah. How does it behave far ahead? The forecast drift of the scores reverts to the hierarchical target δ_hier (Step 3), so in the long run the male − female difference of logit(q_x) at age x changes at the constant rate \((L_{\text{male}} - L_{\text{female}})\,\delta_{\text{hier}}\) (mdmx.compare.sex_difference_slope). On the logit scale any non-zero rate means that the difference keeps changing, so the question is how fast. The cell computes the rate for every population at the latest data year, 2025 — split into the part that comes from the HMD-wide drift (common to the populations) and the population’s own part — and compares the change it implies over 100 years with the change actually observed over each population’s last 50 years (as pre-specified).


MDMx’s long-run age-specific sex difference: the rate per population, and Sweden over 100 years (cached)
OV = F["overall"]
LR_H = int(OV["longrun_horizon"])
lr_origin = int(years[-1])
lr_jobs = fc.cv_jobs(observed, pops, years, [lr_origin], LR_H, F["min_train_years"], 0)
lr_set = dataclasses.replace(SET, horizon=LR_H)
lr = artifacts.stage(
    "forecast_longrun",
    functools.partial(fc.mdmx_origin, M, observed, pops, years, lr_origin, lr_jobs, lr_set, workers=WORKERS,
                      anchor=E["mdmx_anchor"]),
    inputs=["tensor"], params={"settings": lr_set.as_dict(), "jobs": artifacts.content_hash(lr_jobs),
                               "anchor": E["mdmx_anchor"]},
    code=MDMX_CODE, desc=f"MDMx forecasts {LR_H} years ahead from {lr_origin} (long-run sex differences)")
lr_p = SET.n_pc
lr_target = lr["jobs"][[f"target_{i + 1}" for i in range(lr_p)]].to_numpy()          # (J, p), per year
# The HMD part of each target: w_HMD·δ_HMD, or all of it where the population's own drift was undefined.
lr_hmd = (np.where(lr["jobs"]["own_drift"].to_numpy(bool), SET.weight_hmd, 1.0)[:, None]
          * lr["hmd_drift"][None, :lr_p])
lr_rate = cp.sex_difference_slope(lr["L"], lr_target)                                # (J, A), logit per year
lr_rate_hmd = cp.sex_difference_slope(lr["L"], lr_hmd)


lr_century = 100 * cp.group_means(lr_rate, GROUPS)     # (J, G): change per century implied by the rate
lr_century_hmd = 100 * cp.group_means(lr_rate_hmd, GROUPS)
# Observed: the change of the difference over the last `longrun_lag` years of each population.
lr_obs = cp.observed_sex_difference_change(M, observed, years, [PIDX[p_] for p_ in lr["jobs"]["pop"]], GROUPS,
                                           lag=int(OV["longrun_lag"]), window=int(OV["longrun_window"]))
lr_tab = pd.DataFrame({
    "100 y (median)": np.median(lr_century, axis=0),
    "100 y, HMD part (median)": np.median(lr_century_hmd, axis=0),
    "|100 y| (median)": np.median(np.abs(lr_century), axis=0),
    "last 50 y observed (median)": np.median(lr_obs, axis=0),
    "|last 50 y| (median)": np.median(np.abs(lr_obs), axis=0),
}, index=list(GROUPS))
for lab, row in lr_tab.iterrows():
    word = lab.split()[0]
    latex.report(f"fcLongrunCentury{word}", row["|100 y| (median)"], digits=2,
                 desc=f"MDMx: median |long-run change of the male-female logit difference| per century, {lab}")
    latex.report(f"fcLongrunObserved{word}", row["|last 50 y| (median)"], digits=2,
                 desc=f"Median |observed change of the male-female logit difference| over the last 50 years, {lab}")
latex.report("fcLongrunOrigin", lr_origin, text=str(lr_origin), desc="Origin of the long-run forecasts")
latex.report("fcLongrunPops", len(lr["jobs"]), desc="Populations forecast in the long-run check")
latex.report("fcLongrunObsPops", len(lr_obs), desc="Populations with 55 observed years for the observed change")
# Sweden, 100 years ahead: e₀ of the two sexes and their gap.
lr_sw = lr["points"][lr["points"]["pop"] == SHOW].pivot(index="year", columns="sex", values="e0_fc")
lr_gap = lr_sw["female"] - lr_sw["male"]
latex.report("fcLongrunGapSWEStart", float(lr_gap.iloc[0]), digits=1,
             desc=f"MDMx: female-male e0 gap of {SHOW}, first forecast year from {lr_origin}")
latex.report("fcLongrunGapSWEEnd", float(lr_gap.iloc[-1]), digits=1,
             desc=f"MDMx: female-male e0 gap of {SHOW}, {LR_H} years ahead")
# Like for like: the observed change scaled to a century.
change_ratio = lr_tab["|100 y| (median)"] / (100 / int(OV["longrun_lag"]) * lr_tab["|last 50 y| (median)"])
slower = [lab.lower() for lab in change_ratio.index[change_ratio < 1]]
latex.report("fcLongrunMinYears", F["min_train_years"],
             desc="Observed years up to the origin a population needs for the long-run check")
latex.report("fcLongrunHorizon", LR_H, desc="Horizon (years) of the long-run MDMx forecasts")
latex.report("fcLongrunLag", int(OV["longrun_lag"]), desc="Years over which the observed change of the sex difference is measured")
latex.report("fcLongrunGroups", len(change_ratio), desc="Age groups of the long-run check")
latex.report("fcLongrunSlowerGroups", len(slower),
             desc="Age groups in which the forecast changes the sex difference more slowly than observed (per century)")
lr_note = (f"Over 100 years the model's long-run rate changes the male − female logit difference by a median "
           f"{lr_tab['|100 y| (median)'].min():.2f}–{lr_tab['|100 y| (median)'].max():.2f} across the age groups, "
           f"against {lr_tab['|last 50 y| (median)'].min():.2f}–{lr_tab['|last 50 y| (median)'].max():.2f} actually "
           f"observed over the last {int(OV['longrun_lag'])} years ({len(lr_obs)} populations).  Per century (the "
           "observed change scaled to a century) the forecast sex differences change "
           + ("more slowly than the observed ones in every age group." if len(slower) == len(change_ratio) else
              "at least as fast as the observed ones in every age group." if not slower else
              f"more slowly than the observed ones in {len(slower)} of the {len(change_ratio)} age groups "
              f"({', '.join(slower)}).")
           + f"  For {NAME[SHOW]} the female − male gap in e₀ goes from {lr_gap.iloc[0]:.1f} years in "
             f"{lr_gap.index[0]} to {lr_gap.iloc[-1]:.1f} in {lr_gap.index[-1]}.")
print(lr_note)
lr_tab.round(3)

section: 14.7 How often one start would have been enough
text:
14.7 How often one start would have been enough
The long-run forecasts come from one fit per population at 2025, each to the population’s whole history, with the starts of Step 3. The cell counts the fits in which some start, and those in which the single moment-based start (\(\rho\) in the middle of its range), ended more than 0.1 below the maximum log-likelihood.


How far below the maximum the starts of the long-run fits ended
START_GAP = float(F["mle_start_gap_report"])
lr_fits = lr["jobs"]
n_fits = len(lr_fits)
n_gap_any = int((lr_fits["start_gap_max"] > START_GAP).sum())
n_gap_moment = int((lr_fits["moment_gap"] > START_GAP).sum())
# Starts per fit: the best grid points of the profile likelihood, the moment-based start with ρ mid-range,
# and the moment-based starts at each fixed ρ; every fit must have used them all.
n_starts = SET.mle_grid_top + 1 + len(SET.mle_rho_starts)
if not (lr_fits["n_starts"] == n_starts).all():
    raise ValueError(f"The long-run fits used {sorted(lr_fits['n_starts'].unique())} starts, not {n_starts}.")
latex.report("fcNStarts", n_starts, desc="Starts of the optimiser per MDMx fit")
latex.report("fcStartGapThreshold", START_GAP, text=f"{START_GAP:g}",
             desc="Log-likelihood below the maximum at which a start counts as having missed it")
print(f"{n_fits} fits from {lr_origin}: {int(lr_fits['converged'].sum())} converged; best start by kind: "
      f"{lr_fits['best_start_kind'].value_counts().to_dict()}")
print(f"Some start more than {START_GAP:g} below the maximum: {n_gap_any}; the moment-based start: {n_gap_moment}")
latex.report("fcStartGapFits", n_fits,
             desc=f"MDMx fits of the long-run forecasts (one per population, whole history, origin {lr_origin})")
latex.report("fcStartGapAny", n_gap_any,
             desc=f"Long-run fits in which some start ended more than {START_GAP:g} below the maximum log-likelihood")
latex.report("fcStartGapMoment", n_gap_moment,
             desc=f"Long-run fits in which the moment-based start (rho mid-range) ended more than {START_GAP:g} "
                  "below the maximum log-likelihood")
start_note = (f"In {n_gap_any} of the {n_fits} fits at least one start ended more than {START_GAP:g} below the "
              "maximum log-likelihood"
              + (f", and in {n_gap_moment} the moment-based start did: with that start alone, "
                 f"{'that fit' if n_gap_moment == 1 else 'those fits'} would have stopped short of the maximum."
                 if n_gap_moment else
                 f"; the moment-based start came within {START_GAP:g} of the maximum in every fit."))
print(start_note)

title: 14  Two forecasters
text:
14.9 Summary
MDMx and the flow field forecast the same object, the complete schedule of both sexes, in the same space, and both start from the observed schedule, its departure from the scores smoothed over age. MDMx extrapolates each population’s own damped trend, pulled towards the HMD-wide drift; the flow field moves each population along the paths that populations at its level of mortality followed, at the leaders’ pace beyond the frontier. Chapter 12 evaluates both, with the established methods, from every origin between 1900 and 2015.

title: 15  Forecast evaluation
text:
15.1 The design
This chapter compares the two forecasters of chapter 11, MDMx with its jump-off anchor and the flow field, with the established methods: Lee–Carter, Hyndman–Ullah’s functional model, the coherent functional model, and the UN’s bayesLife, each fitted either to every year of a population’s history or to its last 50 years. An equally weighted ensemble of anchored MDMx, the flow field and Lee–Carter on the last 50 years is the twelfth entry. A random walk with drift is the yardstick that scales every measure.
The design was frozen before any of its numbers existed: the origins, the entries, the views, the measures and the rule that names the headline (paper §10.5). Not everything stayed as frozen. After the comparison and the held-out block had first been scored, independent reviews found that the frozen overall comparison counted the level of e₀ in overlapping families, rewarded errors that offset, and scored intervals calibrated in different ways. The overall comparison was revised (Deviation 2), and the corrections of four further reviews followed (Deviation 3: life expectancy from death rates with a₀ = 0.3 at age 0, the book’s life-table convention). Deviation 3 changed the entries that convert death rates: Lee–Carter, Hyndman–Ullah and the coherent model, bayesLife (whose input series changed, so its runs were all made again) and, through Lee–Carter, the ensemble. Anchored MDMx, the flow field and the naive convert no rates and did not change. This chapter reports the revised and corrected comparison; the frozen one is kept beside it as the record of that path. Because the revision came after the held-out block had been scored, the block is not a blind test of the revised comparison.
Forecasts are made from an origin every five years from 1900 to 2015 (paper §10.1). A population is forecast from an origin if it has at least 30 observed years up to the origin and 3 after it, and each forecast runs 50 years. The origins form three groups:
Truth is the HMD’s observed e₀ in normal years: the years of the event dictionary (chapter d3) are left out of the scoring, among them wars, 1918, and three pandemics masked in every population whether or not its mortality rose there: the influenza pandemics of 1957–58 and 1968–69, and COVID-19 (counts below). Every comparison is made on the same points: the population-years at which every entry forecasts both sexes and their average, and all three are observed.

title: 15  Forecast evaluation
text:
15.2 The runs
Every entry is run at every origin under each of its fitting periods, and each model is fitted only to data for years up to its origin, taken from the HMD release this book uses (29 October 2026, chapter d1), not the data available at the time. The forecasts are therefore out of sample from rolling origins; they are not the forecasts that could have been made at the time, which would have used the data then available. A few inputs draw on data for years after the origin, and they are listed here in one place (paper §10.9):

pooling: at the ages where small populations record zero deaths, the data pipeline pools deaths and exposures over blocks of adjacent years formed on the whole series, so a block can span an origin (counts below);
intervals: the comparison’s intervals are calibrated on the errors at the other origins of the era, later ones included (intervals from past errors only are reported beside them);
bayesLife: its default priors come from WPP data that extend beyond most origins, and the σ of its gap model’s second equation is bayesLife’s own WPP-derived value at the origins up to 1990;
MortCast: the rotation of bayesLife’s schedules uses MortCast’s default rotation settings, estimated on recent data;
the age rank of the decomposition (chapter 04) was chosen on all the data;
MDMx’s settings (the drift weights and the number of components) were set before this evaluation, on data that include years after most origins (alternatives are reported below);
the event dictionary marks the crisis years with hindsight, and the truth leaves them out;
which populations are scored: a population enters an origin’s jobs only if it is observed for at least 3 years after the origin, and the jobs also decide which populations form bayesLife’s world level (and Li–Lee’s group, below).

The exceptions touch different entries: bayesLife’s priors and MortCast’s rotation the comparators, the age rank the two new forecasters, MDMx’s settings MDMx, the pooling the entries trained on pooled data, and the intervals every entry (their bias adjustment helps most the entries with a persistent bias). Their effects are not measured, except for MDMx’s settings and the intervals, whose alternatives are reported below. Chapter 11 describes the two forecasters. The comparators run in R, through the package demography (R/demography_forecasts.R, settings in config/params.d/forecast.toml): Lee–Carter on each sex’s rates, with k_t refitted to the observed total deaths (adjust = "dt", as Lee and Carter 1992); Hyndman–Ullah’s functional model on the rates smoothed year by year; and the coherent functional model, which forecasts the product and the ratio of the sexes’ smoothed rates. The runs are cached per origin; tools/warm_evaluation.py computes the same runs ahead of a render. bayesLife’s 48 runs (24 origins, two fitting periods) are made off-site, in a project that tools/bayeslife_bundle.py writes from the book’s own inputs and R scripts (R/bayeslife_forecast.R and its patches); they are imported below after checks that they are the book’s own runs.

The R warnings all come from Lee–Carter’s lca. Where a small population has no deaths at some age in some year, the log rate is infinite: lca replaces it (“Inf replaced by maximum positive value”) or estimates the zero rate (“Replacing zero values with estimates”). “No root exists. Returning closest” means that in some year no k_t reproduces the observed deaths exactly, and lca keeps the closest value. These are the package’s documented behaviour; no forecast is missing because of them.

15.2.1 bayesLife: the off-site runs
The off-site project’s runs, gathered from the machines that made them, are copied into work/bayeslife/chapter-12-input/ by tools/fetch_bayeslife_offsite.py. Each run is accepted only if the project’s files match its manifest, the run finished, and its input e₀ and settings are byte-for-byte those the book itself would have sent (bayeslife.offsite_runs). bayesLife forecasts e₀ only; its schedules come from its median e₀ path by MortCast’s coherent rotated Lee–Carter, fitted to each population’s smoothed rates over the job’s fitting window. MortCast matches e₀ in its own life table (a₀ by Andreev and Kingkade, ages to 130), whose e₀ differs from the book’s (a₀ = 0.3) where infant mortality is high. The schedules are scored in the book’s life table, so MortCast’s target is moved by the remaining difference until the schedules’ e₀ there is bayesLife’s median, to 0.025 years (MortCast itself meets its target to 0.01 years).

The correction of Deviation 3 is at age 0. Before it, the comparators turned their death rates into probabilities of dying with a₀ = 0.5, the a_x they use above age 0, while the book’s life table uses a₀ = 0.3; bayesLife was fitted to e₀ series converted in the same way. The difference matters where infant mortality is high. Its size, on the comparators’ own input rates of the years before 1950:


The size of the age-0 correction, on the comparators’ input rates
# Each population-year's rates as the comparators receive them, ages 0 to their open age: an age with no
# exposure keeps the rate of the age below (as bl.e0_series), and the open group's rate holds at every
# older age (as fc.comparator_schedules).
_r = ctx["rates"][ctx["rates"]["year"] < int(E["a0_offset_before"])]
_m = (_r.assign(mx=_r["deaths"] / _r["exposure"].where(_r["exposure"] > 0))
      .pivot(index=["pop", "year", "sex"], columns="age", values="mx").ffill(axis=1))
_mx = _m.to_numpy()
if not np.isfinite(_mx).all():
    raise ValueError("a population-year of the comparators' rates has no rate at some age")
_mx = np.concatenate([_mx[:, :-1], np.repeat(_mx[:, -1:], A - _mx.shape[1] + 1, axis=1)], axis=1)  # (N, A)
CMP_AX, BOOK_A0 = float(ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"]), float(P.section("data")["a0"])


def e0_converted(a0):
    """e₀ in the book's life table of the rates ``_mx`` converted to q_x with ``a0`` at age 0."""
    return lifetable.e0_from_qx(lifetable.qx_from_mx(_mx, lifetable.conversion_ax(A, CMP_AX, a0=a0)), a0=BOOK_A0)


# The change of e₀, the average of the sexes, in the population-years with both sexes.
A0_SHIFT = (pd.Series(e0_converted(BOOK_A0) - e0_converted(CMP_AX), index=_m.index)
            .unstack("sex").dropna().mean(axis=1))
latex.report("evAzeroOffsetEarly", float(A0_SHIFT.median()), digits=2,
             desc=f"Median rise of e0 (average of the sexes) from a0 = {CMP_AX:g} to the book's a0 at age 0, the "
                  f"comparators' input rates before {int(E['a0_offset_before'])}")
print(f"{len(A0_SHIFT):,} population-years before {E['a0_offset_before']}: e₀ rises by a median "
      f"{A0_SHIFT.median():.3f} y (5th–95th percentile {A0_SHIFT.quantile(0.05):.3f}–{A0_SHIFT.quantile(0.95):.3f})")


1,542 population-years before 1950: e₀ rises by a median 0.155 y (5th–95th percentile 0.019–0.446)


With a₀ = 0.5 the comparators’ e₀ (the average of the sexes) was a median of 0.15 years lower in these years than in the book’s life table.


15.2.2 The entries on common points
The ensemble is the equally weighted mean of its members’ e₀ forecasts and of their logit(q_x) schedules, where all three members forecast. Every comparison below is made on the points at which all twelve entries forecast both sexes and their average, and all three are observed.


Every entry’s points and schedules; the naive; the common points; errors
results = ev.entry_results(ctx, runs, BL_RUNS, BL_SCHED)
points = ev.long_points(results)
naive_q = cp.naive_e0(truth, ctx["jobs"]["full"], LEVELS)
points = pd.concat([points, naive_q.assign(entry=ev.NAIVE, h=naive_q["year"] - naive_q["origin"])
                    [["entry", "pop", "sex", "origin", "year", "h", "e0_fc"]]], ignore_index=True)
points["era"] = points["origin"].map(ERA_OF)
keys_all = ev.paired_keys(points, truth, ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE])
keys_all["era"] = keys_all["origin"].map(ERA_OF)
# The held-out block is scored only when the design switches it on (score_held_out).
keys = keys_all if HELD else keys_all[keys_all["era"] != "held"].reset_index(drop=True)
errs = ev.errors(points, truth, keys)
errs["era"] = errs["origin"].map(ERA_OF)
n_expected = points[(points["entry"] == ev.NAIVE) & (points["sex"] == "both")].merge(
    truth[truth["sex"] == "both"], on=["pop", "year"])
n_expected = n_expected[n_expected["origin"].map(D.era) != "held"] if not HELD else n_expected
latex.report("evNPoints", len(keys), desc="Common points (population-years) scored")
for era in ERAS_ALL if HELD else D.eras:
    latex.report(f"evNPoints{era.capitalize()}", int((keys["era"] == era).sum()), desc=f"Common points, {era} era")
print(f"Common points: {len(keys):,} of {len(n_expected):,} observed naive points "
      f"({100 * len(keys) / len(n_expected):.1f} %); by era: {keys['era'].value_counts().to_dict()}")

# The truth leaves out every year of the event dictionary (chapter d3).  Three pandemics are masked in every
# population with data, whether or not its mortality rose: 1957–58 and 1968–69 are disclosed as such, COVID-19
# beside them.
HAS_DATA = np.isfinite(M).all(axis=(0, 1))                       # (C, T): the masked years keep their data
masked_jobs = ctx["jobs"]["full"][ctx["jobs"]["full"]["origin"].map(ERA_OF).isin(ERAS)]
MASKED = va.masked_event_counts(dt.load_events().query("populations == 'ALL'"), HAS_DATA, observed, years, pops,
                                masked_jobs, D.horizon)
for r_ in MASKED.itertuples():
    tag = "".join(w.capitalize() for w in "".join(ch for ch in r_.event if ch.isalpha() or ch == " ").split())
    latex.report(f"evMasked{tag}PopYears", int(r_.popyears),
                 desc=f"Population-years masked from the truth in every population: {r_.event} {r_.start}-{r_.end}")
    latex.report(f"evMasked{tag}Points", int(r_.forecast),
                 desc=f"Forecast years (job × year, scored eras) in those population-years, not scored: {r_.event}")
MASKED_TAB = MASKED.assign(years=MASKED["start"].astype(str) + "–" + MASKED["end"].astype(str))[
    ["event", "years", "popyears", "forecast"]].rename(columns={"popyears": "population-years masked",
                                                                 "forecast": "forecast years not scored"})
print("Events masked in every population with data:\n" + MASKED_TAB.to_string(index=False))


Common points: 15,261 of 15,261 observed naive points (100.0 %); by era: {'late': 8763, 'early': 5347, 'held': 1151}
Events masked in every population with data:
              event     years  population-years masked  forecast years not scored
    Asian influenza 1957–1958                       63                        250
Hong Kong influenza 1968–1969                       78                        270
           COVID-19 2020–2022                      108                        776


The influenza pandemics of 1957–58 and 1968–69 are masked in every population with data: 63 and 78 population-years, in which 250 and 270 forecast years of the scored eras go unscored. The models are fitted without them too. Chapter 08 estimates no excess (a negative intensity) for many respiratory event-years, so masking these two pandemics in every population is a choice, not a finding; a sensitivity analysis that keeps them has not yet been made.

text:
15.3 Accuracy by era and horizon
The mean absolute error of e₀ (the average of the sexes) in each horizon band (paper §10.3), on the common points. The late era is the primary view; the early era, outside the regime the forms were chosen in, is reported with the same prominence. Few origins reach the longest horizons (in the late era only those up to 1985 reach 36–50 years), so the right-hand columns rest on few forecasts; every claim beyond 20 years is descriptive (the held-out block reaches no further).


Code
both_err = errs[errs["measure"] == "e0_both"]
bands = ev.band_table(both_err, D, ["entry", "era"])
band_tab = (bands.pivot_table(index="entry", columns=["era", "band"], values="mae", observed=True)
            .reindex(index=ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE]))
band_tab = band_tab.reindex(columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([ERAS, BANDS]))
# A band as scored: the held-out block reaches only H_MAX["held"] years ahead, so its last band is labelled by

Forecasts from the early origins, 1900–1950, outside the regime of modern mortality decline, under-predict life expectancy most: the flow field’s mean error at 36–50 years ahead is −7.7 to −2.0 years. Among the late origins, those around 1970 are a turning point: from 1965, 1970 and 1975 the flow field’s mean error is −2.36, −4.27 and −3.01 years, while from 1955, 1960 and 1985 it is within a year of the outcome (0.13, −0.20 and 0.75). Among the late origins the comparators in the table also under-predict most from 1970; anchored MDMx’s persists after it (−3.77 at 1980, −3.07 at 1985). The methods that extrapolate recent rates of improvement under-predicted from 1965–1975, while the naive, a linear trend in e₀ over each population’s whole history, over-predicted from every late origin that reaches these horizons (by 3.3 to 5.4 years). In the literature’s account, the data of the origins 1965–1975 end in the stall of adult male mortality of the 1950s and 1960s, just before the sustained decline of old-age, mostly cardiovascular, mortality from about 1970.

15.4 Predictive intervals
Each entry is scored with its own predictive distribution (paper §10.4): MDMx’s delta-method intervals scaled by κ; the flow field’s empirical quantiles of its own errors; Lee–Carter’s k_t interval mapped through e₀(k); the functional models’ simulations; bayesLife’s MCMC; the naive’s normal random walk; and the ensemble’s average of its members’ quantiles. MDMx’s κ and the flow field’s error quantiles are calibrated within era, leaving out the origin being calibrated; the held-out origins are calibrated on the late development origins only. Leave-one-origin-out calibration uses the errors of other origins, later ones included. The flow field’s quantiles, by horizon and sex, are then near nominal on the development origins by construction; MDMx’s κ, one factor pooled over horizons 1–50 and centred, is not, so its coverage by horizon is a finding. The held-out block tests both on outcomes mostly outside the calibration.

text:
15.5 The overall comparison
The overall comparison (the article’s §10.5–10.6; the detail is in this chapter only) ranks the entries on five families of measures, each counting a quantity once:

level: the MAE of female e₀ and of male e₀ (each sex once);
gap: the MAE of the female − male gap;
age-specific sex differences: the RMSE of the male − female difference in logit q_x, each age weighted by the observed deaths d_x;
age pattern: the RMSE of logit q_x weighted by the observed deaths, and the MAE of life expectancy at 65 for each sex;
intervals: the weighted interval score of female and of male e₀, every entry’s intervals made by one rule: the empirical quantiles of its own errors at the other origins of its era, later ones included (the held-out origins: the late era’s). The median of such an interval is the forecast shifted by the median error of those origins, so this family scores the calibrated dispersion of a bias-adjusted forecast, not the entry’s own statement of its uncertainty; that is tested by the coverage of each entry’s own intervals (above) and, on outcomes mostly outside the calibration, in the held-out block.

Each measure is divided by the naive’s value of the same measure, so 1 is the naive’s level, and a family’s loss is the mean of its measures. The entries are ranked over draws of family weights (Dirichlet(1, …, 1)), each draw with a bootstrap of population families: stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis (SMAA). The full-output composite uses all five families; the e₀-only composite the level, the gap and the intervals. The families are not independent: across the entries the interval losses follow the level losses closely (the correlations below). Bias is not a measure: MAE contains it, and a bias term beside MAE rewards errors that offset (bias is reported by era, band and origin above). bayesLife enters the schedule families through its MortCast schedules.
Deviation 2. This is not the overall comparison of the frozen design. Two independent reviews of that design, made after the held-out block had been scored, found that the level of e₀ was counted in three overlapping families (about 60 % of the expected weight), that its bias terms rewarded offsetting errors, that its survivor-weighted age measures were dominated by noise at young ages, and that the methods’ own intervals were calibrated in different ways or not at all. The revision was made for these reasons; its effects on the ranking follow the headline below. The frozen comparison is reported beside this one as the record of the path.
The views: the primary view (late era, 1–15 years) decides the headline; the secondary view (early era, 1–15 years) is the out-of-regime check; the eras pooled; a sensitivity at 16–25 years in the late era; and, scored once, the held-out block.

def view_span(view):
    """A view's first and last origin and horizons, from the design."""
    spec = E["views"][view]
    origins = [o for era in VIEW_ORIGINS[spec["origins"]] for o in (D.held_out if era == "held" else D.eras[era])]
    return {"origins": (min(origins), max(origins)), "horizons": tuple(spec["horizons"])}

In the early era (origins 1900–1950), the flow field ranks first (55%); anchored MDMx ranks 4th when fitted to all years and 2nd when fitted to the last 50. Under the frozen design: on forecasts from origins 1955–2000 at horizons of 1–15 years, the flow field ranks first in the overall comparison of age-specific and summary forecasts (100% of the draws), ahead of anchored MDMx, which ranks 3rd when fitted to all years and 4th when fitted to the last 50.
By mean rank the runner-up in the primary view is bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years. In the early era the flow field is first both in the most draws and by mean rank (1.98). The share of first places counts draws of family weights and of population families; it does not cover the uncertainty from the few late origins, whose outcome years overlap (a bootstrap of origins and leaving one origin out, in the robustness checks below).

15.5.2 Sensitivities
Each sensitivity (paper §10.7) changes one thing and ranks the entries again in the primary and secondary views. None is used for the headline.

The frozen design (as pre-registered; the table above).
Each method’s own intervals instead of the one rule.
Survivor weights for the age measures (as in the frozen design), and the age family without the old-age measure.
Bias added back, without cancellation: the level and gap families also get the mean over origin × horizon-band cells of the absolute mean error.
Without the interval family, which partly re-scores the level of the errors (the correlations above).
The ensemble with the naive as a fourth member.
α_k = 1 for the forecasts that start beyond the frontier point: these jobs keep their deviations from the shape law unrelaxed.
MDMx with the decaying anchor (half-life 2 years), and unanchored, in place of anchored MDMx fitted to all years.
The comparators averaged across windows: each comparator’s forecast is the mean over the windows 25, 50, 75, 100 years and all years (development origins only).
The comparators’ actual jump-off: Lee–Carter and Hyndman–Ullah started from the observed rates of the jump-off year (jumpchoice = "actual"; the coherent model has no such option), as MDMx and the flow field start from their observed jump-off.
The ages from 100 as one open interval: the comparators forecast one rate for the open interval and their schedules repeat it at every older age, so the age measures, summed over single ages, count that one forecast once per age. Here the schedule and sex-difference measures fold those ages into one cell, the logit of the probability of dying between that age and the last age of the table, for every entry, the naive and the truth alike; e₆₅ is unchanged.
Intervals from past errors only: every entry’s intervals from its errors at the earlier origins whose outcome had been observed by the origin (described with the interval checks below), in place of the within-era rule, on the points where every entry has one.
Leave one origin out: the range of each entry’s share of first places when each origin of the view is left out in turn.

15.5.4 The anchor’s residual and the sex differences by age
Both anchored forecasters carry the jump-off residual, the part of the jump-off year’s observed schedule that the scores do not represent, smoothed over age (Section 14.2.5). Unsmoothed, the residual would hold the noise of that one year’s single-age rates as well as the population’s own detail, and the forecasts would carry it at every horizon. Which measures such noise reaches depends on how they weigh the errors over age. The measure of the sex differences by age squares the error at each age and so charges single-age noise in full; the gap in e₀ sums the errors over the ages, so noise of opposite signs at neighbouring ages cancels and what remains is the systematic part. To show what the smoothing does, the anchored forecasts are scored again on the primary view’s points with the residual as observed, the forecast change of the scores left as it is. This is a sensitivity, not an entry of the comparison.

With the residual as observed, the flow field would score 0.95 of the naive’s error on the sex differences by age and anchored MDMx 0.93 (all years), close to the observed jump-off schedule held fixed, 0.93: unsmoothed, the jump-off year’s noise would dominate the measure. With the residual smoothed they score 0.80 and 0.78, against bayesLife’s 0.88 (last 50 years) and 0.87 (all years), and the age pattern improves with them (the flow field 0.82 against 0.89), while the flow field’s female and male e₀ hardly move (0.64 and 0.77 against 0.64 and 0.78). Much of what is left is noise of the outcome year: the observed schedules themselves, smoothed over 7 ages, score 0.48. bayesLife’s schedules come from MortCast fitted to smoothed rates, so their sex difference is smooth across ages, but their systematic error is larger: the mean error of the difference at ages 0–39 is 0.14 in logit(q_x) for bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years and 0.02 for the flow field, and 59 % of bayesLife’s squared error lies at ages 90 and over, where its schedules repeat the rate of the open age group.

text:
15.6 Variants and benchmarks beside the comparison
The comparison ranks the twelve entries fixed in the frozen design. Beside it, never ranked and reported in full only in the companion, are the forms and benchmarks the independent reviews asked for. Each is computed and scored at the development origins only (1900–2000, both eras), on the comparison’s own points, so that the held-out block stays reserved for the ranked entries:

the flow field’s other forms: FR0-all, whose speed beyond the frontier point stays at its value there, and FR2-all, the form the frontier rule as written chose (Deviation 1), both with every part estimated on every year;
a drop-one-component ablation of FR1-50, whose plan was committed before its results;
Li–Lee’s coherent model in two forms: the group form, in which the origin’s populations share a common factor for each sex, and the sex-coherent form, in which the two sexes of a population share one;
anchored MDMx fitted to every year with other drift weights and numbers of components.

No choice of form or design depends on these results.


The unranked variants at the development origins (cached per origin; computed ahead by tools/warm_variants.py)

def variant_bands(entries, common=True):
    """Band errors of the named variants and entries on the comparison's development points."""
    pick = {lab: (VRES[lab] if lab in VRES else results[lab]) for lab in entries}
    return va.band_errors(pick, truth, KEYS_DEV, D, M, pops, years, GROUPS, old_age=OLD_AGE, common=common)


def report_bands(tab, labels, prefix, what, stats=(("mae", "Mae"), ("me", "Bias")), measure="e0_both"):
    """Macros ev<prefix><Mae|Bias><tag><Era><Band> of one measure of a band table."""
    for stat, word in stats:
        wide = va.band_wide(tab, measure, stat, D, labels)
        for lab in labels:
            for era in D.eras:
                for b in BANDS:
                    v = wide.loc[lab, (era, b)]
                    if np.isfinite(v):
                        latex.report(f"ev{prefix}{word}{VTAG.get(lab, TAG.get(lab))}{ERA_TAG[era]}{BAND_TAG[b]}", v,
                                     digits=2, desc=f"{what}: {stat} of {measure}, {lab}, {era} era, horizons {b}")


def bands_out(tab, labels, measures=(("e0_both", "mae", "e0 MAE"), ("e0_both", "me", "e0 bias"))):
    """A band table for the paper in long form: (measure, era, entry) × horizon band."""
    rows = [va.band_wide(tab, measure, stat, D, labels).xs(era, axis=1, level=0)
            .assign(Measure=name, Era=era).rename_axis("Entry").reset_index()
            for measure, stat, name in measures for era in D.eras]
    return pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)[["Measure", "Era", "Entry", *BANDS]]


def below(w, a, others, era):
    """The bands of ``era`` in which row ``a`` of a band table (:func:`mdmx.variants.band_wide`) is below
    every row of ``others``."""
    others = [others] if isinstance(others, str) else list(others)
    return [b for b in BANDS if w.loc[a, (era, b)] < w.loc[others, (era, b)].min()]


def above(w, a, others, era):
    """The bands of ``era`` in which row ``a`` of a band table is above every row of ``others``."""
    others = [others] if isinstance(others, str) else list(others)
    return [b for b in BANDS if w.loc[a, (era, b)] > w.loc[others, (era, b)].max()]


def plain(label):
    """A measure's label without LaTeX, for the prose: "female $e_{65}$" → "female e₆₅"."""
    sub = str.maketrans("0123456789", "₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉")
    return re.sub(r"\$e_\{?(\d+)\}?\$", lambda m: "e" + m.group(1).translate(sub), label)


def bands_text(bs):
    """Horizon bands as words."""
    if len(bs) == len(BANDS):
        return "at every horizon band"
    if not bs:
        return "at no horizon band"
    return "at " + (", ".join(bs[:-1]) + " and " if len(bs) > 1 else "") + bs[-1] + " years"

The comparison’s intervals are calibrated on the other origins of the era, later ones included, so they use errors that had not been observed by the origin. Intervals from past errors only use, at origin o and horizon h, only the errors at earlier origins o′ whose outcome had been observed by the origin (o′ + h ≤ o), where at least 20 such errors exist. The two rules are compared on the points where both give an interval; the early era has few, because its first origins have no earlier errors.

The second removes the leak. At every origin the pooling of chapter d5 is planned again on the years up to the origin alone (the same valley ages and settings), and every entry whose inputs are pooled is forecast again from the result: the flow field and anchored MDMx from the tensor, Hyndman–Ullah and the coherent model from the rates smoothed after the same pooling, for the populations whose cells change. Lee–Carter and bayesLife’s e₀ read the unpooled rates and keep their forecasts; the ensemble is rebuilt from its members, and the naive is fitted to the published series. With the pooling planned on the years up to each origin (21 populations change at 24 origins), an entry’s late-era MAE of e₀ in a band changes by at most 0.03 years, and on e₀ only the flow field ranks first in 54 % of the draws (49 % in the comparison).

15.6.1 Paired differences of the error
The SMAA ranks the entries over many measures at once. Beside it, one measure between two forecasters at a time: the MAE of e₀ (the average of the sexes) of the flow field minus that of another forecaster, on the late-era points where both are scored, in the first horizon bands. The late era’s origins share their periods, so the interval resamples whole origins (a block bootstrap); the share of draws below zero describes the resampling and is not a p-value. The other forecasters: the ensemble, bayesLife and anchored MDMx (ranked entries), Lee–Carter from the observed rates of the jump-off year (a sensitivity above) and FR2-all (a variant).

15.7 Generality
Three properties of a general forecaster, in the companion only, for every entry but bayesLife and the ensemble:

More history must not hurt: the MAE with every year minus the MAE with the last 50 years, at horizons up to 15, in each era, must not exceed the margin: twice the typical standard error of a regret between forecasters in that era and band (the median, over the other entries, of the standard error of the difference of MAE between the flow field and that entry, over a bootstrap of population families). For the flow field the comparison is with its windowed variant. The entry already estimates its shape law and its pace beyond the frontier point on the last 50 years, so this test varies the window of its remaining speed only; the window curve below varies every component.
Stable structure across origins: the flow field’s frontier point, its speed there, its pace beyond, the shrinkage weight and the relaxation rates by origin (chapter 11, Table 14.1); MDMx’s damping ρ by origin (Table 15.31, after the generality table).
Bounded regret out of era: each entry’s early-era MAE minus the best entry’s, by band.



Code
dev_both = both_err[both_err["era"].isin(list(D.eras))]
WM = E["window_margins"]
MARGIN_TAB = ev.regret_margins(dev_both, D, ev.FLOW_FIELD, [e for e in ENTRIES if e != ev.FLOW_FIELD], FAMILY,
                               WM["bands"], multiplier=float(WM["multiplier"]), draws=int(WM["draws"]),
                               seed=int(WM["seed"]))

for _, r_ in MARGIN_TAB.iterrows():
    latex.report(f"evMargin{ERA_TAG[r_['era']]}{BAND_TAG[r_['band']]}", r_["margin"], digits=2,
                 desc=f"Margin of the test that more history must not hurt (years), {r_['era']} era, horizons "
                      f"{r_['band']}: {WM['multiplier']} × the median bootstrap SE of a difference of MAE")
latex.report("evMarginDraws", int(WM["draws"]), desc="Bootstrap draws of the margins of the generality test")
gen_pairs = {"MDMx + anchor": ("MDMx + anchor, all years", "MDMx + anchor, last 50 years"),
             "Lee–Carter": ("Lee–Carter, all years", "Lee–Carter, last 50 years"),
             "Hyndman–Ullah": ("Hyndman–Ullah, all years", "Hyndman–Ullah, last 50 years"),
             "Coherent FDM": ("Coherent FDM, all years", "Coherent FDM, last 50 years")}
ffw = ev.long_points({"Flow field, windowed": ff_form("Flow field, windowed")})
ffw_err = ev.errors(ffw, truth, keys)
ffw_err = ffw_err[ffw_err["measure"] == "e0_both"].assign(era=lambda d: d["origin"].map(ERA_OF))
grows = []
for name, (all_, win_) in [*gen_pairs.items(), ("Flow field", ("Flow field", "Flow field, windowed"))]:
    e_all = dev_both[dev_both["entry"] == all_]
    e_win = ffw_err if win_ == "Flow field, windowed" else dev_both[dev_both["entry"] == win_]
    rob = ev.window_robustness(ev.band_table(e_all.assign(entry=name), D, ["entry", "era"]),
                               ev.band_table(e_win.assign(entry=name), D, ["entry", "era"]), MARGINS, ["entry"])
    row = {"Entry": name}
    for era in D.eras:
        r_ = rob[rob["era"] == era]
        row[f"{era}: largest excess"] = float((r_["diff"] - r_["margin"]).max())
        row[f"{era}: hurts"] = "yes" if bool(r_["hurts"].any()) else "no"
    grows.append(row)
early_bands = ev.regret(bands[(bands["era"] == "early") & bands["band"].isin(BANDS[:3])
                              & bands["entry"].isin(ENTRIES)])
reg = early_bands.pivot_table(index="entry", columns="band", values="regret", observed=True)
gen_tab = pd.DataFrame(grows)
for name, (all_, _) in [*gen_pairs.items(), ("Flow field", ("Flow field", None))]:
    for b in BANDS[:3]:
        gen_tab.loc[gen_tab["Entry"] == name, f"early regret {b}"] = reg.loc[all_, b]
GEN_OUT = gen_tab.rename(columns={
    **{f"{era}: largest excess": f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}: Largest\nexcess" for era in D.eras},
    **{f"{era}: hurts": f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}: Hurts" for era in D.eras},
    **{f"early regret {b}": f"Early-era regret: {b}" for b in BANDS[:3]}})
save_table(GEN_OUT, "tbl-ev-generality",
           "Generality of the forecasters (origins 1900--2000).  More history hurts if the MAE of $e_0$ with "
           "every year exceeds the MAE with the last 50 years by more than the margin in some band up to 15 "
           "years: twice the typical standard error of a regret between forecasters in that era and band "
           "(largest excess over the margin shown; negative: within it).  For the flow "
           "field the comparison is with its windowed variant.  Early regret: the entry's early-era MAE "
           "minus the best entry's (all-years fits).",
           short_caption="Generality of the forecasters", formats=formats(GEN_OUT, 2), spanners=": ",
           rank=[ranked(GEN_OUT)], rank_note="in each column, the best being the smallest excess and regret")
HURTS = {r_["Entry"]: [era for era in D.eras if r_[f"{era}: hurts"] == "yes"] for _, r_ in gen_tab.iterrows()}
best_early = reg.loc[:, BANDS[:3]].idxmin().unique()
GEN_TAG = {"MDMx + anchor": "Mdmx", "Lee–Carter": "Lc", "Hyndman–Ullah": "Hu", "Coherent FDM": "Cfdm",
           "Flow field": "Ff"}
for _, row in gen_tab.iterrows():
    for era in D.eras:
        latex.report(f"evHistoryExcess{GEN_TAG[row['Entry']]}{ERA_TAG[era]}", row[f"{era}: largest excess"],
                     digits=2,
                     desc=f"{row['Entry']}: largest excess of MAE(all years) − MAE(last 50) over the margin, {era} era")


def hurt_text(era):
    """The comparators that more history hurts in ``era``, each with its largest excess over the margin."""
    names = {"Lee–Carter": "Lee–Carter", "Hyndman–Ullah": "Hyndman–Ullah", "Coherent FDM": "the coherent model"}
    parts = []
    for e, name in names.items():
        if era in HURTS[e]:
            key = f"evHistoryExcess{GEN_TAG[e]}{ERA_TAG[era]}"
            # An excess that prints as 0.00 is still above the margin: say so rather than print zero.
            by = "less than 0.01 years" if round(val(key), 2) == 0 else f"{num(key)} years"
            parts.append(f"{name} (by {by})")
    if not parts:
        return "none of the comparators"
    return parts[0] if len(parts) == 1 else ", ".join(parts[:-1]) + " and " + parts[-1]

Figure 15.4: The window curve: mean absolute error of e₀ (average of the sexes) by fitting window, horizons 1–15 (top) and 16–50 (bottom), early era (left) and late era (right), development origins, on the common points.





Anchored MDMx barely depends on its window: its late-era error at 1–15 years ranges from 0.90 to 0.92 years across the windows. In the late era Lee–Carter is best with 50 years (0.85, against 0.94 with every year and 1.05 with 25); in the early era all three comparators are best with the shortest window (Lee–Carter 1.99 with 25 years against 2.70 with every year). The flow field’s long-horizon error depends on the window of its shape law, in opposite directions in the two eras: at 16–50 years a shape law on the last 25 years gives 1.44 in the late era against 2.09 on every year, but 3.97 in the early era against 3.21. The entry’s form (the shape law on the last 50 years) gives 1.57 and 3.41.
What this says about the guiding principle of the forecasters, one general model that uses all the data (in the companion only). Its strong form, that a general model should not need to discard history, does not hold for the flow field: two of its three components, the shape law and the pace beyond the frontier point, use only the last 50 years, a window chosen on the late origins (Deviation 1), and the shape law’s window moves the error in opposite directions in the two eras. The narrowed form, pre-registered as the fallback, is that the weight of each datum reflects its relevance and may approach zero. The flow field meets it only coarsely: its window gives the older years a weight of zero, set by a choice rather than estimated in the model. Its remaining component, the speed, uses every year, and there more history does not hurt (the generality table).

15.8.1 By age
Arriaga’s decomposition (paper §10.8) splits each e₀ error into the contributions of age groups, by sex; the contributions add up to the error exactly (checked). Late era, the longer horizons, for every entry with schedules.

15.10 The held-out block
The origins 2005–2015 (paper §10.1 and §10.6) were held out from every formal choice of form and design (what had been seen there is listed with the design above). They were scored once, under the frozen design, by the run that set score_held_out = true and changed nothing else, as the design required. The overall comparison was revised afterwards (Deviation 2) and corrected (Deviation 3), so the revised comparison’s held-out view, reported first below, is not a blind test of the revised design; the frozen design’s view is reported beside it. The block reaches at most 20 years ahead, so this section reports the primary view’s comparison and the bands up to that horizon.

On the held-out origins 2005–2015, scored once under the frozen design and compared here under the comparison revised afterwards, the flow field ranks first in the same view (94%); anchored MDMx ranks 4th when fitted to all years and 3rd when fitted to the last 50. Under the frozen design, by which the block was scored that once: on the held-out origins 2005–2015, held out from every formal choice of form and design, the flow field ranks first in the same view (97%); anchored MDMx ranks 3rd when fitted to all years and 2nd when fitted to the last 50. bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years ranks 5th and the ensemble 6th. At 1–5 years ahead the flow field’s error of e₀ is 0.25 years, anchored MDMx’s 0.28 (last 50 years), bayesLife’s 0.32, the naive’s 0.38, and Lee–Carter’s 0.57: the functional comparators all lose to the naive there. The entries’ own intervals cover more than their nominal level on these outcomes: the flow field’s 80 % intervals, calibrated on the late era’s errors (16 % of which fall after the earliest held-out origin), cover 90 %, and anchored MDMx’s 93 % (all years). The frozen design, which scores each method’s own intervals, leaves out 4 points where a comparator’s interval simulation failed (CFDM for RUS from 2010, last 50 years: ‘ar’ part of model is not stationary); the revised comparison, whose intervals come from one rule, leaves out 0.

The flow field’s two other forms, FR0-all (the speed beyond the frontier point held at its value there) and FR2-all (the form the frontier rule as written chose), are variants, never ranked. They were not run on the held-out block when it was scored; they are run here, after it, and described beside the ranked flow field (FR1-50) on the same points. No choice depends on them.

if HELD:
    HF_FORMS = {k: v for k, v in va.flow_variant_forms(ctx["flowfield"]).items() if k in ("FR0-all", "FR2-all")}
    held_jobs = ctx["jobs"]["full"][ctx["jobs"]["full"]["origin"].isin(D.held_out)].reset_index(drop=True)
    HF_RUNS = va.run_flow_variants(ctx["M"], ctx["observed"], ctx["pops"], ctx["years"], held_jobs, ctx["mdmx"],
                                   HF_FORMS, ctx["e0"], horizon=D.horizon, design=D, name="evaluation_ffvar_held",
                                   allow_held=True)
    HF_RES = va.variant_results({"flow": HF_RUNS}, n_ages=A, ax=ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"])
    hf_err = ev.errors(ev.long_points({lab: HF_RES[lab] for lab in HF_FORMS}), truth, keys)
    hf_err = pd.concat([both_err[both_err["entry"] == ev.FLOW_FIELD], hf_err[hf_err["measure"] == "e0_both"]],
                       ignore_index=True)
    hf_err = hf_err[hf_err["origin"].isin(D.held_out)]
    hf_bands = ev.band_table(hf_err, D, ["entry"])
    if hf_bands.groupby("band", observed=True)["n"].nunique().max() != 1:
        raise ValueError("FR0-all and FR2-all are not scored on the flow field's held-out points")
    HF_LABELS = [ev.FLOW_FIELD, *HF_FORMS]
    HF_TAG = {ev.FLOW_FIELD: "Ff", "FR0-all": "FrZeroAll", "FR2-all": "FrTwoAll"}
    for r_ in hf_bands[hf_bands["entry"] != ev.FLOW_FIELD].itertuples():
        b_ = shown("held", r_.band)
        for stat, word in (("mae", "Mae"), ("me", "Bias")):
            latex.report(f"evVar{word}{HF_TAG[r_.entry]}Held{BAND_TAG[b_]}", getattr(r_, stat), digits=2,
                         desc=f"{r_.entry} (variant, described): {stat} of e0 (average), held-out block, horizons {b_}")
    HF_OUT = pd.concat(
        [hf_bands.pivot_table(index="entry", columns="band", values=stat, observed=True).reindex(HF_LABELS)
         .rename(columns=lambda b: shown("held", b)).rename_axis("Entry").reset_index().assign(Group=name)
         for stat, name in (("mae", "MAE of $e_0$"), ("me", "Mean error of $e_0$"))], ignore_index=True)
    HF_OUT["Entry"] = HF_OUT["Entry"].replace({ev.FLOW_FIELD: "Flow field (FR1-50, ranked)"})

    save_table(HF_OUT, "tbl-ev-held-forms",
               "The flow field's three forms at the recent origins "
               f"({min(D.held_out)}--{max(D.held_out)}): the ranked form, FR1-50, and FR0-all and FR2-all, which "
               "are not part of the overall comparison.  MAE and mean error of $e_0$ "
               "(the average of the sexes, years) by horizon band, on the same points; the last band ends at the "
               "data's last year.",
               short_caption="The flow field's forms at the recent origins", formats=formats(HF_OUT, 2),
               groups="Group", spanners=": ", rank=ranked_bands(HF_OUT),
               rank_note=RANK_BANDS.replace("in each column", "among the three forms in each column"))
    HF_W = hf_bands.pivot_table(index="entry", columns="band", values="mae", observed=True)
    HF_BEST = {shown("held", b): HF_W[b].idxmin() for b in HF_W.columns}
    display_hf = HF_OUT.round(2)
else:
    HF_BEST = {}

15.11 The headline on the release on which the design was chosen
The forms and the evaluation’s design were chosen on an earlier HMD release. The article gives the headline on the later release only. title: Appendix A — Computing environment
text:
The Python environment is fully specified by pyproject.toml and locked by uv.lock; the R packages by R/install-packages.R. The versions actually used to render this copy of the book are:


Record the environment of this render
import json, platform, shutil, subprocess
from mdmx import provenance
env = provenance.environment()
print(json.dumps(env, indent=1))
for tool in ("quarto", "Rscript", "latexmk"):
    path = shutil.which(tool)
    if path:
        out = subprocess.run([path, "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True)
        print(f"{tool}: {(out.stdout or out.stderr).splitlines()[0] if (out.stdout or out.stderr) else '?'}")
    else:
        print(f"{tool}: not found")
